# ON MOSAIC PHILOSOPHY.

...will be proven, etc. But if an image comes immediately from the senses into the phantastic spirit <note>The "phantastic spirit" refers to the imagination or the faculty of the soul that processes sensory images.</note>, then such an object also deceives the intellectual vision. For example: a straight stick placed in water will appear curved to the sight, and in such a manner it will be depicted in the phantastic spirit. Trees, cities, and mountains will seem to move to those who are sailing. A post or a column will appear to the fantasy as a man during the night. Similarly, to the hearing, the sound of a cannon <note>original: "bombardæ"</note>—as well as the flash of the ignited powder—will be taken by the imagination for thunder and lightning. So too the howling of a cat is taken for the cry of a child, and so on. Furthermore, the fantasy represents false images both in sleep and while awake by itself, as may be seen in those seized by delirium, frenzy, or mania. Indeed, it even sometimes feigns things that never were, are, or shall be. 

From this it follows that so many errors have crept into the world, by which the sense and intellect of the animal man <note>The "animal man" (homo animalis) refers to the natural, unregenerate human who relies solely on earthly reason and senses.</note> are led by mere resemblances of truth in place of the real truth itself; relying on mere probability, he is deceived and led onto a contrary path. He seems to understand nothing except the bodies offered by the phantastic sense, or those created within the spirit of the fantasy, which is merely imaginary in itself. 

From here arose that worldly or human wisdom, and consequently that vain philosophy of the Pagans <note>original: "Ethnicorum," referring to non-Christian Greek and Roman philosophers</note>, which proceeded from the tradition of men and according to the elements of this world, and not according to Jesus Christ, the true wisdom specified by the Apostle. From this kind of deceptive vision of the intellect, the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy</note> with their leader imagine and dream of the eternity of the Elements (earth, water, etc.), of the heavens, the stars, and of the world itself. They have feigned a Dominion of Fortune in the world, they say that God acts by necessity regarding generation and corruption, and they speak of a Vacuum which they can imagine within worldly substance. They believe the celestial spheres are carried by the "snatched" and violent motion of the "First Mover" <note>The *Primum Mobile*, the outermost sphere in Aristotelian cosmology</note>. 

They think that Meteors are made from fumes and vapors raised from the earth and waters, and are heaped together by <term>Antiperistasis</term> <note>An ancient physical theory that a quality intensifies when surrounded by its opposite, such as cold concentrating heat.</note>; and they estimate that these are sublimated into the heights by the attractive force of the sun and stars. They feign that earthquakes are caused by winds enclosed in the bowels of the earth; they maintain that springs are generated from vapors condensed in the veins of the earth, and that clouds are procreated from those same vapors elevated on high and thickened by means of Antiperistasis. They gather this from their senses and imprint it in the spirit of their fantasy because they observe in distillations that vapors ascending from a pot or a gourd-shaped vessel <note>original: "cucurbita"</note> into the top of an Alembic <note>A cap used in distilling</note> grow into drops and coagulate. Furthermore, they assert that winds are made from exhalations ascending from the earth and by their repercussions from others descending, because they observe the smoke of liquids or of ignited coals being pushed laterally in its ascent by a wind descending in the air. They even estimate that thunders are made by the murmuring of fire in water, be-

<column-break/>

-cause they notice that glowing iron itself, when thrown into water, makes such murmurs and noises, and so forth. 

Wherefore it is evident that the mind or intellect of the animal man uses two kinds of visions in the fantasy: namely, those from the corporeal sensations of the senses, and those from spiritual images imprinted within it. Such a mind, by neglecting internal and central things—that is, superior and divine truths—is utterly addicted to gazing upon external and superficial things. From this it follows that his reasoning is frequently deceived regarding the objects he investigates, so much so that for the most part he accepts scarcely probable things as true. This is because the notions he seeks from sensory impressions in the fantasy are uncertain; for the images of things present, past, and future delineated in his spirit in an imaginary fashion are for the greater part feigned and imaginary—appearing as such things which, in the reality of the matter, they are not. 

Such, therefore, is the condition of the natural or animal man; such (I say) is the root and foundation of human or worldly wisdom. Indeed, his mind does not understand or perceive with spiritual eyes or with the "taste of wisdom," whose role it is to look upon those things which have neither bodies nor the forms of bodies—such as God, Mind, the Word, Wisdom, Justice, Truth, and the essential good affections of the soul.

<margin>James 3:15</margin> The Apostle intends to speak of this kind of wisdom when he says: *That the wisdom which is from below is earthly, animal <note>sensual</note>, and Devilish.*

<margin>1 Corinthians 2</margin> From which it is clear that the animal man cannot (according to the opinion of Saint Paul) perceive those things which are of the Spirit of God, for they are foolishness to him; nor is it possible for them to be understood by him in any way, as they are to be discerned spiritually. But the spiritual "secretion" <note>or "setting apart"</note> of things is not a natural work, but a supernatural work of faith, insofar as it does not arise from sensory notions, but from supernatural knowledge spiritually infused into the illuminated soul.

But on the other hand, in the third species of the soul's intellectual vision—in which the soul, by the "sharp edge of the mind" and by neglecting lower things, directs its gaze toward the supreme wisdom which is its taste and nourishing mother—the soul possesses an infallible notion of all things. In this vision, it can neither be deceived, deluded, nor led astray. And through this vision, which perceives things that are neither corporeal nor have the forms of bodies (which we listed above), the mind or intellect can arrive at a true recognition of the soul. This can in no way happen through the former means—namely the senses and imaginations—insofar as these instead deceive the mind and make things appear to you which in truth are not. Therefore, by withdrawing from the senses and from the likenesses of bodies, the internal or spiritual man is accustomed to reach the knowledge of himself, of God, of His wisdom, and of the angels. By withdrawing (I say) from the senses, and turning his mind from the multitude...

# BOOK II. OF THE FIRST SECTION.

...by drawing back toward unity—that is, by calling back its rays which were scattered outwardly and retaining them within itself. For the soul is hindered by the senses from being able to discern itself and the created world. If, therefore, the soul is occupied with God, it exults and rejoices in its own good, since the good of the soul is God. But if it is occupied with worldly things, then it will seem to find joy in external things and in the good of the flesh. To ascend to God, however—which is to taste of the supreme wisdom—is to enter into oneself and to penetrate to one's innermost depths. He, therefore, who looks so deeply into the heights that he transcends himself and tastes of the supreme wisdom, truly ascends to God. This, then, is the life of the soul and the heart of man while he contemplates his God. For he who lives in God knows his own being, as it were, to be the very being of God and the Word of God. Whence <term>Mercurius Trismegistus</term><note>A legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the Hermetic writings, often cited by Renaissance philosophers as a pagan prophet of Christian truths.</note> says: *Believe that the Word of God sees and hears within you.* 
<margin>John 1</margin> And the Evangelist: *In the Word was life, and that life was the light of men.* And elsewhere: *You are the Temple of the Holy Spirit and members of Christ.* Oh, how noble is that spirit which, led by a taste of true wisdom, perceives with spiritual eyes that it was created out of light and life! For the spirit that discovers itself to be composed of life and light will transcend back toward life and light. By this reasoning, the soul, transcending itself, expands at will toward things below and things above; and for the purpose of knowing and contemplating God above itself, itself within itself, and the angels alongside itself, and whatever is contained within the circuit of heaven, it is divinely illuminated beneath itself. Then, in this condition, by means of the senses, it observes bodies without error; by the imagination, the likenesses of bodies; by reason, their natures; by the intellect, the created spirit; and by the <term>intelligence</term><note>In this context, "intelligence" refers to the highest faculty of the mind, capable of perceiving divine truths directly.</note>, that which is uncreated. For the intelligence, after tasting the highest wisdom, can discern between the true and the false when the senses inform the imagination and the imagination informs the reason, and from there produces that knowledge which is called prudence (so that it may then instruct the reason with the divine presence and bring forth truth through wisdom). And this is the true and unique vision of the spiritual and mentally upright man, by which he beholds that wisdom which descends from above, which is Jesus Christ, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, which the "animal" or natural man cannot comprehend, but (as the Apostle witnesses) considers it foolishness. These are the words of that spiritual man: *We have received not the spirit of this world, but the spirit which is from God, that we might know the things that are given to us by God, which things also we speak, not in the learned words of human wisdom, but in the doctrine of the spirit, comparing spiritual things with spiritual.* For the natural man 
<margin>1 Corinthians 2:12, 13</margin> does not perceive those things which are of the Spirit of God: for they are foolishness to him, and he cannot understand them, etc. Upon this wisdom, therefore, the true <term>Mosaic philosophy</term><note>A tradition of natural philosophy that sought to derive all scientific knowledge from the writings of Moses (the Pentateuch) rather than from Aristotle or other pagan sources.</note> is founded, revealed to the world by spiritual and God-taught men cited in the Holy Bible through the instinct of the Holy Spirit.

---

And it is contradictory in all things to the worldly philosophy handed down by "animal" men. For this true Philosophy recognizes that God is a pure and incomprehensible spirit, not at all grasped within the boundaries of the phantasy <note>The "phantasy" or "fancy" was considered the faculty that processes sensory images; the author argues God cannot be imagined as a physical shape.</note>, nor is His word or His eternal wisdom. It establishes that the Angels are spirits serving the divine power, and even the Demons, who are not at all to be conceived in their essence by the intellect of the natural man—much less described essentially in his phantasy as they truly exist. It also confesses, against the laws of the Pagans, that the world and consequently the earth, water, and the other elements, as well as the heaven, the stars, and everything else in the world, were created by the divine Word; and consequently not from eternity (as they falsely believe). It concludes that <term>Peripatetic Fortune</term><note>The Aristotelian concept of chance or luck; the author argues that nothing happens by "luck" but by God's will.</note> has no place in the world, nor does it impose a necessity of acting upon God, but witnesses that He works in this world according to His own will. It does not speak of a "void" of worldly substance, but makes mention of the emptiness or absence of the divine Spirit which informs all things, by whose presence all things are said to be full. They assert that the heavens are turned by eternal wisdom and not by the compulsion of a "prime mover." They tell that meteors are not made from smoke and vapors, but are produced by the divine breath from heaven, which is His treasury; and this without any attraction from the sun or stars, whose property it is not to attract but rather to disperse. They maintain that earthquakes are caused by a hidden angelic power and not by winds trapped in the earth. They establish that clouds are produced not from vapors, but by the condensation of air through the act of wisdom. They say that winds are derived from the treasures of God and are not generated from imaginary exhalations. They write that thunder does not arise from the collision of clouds and exhalations, since it is the voice of Jehovah; nor do lightnings proceed from the ignition of exhalations, but from the mouth and throne of God. And so it is with the rest. These are the institutes of true wisdom, established by the authority of the sacred scriptures. From this it is evident what human or worldly wisdom is: namely, that which arises from the external or sensible vision of the intelligence and the appearance of bodily notions, or of bodies subjected to the external senses, or of images impressed upon the phantasy in the spirit of bodies. From this arose human Philosophy, whether born from the tradition of men or from the elements of this world. And consequently, it will be very easy to discern from these things what the "animal" or natural man is: namely, an intelligence whose reach cannot perceive further than sensible and fantastic worldly things, because he does not know how to taste of the supreme wisdom or turn the edge of his mind toward the spiritual and ideal notions of the divine word. Similarly, from the opposite side, it is right to gather from these things what [the spiritual man] is...

# ON MOSAIC PHILOSOPHY.

True wisdom, indeed, that which descends from on high from the Father of Lights <note>original: "Patre Luminum"; a reference to James 1:17</note>, is that which is born from the intelligence or the soul. By neglecting lower and sensible things, it keeps its gaze fixed upon higher things; that is, by rejecting physical bodies and their phantoms <note>original: "simulachra"; referring to the deceptive mental images of material things</note>, it turns the sharp edge of its light toward those things which are neither bodies nor the likenesses of bodies, but the pure and infallible ideas of truth. For if one faithfully directs the sharp edge of their vision toward the existence of the Word, or the supreme wisdom, or the spiritual Christ, they will find there Him who is all in all; and consequently, they will behold all things in Him—who is all things—without fallacy or deception. For he whose Spirit is one with Christ, his spirit will have been made one in Him, and by consequence, it will not be difficult for him to know all things without the hazard of doubt. Nor should this seem a wonder to you, Reader, since all things in the greater world <term>macrocosm</term><note>The "macrocosm" refers to the entire universe as a structured whole.</note> are retained in the <term>microcosm</term><note>The "microcosm" or "little world" refers to man, viewed as a miniature map of the entire universe.</note> according to their due proportion. Nor indeed is that uncreated divinity—which fills the world and everything in it, and occupies man entirely, centrally and by irradiation from the center—divided from itself. For this reason, it is certain that those things which are understood everywhere in the scriptures concerning God, the Word, Eternal Wisdom, Justice, Virtue, and others in the microcosm,

<column-break/>

are also to be understood in the microcosm itself. For just as the earth, water, air, fire, ether, and the empyrean spirit, as well as intellect, reason, mind, wisdom, the Word, and God are contained in the macrocosm, so also are all these things contained proportionally in the microcosm, such that they are no more divided from those in the macrocosm than solar rays are divided from the sun. Truly, just as it is in human nature sometimes to look toward the lower things of the world—which is the task of the animal or natural man—and sometimes to turn the edge of his contemplation toward higher things—which is the affection of the spiritual man—so man is rendered, in a general sense, more prone either to human wisdom (and consequently to inventing and fashioning worldly philosophy, which is false, being foolishness and vanity before God) or to proclaiming and establishing that divine wisdom in both worlds, which is just and acceptable before God. Therefore, these things having been considered with diligence, so that every doubt may be removed from the scholars of this world in the investigation of this philosophy of ours, we shall proceed in this manner.

### CHAPTER III.

->*In which the origin and essential principle of true wisdom and philosophy is explained, and its nature and power are truly revealed in a few words.*<-

---

In order to proceed methodically in this business of ours, it now remains for us to first seek out with diligence, from the testimonies of the sacred writings, the essential origin, fountain, and spring of Wisdom and philosophy. Afterward, we shall express with greater ease the definition and nature most suited to it. Then, we shall show that it is the real foundation not only of true philosophy and the sciences depending on it, but also the revealer and discoverer of all hidden mysteries or secrets—indeed, of all things, both past and future. As for the origin of this most holy wisdom, I shall prove by the testimony and consensus of the sacred page that its fountain is God Himself, who is the Father of Lights.

By these words we are able to discern how immense is the difference between that false or worldly and earthly wisdom of the Heathens <note>original: "Ethnicorum"; referring here to non-Christian classical philosophers like Aristotle or the Stoics</note>, and that true, sincere, and essential wisdom whose root is God, insofar as its source is the word or voice of the Father of Lights. <margin>Ecclesiasticus 1:6</margin> The fountain of wisdom (says the text) is the Word on high: and its entrance is the eternal commandments. Truly, this omnipotent power of His, in and over all things, is explained with excellence in these words of Paul—the Philosopher and Theosopher <note>A "Theosopher" is one who possesses "divine wisdom," a term often used in this era to distinguish spiritual insight from mere academic philosophy.</note>. Christ (he says) is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature: For in Him all things were founded, in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible; whether Thrones or Dominions; whether Principalities or Powers, all things were created through Him and in Him, and He is before all, and all things consist in Him, etc. This Doctrine of the Apostle will, without doubt, seem quite foreign or strange to those Academics who trust too much in the basic principles of Heathen philosophy; for that philosophy recognizes no such wisdom—namely, the celestial Word of God—nor does it recognize that by its mediation the heaven, earth, and Angelic Intelligences were created, or that in it and through it all things were and still exist in their current state. Instead, it presupposes for us many subordinate "efficient natures"—namely those of the intelligences, the stars, the elements, the meteors, and such like—which they want to believe perform all things, both above and below, by themselves. They even claim the world is eternal, that is, without beginning or end. Yet, on the contrary, we are taught by that true and sacred Philosophy that God created all things by His Word or Wisdom, that He Himself works all things in all, and that He is all in all: For the aforementioned text expressly says that all things consist in Him. <margin>Colossians 2</margin> But to the point: The text regarding the antiquity and power of this wisdom seems <margin>Proverbs 8:22</margin> to confirm this: Jehovah possessed Wisdom (it says) in the beginning of His way, before His works, before any time, before any age: When there were no abysses, she was brought forth; when there were no fountains abounding with water: before the mountains were settled: when Jehovah had not yet made the earth: When He prepared the heavens, she was there: When He set a compass upon the face of the abyss: when He established the upper clouds above: When He strengthened the fountains of the deep: when He gave the sea its decree: When

He set a compass upon the face of the abyss: when He established the upper clouds above: when He strengthened the fountains of the deep: When He appointed the foundations of the earth, wisdom was with Him, composing all things, etc. By this thread of discourse, he first depicts the antiquity of this most holy wisdom, and then teaches that she was the composer of heaven and earth, and consequently of every created thing, whether invisible or visible. All of this agrees with the sense and opinion of the sacred philosopher Moses, who recognizes in the first order that the Abyss was without form. In the second, he relates that the matter of this abyss was formless and void of the presence of that divine Spirit: that the *Elohim Ruach* <note>original: "Elohim Ruach"; Hebrew for the "Spirit of God" (Genesis 1:2)</note> was universally informed and marked with the name of "waters." In the third sequence, he shows how, by the operation and act of that Divine and essential Spirit—the Voice or Word "LET IT BE" <note>original: "FIAT"</note> brought forth by the Almighty—that most effective creature, Light, was produced from the beginning into the mass of waters as a created form. In the fourth place, he teaches that by a second issuance of spagyric <term>spagyric</term><note>An alchemical term meaning "to separate and to combine." Here, it refers to God's power to divide the elements during creation.</note> power, the upper waters were divided from the lower ones by the placement of the firmament, and thus by the second "LET IT BE" the heavens were established, just as by that same Word of God in the third sequence the lower waters were arranged into the Elements. Or rather, the single aqueous Element of the lower world was altered fourfold, or into a fourfold nature of spirits or winds; these natures, thus altered within one and the same aqueous element or Spirit, the Heathens were moved to call "Elements." Does <margin>Psalm 33:6</margin> not the Psalmist seem to assert this same thing in these few words? By the Word (he says) of the Lord the heavens were made firm, and all their power by the spirit of His mouth? And St. Peter: The heavens were of old, and the earth consisting of water and in water by the Word of God. Similarly, St. John: By Him all things were made, and without Him nothing was made. Namely, the world was made by that very spirit of light, and the world knew Him not. And Solomon: By wisdom God founded the heavens, <margin>Proverbs 3:19</margin> He established the earth in prudence. Finally, the whole harmony of the sacred page (which would be too long to recite in this place) seems to expressly confirm this same thing: namely, that whatever thing was made, of whatever nature or condition it may be, it was made, arranged, and completed through and by means of that divine power or emanation, which is that divine act whose root is the Word. <meta>This page continues Fludd’s argument that the Divine Word is the active, sustaining force of the universe. He moves here into a specific theological debate: whether God is present in his creation only "virtually" (by His influence) or "essentially" (by His very being). Fludd argues for the latter, asserting that if God were not essentially present, the world would instantly cease to exist.</meta>

Fol. 9.

# ON MOSAIC PHILOSOPHY.

...it stands, that the creature acts by itself—that is, by a certain free choice or its own will, which is absolutely divided and clearly distinguished from the immediate act of Divinity. To these arguments, which are poorly consistent with our established rules or canons regarding the Divinity, I respond: that the divine essence is indivisible. Therefore, it is evident that God does not typically impart any essential act—such as the soul, life, and the functions depending upon them—to any creature in a way that could be discontinued or separated from His own nature, according to that axiom: *what God gave, He never let go.* And for this reason, Christ, who is the eternal spirit of wisdom, is said to fill all things.

But indeed (the worldly-wise man of this age will reply), he who attempts to distract men from the simple truth with vain distinctions will say: that this presence of divinity is in every thing <term>virtually</term> <note>By "virtually," the opponent means God is present only through His power or effects, like the sun's heat felt at a distance, rather than His actual being.</note> and not <term>essentially</term> or substantially. To him I say (considering academic distinctions of that sort as nothing): For St. Paul commands Timothy: if anyone, he says, teaches another doctrine and does not agree to the sound words of our Lord Jesus Christ and to the doctrine of the fear of God, he is one who lifts himself up; and though he knows nothing, he is sick with disputes and questions of words, from which come envy, contention, slander, and evil suspicion. And it is the friction of the sons of men, whose minds are corrupt, and who are deprived of the truth and think that godliness is a source of gain. But you, stay away from such people. 

I would gladly (I say) like to know: is the power of God not His essence? Or can one be distinguished or separated from the other? If he should answer that the divine power is not the essence, but an <term>accident</term> <note>In Aristotelian logic, an "accident" is a property that a thing can have or lose without changing its fundamental nature. Fludd argues God has no accidents; He is entirely His own nature.</note>, it is certainly to be believed that such an answer is erroneous. For it is manifest and known even to the Jews and Gentiles that God is free from every accident, since He is the most essential essence of all things, existing in and by Himself, subject to no accident. Furthermore, where His essential act is present, there also is His power; and where His power is, there equally is His essence. Indeed, if this were not so, the word of God or the divine act—whose role is to give life to all things and to make every creature agile and mobile—would seem to be nothing but a mere accident; or rather, an accident divided from the divine essence. How absurd this would be is proven by the immortality of the very root of life.
<margin>Psalm 32:6 <note>In modern Bibles, this is Psalm 33:6.</note></margin>
For David has it in the aforementioned text: *By the spirit from His mouth is all their power*—namely, of the heavens, etc. I believe no one is so lacking in mind as to hold that power for an accident. It follows, therefore, that divine power is the same as the divine essence, and consequently is never divided in God Himself or from God—that is, from the divine spirit. But why say more? Since we have this expressly confirmed by the scriptures: The Spirit (says

<column-break/>

Solomon) is a breath of the power of God and a pure emanation from the glory of the Almighty, and a brightness from the eternal light, etc. What? Shall we call this power or brightness proceeding from the eternal light an accident, when it is the holy spirit of wisdom, as the wise man confesses? Hence 
<margin>Colossians 1:16. John 1.</margin>
also Saint Paul in the place cited before: *In Him all things were founded in heaven and on earth, both visible and invisible; all things were created in Him and through Him, and all things consist in Him,* etc. By these words it is clear that outside of Him, in spirit, there is nothing. And John says: *In the Word was life,* etc. And consequently, it is clear that the creature is continued and annexed to the divinity by the bond of that divine nature—that is, by one and the same spirit of Life which is within it. Without this connection, union, or relation to one another, it is impossible for a creature to exist for even a moment of time. Therefore 
<margin>Psalm 104:24 etc.</margin>
the Royal Psalmist says: *All creatures look to you to give them food in its time; when You give it to them, they gather it; when You open Your hand, they are satisfied with good. When You hide Your face, they are troubled; when You take away their spirit, they expire; when You send forth Your spirit, they are recreated with good,* etc. 

By this one may see that it is the immediate act of this wisdom that makes the creature live and exist, and that it is she who works all things. For the scriptures testify that God gives life to all things; and that *in Him we live, move, and have our being.* And not only us, but also all flesh in general, as we gather from this very text. And also from this testimony of Job: *If God, applying His soul to man, should take back His spirit or His breath to Himself,* 
<margin>Job 34:14.</margin>
*all flesh would fail at once and man would return to ash,* etc. Behold, therefore, the Cornerstone upon which all flesh is built, and without which it is reduced to nothing. Furthermore, the Prophet says: *God gives breath to the people who are upon the earth, and spirit to those who walk upon it,* etc. How (I beseech you) is it possible that this spirit of life could be present in and with all things, and thus essentially in every thing, and yet cease and rest from its immediate action—when it is in itself the swiftest of all things, and most 
<margin>Wisdom 7.</margin>
agile and mobile, as we are taught by Solomon? That this spirit is present to all things is clear from the fact that all things act, move, and live in it and through it. For 
<margin>Colossians 1. 1 Corinthians 12:6. 2 Peter 3:5. Wisdom 12:1. Psalm 139:7.</margin>
it stands. And elsewhere: *He Himself works all in all.* And St. Peter: *The heavens and the earth, and consequently all things that were from the water, consist by the Word of God.* And Solomon: *The incorruptible spirit of God is in every thing; and the holy spirit of discipline fills the world.* And the Psalmist: *Whither shall I go from your spirit, or whither shall I flee from your face? If I should ascend to the heavens, you are there; if I should make my bed in the grave, behold, you are present. If I should take the wings of the morning to dwell in the furthest parts of the sea, even there your hand would lead me and your right hand would hold me.* But if I should say...

...thing; surely the darkness covers me as if in twilight, and night is light around me. <note>Original: "tenebrae velut crepusculo obvoluant me..." Fludd is paraphrasing Psalm 139:11-12 to show that God is present even in darkness.</note> Though the darkness may indeed be so thick that you cannot see through it, yet the night shines as the day, and so forth. For this reason, it is manifest that it is the real Spirit of God—and not some accidental power (as some falsely imagine)—which fills all things. Regarding this, the prophet Isaiah says: *Heaven is my throne; the earth is my footstool.* And Jeremiah: *Do I not fill heaven and earth?* Now, so that you may know how this happens, I would have you listen closely to the words of King David, who says: *In wisdom you have made all things: the earth is filled with your possession.* <note>Psalm 104:24</note> That is to say, it is filled with your Spirit, which fills all things, gives them form, and brings all things into actual being. Hence also the son of Sirach says: *God poured out his wisdom over all his works and over all flesh according to his gift.* It is as if he had said that the Spirit is fertile to a greater or lesser degree in every thing, namely, according to that proportion which it pleased the Creator to assign to this or that creature. And this is the reason why Solomon asserts in another place that Wisdom works all things, just as the Apostle said above: *God works all things in all.* Since this is so, what, I ask, prevents us from boldly inferring that this Spirit is presentially and essentially everywhere, and consequently in every thing? What more? Does not Moses—that most excellent teacher of ours in sacred philosophy—teach us that when the foundations of the heavens and the Elements were established, every creature was fashioned from them and lives and moves within them? He teaches that they receive both their existence and their preservation from that unique Spirit: namely, that the Sun, Moon, and the other stars of heaven, the seeds of things, the trees, the herbs, and all other things of the vegetable kind, as well as the reptiles, quadrupeds, and birds of the animal kingdom, and even man himself, were created by one and the same Spirit. But in truth, God assigned a greater portion of his Spirit to man,

<column-break/>

so that man might excel the other living creatures by a more ample presence and possession of that Spirit.

To commit the entire scope of this philosophical matter to writing, as it is expressly and openly recited from the Scriptures, would be too laborious. For if we look at the works of Moses, read the books of Joshua and Judges, observe the history of Kings and Chronicles, listen to the account of Job, search the Psalms of David, the Proverbs and Ecclesiastes, the Song of Songs and the Wisdom of Solomon; if we scrutinize the monuments of the Prophets, the subject of Ecclesiasticus and the Maccabees, and finally, if we notice with diligence the reports and sayings of Christ and the Apostles; we shall perceive evidently that this sacred Wisdom, with her essential virtues, acts, and effects in the vast cavity of the entire world (both the supernal and the infernal), is the basis and foundation of all doctrine and science. This applies to natural things as well as supernatural—or rather, those things which concern the acts of God in his created "tabernacles," or his "watery coverings," <note>Fludd often uses "watery coverings" to describe the material world or the physical bodies that "clothe" the divine light.</note> which he either puts on or puts off according to his will, as those sacred writings testify almost everywhere.

Now, leaving generalities, I shall descend to particulars. I will show how this eternal Wisdom is the central source and cornerstone, first of all the arts: namely, Theology and Medicine, Astronomy, Music, Arithmetic, Geometry, Rhetoric, and then how the science of Meteorology depends upon her act and virtue. Next, I will show by what reason the science of Ethics (or Morals) and political Governance arise from her instructions and directions. And finally, I shall declare how all secret acts, mystical revelations, and miracles are perfected by her; thereby confirming that place of Scripture where it is said: *The other sciences are handmaids to this one.* <note>A common Renaissance sentiment placing Divine Wisdom as the "Queen of the Sciences."</note> Concerning all these things, then, we shall speak in order in the following sections.

Fol. 10.
# ON THE MOSAIC PHILOSOPHY.

...let them say that those words of Solomon are understood in a sense other than those of the sciences which are included under natural philosophy: I therefore warn such people, for their better direction, to turn their minds to the teachings of the wise man, who quite clearly sets out to erase their doubt: <margin>Wisdom 7:2, 7.</margin> "By the spirit of wisdom," he says, "it was given to me to know the constitution of the world and the force of the Elements; the Beginning, middle, and end of times; the changes of the solstices, and the varieties of times or seasons; the circuits of the year, and the positions of the stars; the natures of living things and the tempers or rages of beasts; the force of the winds or spirits, and the thoughts of men; the differences of plants and the powers of roots: I also knew all things, both hidden and manifest; for wisdom, the craftswoman of all things, taught me," etc. From these words we gather that by the revelation of this divine spirit, this most wise king reached a knowledge of all things and sciences. For since wisdom is the central root, or the Cornerstone of all things, how is it possible for us to reach the knowledge of the center if we are ignorant of the secrets of the circumference? This is especially true since the circumference, or the external part of a thing, is nothing other than that which is ordered and disposed by the center. And for this reason, this divine spirit is not undeservedly called by the most profound Philosopher Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the "Hermetic" tradition of secret wisdom.</note> the center of every thing, whose circumference is nowhere, but which nonetheless encompasses all circumferences within itself. Therefore, from the aforementioned speech of Solomon, we can learn first: that wisdom revealed to him—no differently than to Moses—those hidden mysteries concerning the fabric of the world. Second: that she taught him the nature and power of the Elements, along with the hidden action and miraculous generation and properties of meteors <note>In the 17th century, "meteors" referred to any atmospheric phenomena, including rain, wind, and lightning.</note> which are fashioned from elementary matter. Third: that she provided him with the reason and method for the origin and production of the winds, the astronomical division of the year, and the site or position of the stars in the heaven along with their astrological natures. Fourth: that she opened the chief mysteries of the art of healing; for he confesses that he learned from his mistress, Wisdom, the natures of all creatures, the conditions of beasts, the differences of plants, and the powers of roots. Fifth: he relates that by means of this spirit he was made a participant in all hidden or secret things and consequently in the Mysteries of the Angels; indeed, even in the secrets of God himself.

<margin>THEOLOGY. Concerning the eternal world.</margin>
As far as Theology is concerned, it is well known that the word is derived from *Theos* <note>Greek: "God"</note> and *Logos* <note>Greek: "Word" or "Speech"</note>, signifying as it were a "speech about God." This high science is also founded upon these divine bases, wherefore the wise man says: The spirit of wisdom transfers itself into Holy souls <margin>Wisdom 7:27.</margin> and appoints the friends of God and prophets. For 

<column-break/>

God loves no one, except the one who dwells with wisdom. Again elsewhere: God sends forth wisdom from the holy heavens; from the throne of his glory he sends her to man, so that being present she may work with him in his labor, so that he may know <margin>Ecclesiasticus 24:45.</margin> what is pleasing to him: for she knows all things. For this reason also Wisdom says: I will enlighten all who hope in the Lord. And elsewhere: I am the book of life, <margin>Ecclesiasticus 24:32.</margin> the testament of the most high, and the recognition of the truth. And Solomon: The desire for wisdom leads to a perpetual kingdom. And again: Wisdom is the teacher of the discipline of God and the chooser of his works. And elsewhere: Through <margin>Wisdom 6:21. Wisdom 8:4. Wisdom 8:13.</margin> wisdom I shall have immortality, etc. It would be a weariness to the soul, and would perhaps seem superfluous to the reader, if I were to enumerate in this place more confirmations of Theological doctrine which are indicated and manifested by this spirit. In short, I say that this was the very Spirit in Christ in the Flesh and in his Apostles, which made their bodily organs—namely their tongues—speak, and their hands and pens commit to writing all that theological doctrine and wisdom which is contained in the New Testament. And it was also this spirit which, like the oracles of divinity, uttered the speeches in the Old Testament through the mouths of the Patriarchs and Prophets. Therefore, it is necessary that we look back to those literal sources of Theology, since under their symbolic or written instructions the hidden spirit of this secret sense lies concealed; which can be extracted and unshelled by means of the precepts of mystical Theology.

<margin>CONCERNING THE ANGELIC WORLD. Colossians 1:16. Colossians 2:9. Ephesians 1:20.</margin>
I shall now proceed in the second place to that science which I will prove shares a foundation with Theology, and which pertains to the everlasting world. "In him" (says St. Paul in the place cited before) "all things were created in the heavens, whether Dominations, or Thrones, or Principalities, or Powers." And elsewhere: "In Christ dwelt all the fullness of the Godhead bodily, who is the head of all Principality and power." And again: "Christ is set at the right hand of God in the heavenly places, and above every Principality and power and virtue and Domination," etc. By these testimonies and many others collected from the sacred page (which I omit for the sake of brevity) it is proved that no secret mystery is contained within the society of angels—whether it pertains to their creation, their essence, their properties and virtues, or their names—which does not exist within the power and knowledge of this most excellent spirit, by whom and through whom it is revealed to men. Nor indeed is it a wonder if it is within his will to uncover everything in all things, since it is known by the wise that he is himself "all in all."

Now I shall descend to the next step on the ladder of the sciences, which is Astronomy, whose essential nature is to fly upon the wings of this most wise spirit and stay fixed upon its base...

<margin>Knowledge of the temporal world.</margin> or seen to rest upon a foundation. And the Psalmist says: *God, in his wisdom, numbers the multitude of the stars, and assigns names to them all. For King David confirms that <margin>Psalm 32:6. 4 Esdras 6:17. Baruch 3:34. Joshua 10:13.</margin> every power in heaven proceeds from this spirit of God. And Esdras says: *The stars were founded in the word of God, who knows the number of the stars.* In this respect also the Prophet Baruch says: *The stars gave light in their watches and rejoiced at the command of God.* And it was from this that, when this spirit fought for Joshua, it made the sun stand still in the sky for several hours. Furthermore, it turned the brightness <margin>Matthew 27:45.</margin> of the sun into darkness during the suffering of Christ. At the command of this spirit, the stars also fought against Sisera, etc. From this it is clear that, just as the heavens and stars were created and animated in the beginning by this spirit <margin>Judges 5:20.</margin> to serve as instruments for administering to the lower, sublunary world: so too, beyond the common course or manner of <term>microcosmic Nature</term> <note>The idea that the human body reflects the structure of the universe</note>, they can be diverted from their own and accustomed action by the will and command of that almighty spirit (which acts in them no differently than the soul in the body); namely, by altering both their motion and the activity of their light and influential spirit. As for the fixed stars, Job says these things in the person of that spirit: *Will you <margin>Job 38:31.</margin> be able to bind the delicate fruits of the Pleiades with your hands, or can you open the late fruits of Orion? Can you bring forth the <term>Mazzaroth</term> <note>original: "MaIaroth"; the signs of the Zodiac</note>, or the celestial signs in their time, and lead Arcturus with the lesser stars as if they were his children? Do you know the laws of heaven? Will you set its dominion upon the earth?* etc. This is as if one were to say that no one is able to understand the course of the stars directly and for certain, or to discern the power and virtue of their influences, without the assistance and indication of that most wise spirit. For this reason, Solomon seems to boast that he understood the course of the year <margin>Wisdom 7:10.</margin> and the positions of the stars and the changes

of the solstices by the teaching of that all-knowing spirit. Therefore, if a professor of Astronomy does not have this true foundation of astrology, all his predictions will undoubtedly be false and mythical—or at least (for the most part) uncertain and full of lies, as may be seen in common astrologers.

<margin>METEOROLOGY in the temporal elementary world.</margin>
It follows that we should speak next of the sciences belonging to the lower region of the temporal world, so that we may show the reason for the operation of this <term>Universal Spirit</term> <note>original: "spiritus Catholici"</note> in the production of multiform meteors in the Universal Elementary kingdom.

On the act and operation of that eternal actor and mover in the Air, Water, and Earth, as if in one Universal element or moist sublunary spirit, for the production of meteors. These things also come from the holy book: *God in his Wisdom fits the weight to the air, and weighs the waters in measure, and makes the laws for the rain, and a way for the lightning of the thunders* <margin>Job 28:25.</margin>, etc. By this thread of discourse Job argues that this eternal spirit—in which there is the vigor and power of both contraction and condensation, as well as expansion and rarefaction—can at its will make the air either denser and heavier by condensation (and consequently produce a consistency within us), or reduce it into a thinner and more subtle substance by expanding or rarefying it into the form of lightning or a flash. Therefore, it must be known that in all such changes, the variety of the form is received from that actor or alterer; and this is according to the will of him who is the disposer or ordainer of all things. And thus clouds, lightning, thunder, comets, frost, snow, hail, ice, etc., and other things of that kind are continually created by the act of this spirit and produced in this sublunary world. Do we not have all these things confirmed by Holy Scripture? *By the Wisdom of God* <margin>Proverbs 3:20.</margin> (says the Wise Man) *the depths broke open, and the clouds grow thick with dew.* And Sirach, in the person of the said spirit: *I, wisdom, covered the whole earth like a mist.* <margin>Ecclesiasticus 24:6. Ecclesiasticus 24:7. Job 28:25. Psalm 134:7. Psalm 147:15.</margin> Again: *I dwelt in the highest places, and my throne is a pillar of cloud.* And Job: *God made the clouds by his wisdom.* And David: *He brings out the clouds from the end of the earth, he makes lightnings into rain. He produces winds from his treasures.* And elsewhere: *With his word running most swiftly, and his command sent out upon the earth, God gives snow like wool, and scatters hoarfrost like ashes. Who can stand before his fury?* etc. Truly, there are many hundreds of other passages that could be cited from the book of truth to prove that all true meteorology is founded upon this spirit. But since we will deal more fully with this subject in the last book of this work—in which we not only recite the true history of Meteors, but also detect the errors and falsehoods of Aristotelian Meteorology.

<margin>MEDICINA.</margin> It remains now for us to say a few words about Medicine, or the art of healing. Concerning this <margin>Ecclesiasticus 38:2.</margin> most excellent science, the wise man says: *All healing is from God* <note>original: "A Deo est omnis medela"</note>, etc. Since this is so, it is evident that the principal act in the art of healing comes immediately from that Spirit. Therefore the Royal Prophet says: <margin>Psalm 106:20. Wisdom 16:11.</margin> *He sent his word and healed them, and rescued them from their destruction.* And Solomon says: *Neither herb nor poultice healed them, but your word, O Lord, which heals all things* <note>original: "Neque herba, neque malagma sanavit eos, sed tuus domine, sermo, qui sanat omnia."</note>, etc. Observe well. Your "Word" or "Speech" (says the text) which heals all things: for that divine Word is the root or fountain of that eternal Spirit, and consequently the basis and foundation of healing consists in it. From this it follows that every power of healing proceeds from it. For this also agrees with the sense of the Apostle: <margin>1 Corinthians 12:4, 9.</margin> *There are differences, or divisions, of graces, but the same Spirit: divisions of operations, but the same God, who works all in all.* To some, indeed, is given the word of wisdom through the Spirit; to others the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit; to others faith by the same Spirit, etc.; to others the gifts of healing by the same Spirit. Now, truly, that this almighty and all-working Spirit is the one who attributes life to the creature is confirmed from many places <margin>Proverbs 2:7, 3:16.</margin> in Holy Scripture. For the wise man says: *Wisdom shall guard health.* And again: *In the right hand of wisdom is length of days: she is a tree of life to all who have taken hold of her,* etc. And this is to be understood as much concerning the soul as the body, just as appeared in the healings successfully performed by Christ and his Apostles, <margin>Proverbs 8:35.</margin> who completed them by means of that Spirit. Furthermore, Solomon says: *He who finds wisdom, <margin>Wisdom 10:9, 9:19.</margin> finds life and shall draw health from the Lord.* And elsewhere: *She shall deliver those who observe her from sorrows.* And again: *Through wisdom they were born, whoever have pleased you, O Lord, from the beginning,* etc. Indeed, any prudent reader ought to consider that there is no animal, vegetable, or mineral used in the art of medicine <margin>Ecclesiasticus 38:4.</margin> which does not have and receive its curative act immediately from that Spirit. For this reason, therefore, the Most High created medicine from the earth, and a prudent man will not abhor it. In which context it must be observed, first, that trees, herbs, roots, and also minerals, since they are earth-born, were ordained by God from the beginning

<column-break/>

of the world for the healing of men: and then afterwards, that the life-giving act within them was imparted to them by that incorruptible Spirit. For that Spirit is said to be in every thing, and to work all things in them, even though it is noted to act in them in various forms, as the Apostle seems to assert in the place cited before, confirming the aforementioned assertion of the wise man, which is <margin>Wisdom 16:12.</margin> that God heals all things by his Word. If, therefore, the Word heals all things, then nothing can heal except by means of the Word or the Spirit of Wisdom, whose fountain is the Word (as was said before). But since that incorruptible Spirit is in every thing, and since it is more agile and mobile than any thing in this world; and since, in respect to its purity, it <margin>Wisdom 12:1, 7:24.</margin> penetrates through all things, and consequently works in all things: What, I pray, shall hinder me or any Christian from saying that God works all in all, by means of the Word, through himself and immediately? And consequently, that no creature can act from itself and by itself. For that doctrine of the Peripatetics <note>The followers of Aristotle, whom Fludd often criticized for their "godless" physics.</note> is absurd, which falsely instructs us (seducing the hearts of sincere Christians from the truth of the Creator). For it attempts to entice pious men with erroneous basics of this kind, so that they may take away from God, who creates all things and who is all in all, that which creatures (which without the presence of the Word are plainly nothing) might arrogantly claim for themselves as an absolute power of acting and working by themselves. To better achieve this, that doctrine mentions many essential and distinct subaltern agents (as was said before), all of which it feigns to have actions and operations by themselves—that is, without the help of another—that they might exist, act, and work. Such agents are the Sun, the Stars, the winds, the Elements, or rather the "Universal Element" in its many forms, and creatures both perfectly and imperfectly mixed. Certainly, in doing this, it deludes the world, making it believe that the organ or instrument acts essentially by itself, and not by the centrally and divinely originated power, which is the foundation of every creature, and the distinguished character or goal <note>term: "meta" (goal or mark)</note> of the highest good of philosophers, at which a lover of true philosophy aims. This, therefore, is the reason that Solomon, the Prophets, and Christ with his holy Apostles exhort all Christians to be lovers of true wisdom, as it is that in which every act is found—both the intellectual act which raises the human mind to the summit of knowledge and wisdom, and the material act, namely that which works toward life-giving, growth, and <margin>Wisdom 7:20.</margin> multiplication. But of this, more elsewhere. I conclude this part of the chapter with this confession of Solomon: *The natures of animals (he says) and the rages of wild beasts... the differences of shrubs and the powers of roots, and even those things which are hidden and manifest, Wisdom, the artisan of all things, made known to me,* etc. By which he proves that Wisdom gave to herbs, animals,

### BOOK II OF THE FIRST SECTION.

To animals and minerals, he has imparted their virtues, both hidden and apparent. I speak of that supreme spirit, who is "all in all" and "works all things in all" <note>original: "omne in omni & operatur omnia in omnibus"</note>; consequently, he is able to teach and instruct through external revelation what occurs within a creature's interior, and by what virtue he operates in each. And although the pagan philosophers and physicians <note>Fludd uses "Ethnici" to refer to non-Christian classical authorities like Galen or Aristotle.</note> discovered the hidden properties of plants only through the effects perceived in practice and through sensory observation—as if by a "demonstration from the effect" <note>original: "demonstratione à posteriore"</note>—finding, for example, that the Linden tree, Oak Mistletoe, and Peonies cure epilepsy; and that the herb Rupturewort <note>original: "Herniaria"</note> treats the condition called a hernia (from which it takes its name); just as Coltsfoot <note>original: "tussilago"</note> is used to cure a cough <note>original: "tussim"</note>; and that Eyebright <note>original: "Euphrasia"</note> helps with the fogging of the eyes; and among animals, that the Toad <note>original: "Buffo"</note> stops blood, while the elk’s foot and frogs are effective against the "falling sickness" <note>term: morbum caducum — an early term for epilepsy</note>; and that scorpions cure the sting of scorpions, and so on. Nevertheless, because these doctors lack the central foundations of <term>sympathy and antipathy</term> <note>These are the core forces in Fludd's universe: "sympathy" is the attraction between like things, and "antipathy" is the repulsion between opposites.</note>—which consist in the "Will" and "Un-will" of one and the same spirit—they can provide no other reason for these wonderful and hidden things, except to say they are "hidden properties." In the end, they can infer nothing further about the matter than that these things are so "because they are so." Thus, from these learned doctors, we receive no conclusion except "the unknown explained by the even more unknown" <note>original: "Ignotum per Ignotius"</note>.

<margin>MUSIC</margin>
That the action and virtue of this spirit is also involved in every kind of Music—not only in the common and artificial kind but also in the more essential and mystical kind, whether it be of the <term>macrocosm</term> <note>the universe as a whole</note> or the <term>microcosm</term> <note>the human being as a "little world"</note>—is a truth that can be drawn out not just by common observation, but by a more internal inspection. Regarding worldly harmony, and the manner in which every sublunary element and every celestial sphere is arranged by a certain essential species of sympathetic concord, the entire series of the Scriptures seems to confirm this: namely, that these things are perfected by the mediation of the Divine Spirit’s act.

<margin>Wisdom 19:17.</margin>
And above all others, Solomon testifies to the wonderful effect of that Spirit in worldly harmony in these words:
> For the elements, while they were being changed among themselves, were like the qualities of a musical instrument changing its tone, yet all kept their own sound. <note>original: "In se Elementa dum convertuntur, sicut in organo qualitatis immutatur, & omnia suum sonum custodiunt."</note>

But the Apostle expresses all of this with even greater excellence and efficacy, saying:
<margin>Colossians 1:19.</margin>
> In Christ all things were created in heaven and on earth, both visible and invisible; all things were created through him and in him. He is before all things, and in him all things hold together. In him it pleased all the fullness of the Divinity to dwell, and through him to reconcile all things in himself, making peace through the blood of his cross, whether things on earth or things in heaven, etc.

Behold here the perfect and universal source of Love, Sympathy, and Harmony! It is he who not only takes away the discordant sins of the world but also cleanses heaven and 

<column-break/>

earth from discord. By his peaceful virtue, he adorns them with harmonic concord and with a sympathetic peace or love. From this, it follows that this spirit is called by the wise and mystical philosopher the "bond" or "ligament" of the elements. By this means, the elements of the discordant world and the microcosm (or man) are bound together and reduced into a fitting harmony and quiet union. Therefore, in imitation of this worldly consonance, the harmony of external music—both vocal and instrumental—is typically formed. In respect to that true and pure Symphony of the Spirit, external music stands as a shadow to the object that casts it, or as an image to the real person it represents.

<margin>ARITHMETIC GEOMETRIA Wisdom 11:22.</margin>
Now we come to Arithmetic and Geometry, which the wise man seems to include in his discourse:
> You have ordered or tempered all things by measure, number, and weight. <note>original: "Omnia mensura, numero & pondere disposuisti"</note>

Where by "measure," he understands the progress of a thing in length, width, and depth, relating to Arithmetic and Algebra <note>term: Cofficam — likely referring to 'Cossic' art, an early term for algebra.</note>. This almighty spirit, in its emanation, makes this measure from a point into a line; from a line or root into a square; and finally from a square to a cube—as if from a point or starting place to a surface, and from a surface to a body or destination. By "numbers," he understands those arithmetic dimensions in a progression by which that spirit moved out from unity into multiplicity. For example: from 1 to 10, as if from the eternal center of all things into the angelic or aeonial state; this progression was the first and simplest degree of composition or mixture. Then from 10 to 100, which multiplicative progress denotes the composition of the temporal world; and finally from 100 to 1,000. This progression proves the composition of creatures from the elements or from various alterations of the Universal Element. Thus, every Christian can see from these things how God is all in all and yet outside of all—and (as it says in the text) in heaven, in the sea, in the abyss, and in the depths. For this reason, the Pythagoreans included all things in these three arithmetic principles: 1, 2, and 3. They attributed 1 to God in his hidden existence; 2 they referred to the matter of all things; and 3 to the universal form of the world. Under these three, therefore, all things are comprehended. I will make a fuller mention of these (God willing) in the second section, where I shall discuss the essentials of sympathy and antipathy.

The patient man <note>Job</note>, speaking in the persona of Jehovah, says:
<margin>Job 38:4.</margin>
> Where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth? Tell me, if you have understanding. Who determined its measurements, if you know? Or who stretched a line upon it? On what were its bases sunk, or who laid its cornerstone?

By these words, he proves that this spirit, which is the cornerstone...

### ON MOSAIC PHILOSOPHY. Folio 12.

The Singular Basis or Foundation of all things (for without Him nothing was made or can exist, as Saint John testifies) not only determined the Earth’s position, dimensions, and geometric placement; but also the Celestial Sun, Moon, Stars, and all things in heaven as well as on earth acquire their weights, proportions, magnitudes, and positions in this world through Him. Indeed, even the air itself is shaped into various meteorological "characters" or images according to different measures and proportions. For the sacred text says: *God in His wisdom provides a weight for the air, and weighs out the waters by measure, and establishes the laws for the rain and a path for the lightning of the thunder, etc.* <note>original: "Deus sapientiâ aptat pondus aëri, & appendit aquas in mensura & facit pluviæ statuta & viam fulgetro tonitruum, &c." — a reference to Job 28:25.</note>

<margin>
RHETORIC.
ORATORY
</margin>
It follows that we should explain and prove in a few words His virtue and power in the science of Rhetoric and the art of Oratory. We shall prove that the Spirit itself is the most exact mistress in teaching these arts, and is the most essential mover in the souls or spirits of men. By His action, men who were once entirely mute and barbaric are rendered eloquent and effectively persuasive; and what is more, He is that essential spirit within the voice and words of orators, by whose mediation the minds of listeners are enticed and drawn toward paying attention and placing faith in their speeches. For Moses, while in dialogue with that divine spirit, said: *I am not, he said, a man of eloquence, nor have I ever been, not even since you have spoken to your servant, for I am slow of speech and slow of tongue.*

<margin>Exodus 4:10.</margin>
Then Jehovah said to him: *Who established the mouth of man, or who can make one either deaf or mute? Is it not I, who am Jehovah? Now therefore go, and I will be with your mouth, and I will teach you what it is proper for you to speak, etc.* By this we are taught that eloquence, the fit arrangement of words, sentences, and speeches—both in the <term>rhetorician</term> <note>One who studies the theory of communication.</note> and the <term>orator</term> <note>One who practices public speaking.</note>—are from God, to whom alone it belongs to give or take away fluency as He pleases.

<margin>
John 6:45.
Isaiah 54:13.

Wherefore the Evangelist says, *they shall all be taught by God.* And the Prophet: *all your sons are taught by Jehovah.* Truly, Christ expresses all this in even more explicit words: *The Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send, he will teach you all things, and will bring to your mind all things, whatever I have said to you.*

<margin>John 14:26.</margin>
Now, that this spirit is that eternal Wisdom which effects and awakens this Rhetorical and Oratorical function in men, the Scriptures teach elsewhere:

<margin>Wisdom 10:21.</margin>
*Wisdom opened (says the Wise Man) the mouth of the mute and made the tongues of infants eloquent.* And the son of Sirach:

<margin>Ecclesiasticus 39:7.</margin>
*Like showers he sends forth the words of his wisdom, and in prayer he shall confess to the Lord, etc.* I could bring forward many other examples from the sacred page in this place to confirm this assertion of mine—namely, to prove that Rhetorical eloquence is from this good spirit of wisdom—but for the sake of brevity I will omit them now, so that I may move on to the <term>mechanical arts</term> <note>In the 17th century, "mechanical arts" referred to any practical craft or trade involving physical labor, such as metallurgy or weaving.</note>. I will prove that the inventions of all these arts had their origin from the instinct and guidance of this good spirit,

<column-break/>

even though today they are defiled and stained, partly by the antiquity of time and partly by the envy and ignorance of men.

<margin>
MECHANICAL
ARTS.
</margin>
Regarding the mechanical arts, it must be known that their invention and origin (as we have said) came from the inspiration of this spirit. For example: the Art of Tailoring or garment-making proceeded from the instruction of this spirit.

<margin>Exodus 28.</margin>
Hence Jehovah to Moses: *Speak to all those wise of heart, whom I have filled with the spirit of wisdom, that they may make garments for Aaron, in which he may minister having been sanctified.*

<margin>Exodus 31.</margin>
Furthermore, the inventions of the Goldsmith's work, the art of the Jeweler, the Carpenter, and the Wood-carver took their beginning from that very source; wherefore Jehovah said to Moses: *Behold, I have called Bezalel and filled him with the spirit of God, with Wisdom, understanding, and knowledge in every work, both for devising whatever can be crafted from gold, silver, and bronze, marble and gems, and various types of wood; and I have given him Oholiab as a companion, and in the heart of every learned man I have placed wisdom, so that they may do all the things I have commanded you, etc.* From these things it is evident that the knowledge of every true mechanical art is in the spirit of God, in whose power alone it is to teach men all things. But all this is expressed more plainly elsewhere:

<margin>Exodus 35:30.</margin>
For Moses says to the children of Israel: *Behold, the Lord has called Bezalel, and filled him with the spirit of God, with wisdom, understanding, knowledge, and all learning for devising and performing work in gold, silver, bronze, and iron, and in carving stones and in carpentry. Whatever can be skillfully devised, He has put into his heart: He has also instructed both him and Oholiab with wisdom, so that they may perform the work of the joiner, the weaver, and the embroiderer in hyacinth-blue, purple, and twice-dyed scarlet, and fine linen, and may weave all things, etc.* Moreover, we read that Noah was instructed by this spirit in the construction of the Ark.

<margin>Wisdom 10:4.</margin>
For the text says: *Wisdom healed the earth, steering the just man by means of a contemptible piece of wood.* Through her mediation, the art of Music was revealed to Tubal: for the text has: *Tubal was the Father of those singing with the lyre and the organ.* <note>The Latin text here attributes the invention of music to Tubal, though Genesis 4:21 mentions Jubal; Fludd often groups these antediluvian figures together as recipients of divine "Prisca Sapientia" or Ancient Wisdom.</note> And Tubal-Cain was the first inventor of works in iron and bronze. And Adah’s son, Jubal, was the Father and author of the art of Tabernacles and the pastoral life. We conclude, therefore, that there is no true mechanical art which does not have its origin from this omnipotent spirit, whose role alone it is to teach all things.

Since this is so, it is clearly evident that there is no true and genuine art or science, whether it be manifest or abstruse and mystical, which is not derived from the doctrine of this true wisdom, since without her nothing real or essential can be either known or acquired in art.

<meta>This page transitions from the discussion of the four cardinal virtues—temperance, justice, prudence, and fortitude—as the pillars of moral philosophy, to a sharp contrast between "true" divine philosophy and the "false" or "spurious" philosophy of the worldly schools.</meta>

# ON THE MOSAIC PHILOSOPHY. Folio 13.

### CHAPTER V:

#### Concerning false wisdom, spurious philosophy, and the counterfeit philosopher, along with their characteristics.

<margin>James 3:17</margin>
Now, since I have already explained clearly enough the nature or essence of true wisdom—and consequently of pure philosophy and the pure philosopher—it is appropriate that I describe the false and counterfeit wisdom of this world. I shall describe the philosophy founded upon it, as well as the signs and characteristics not only of this unclean wisdom and philosophy, but also of the philosopher who is nourished and educated within it like a bastard child. The Apostle says that true wisdom, which arises from the Father of Light, is pure, peaceable, gentle, open to reason, full of mercy and good fruits; it is not judgmental, and is without rivalry or hypocrisy. But on the other hand, he asserts that the wisdom which is from below—and not from the Father of Light—is earthly, sensual, demonic, and contradictory to the truth. Consequently, it is litigious, immodest, stubborn, devoid of good fruit, and full of rivalry, contention, and dispute.

Therefore, just as the basis or foundation of the former philosophy is Jesus Christ—inasmuch as he is true Wisdom—so indeed the foundation of the latter is the tradition and invention of worldly men. This worldly wisdom is animated by the deceptive suggestions of the Devil, so that by this path he might create strife, disputes, and opposition in this world. Hence that divine Philosopher <note>Referring to St. Paul</note> said, in establishing the difference between these two opposites: "In Christ are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge." <note>original: "In Christo sunt omnes Thesauri sapientiæ & scientiæ absconditi"</note>

<margin>Colossians 2:7-8</margin>
By this series of words, Saint Paul seems to assert that all wisdom and knowledge—and consequently all true Philosophy and all sincere sciences derived from it—are contained and are to be sought and found in Christ. He is that eternal wisdom and the true Cornerstone <note>original: "lapis verè Angularis"</note> who fills, informs, and gives life to all things. True wisdom is not found through any human industry investigating the vain knowledge and wisdom of the world and of the Pagans <note>original: "Ethnicorum"</note>; for such knowledge is deceptive and barely adorned with the appearance of probability, since it relies on the obscure and erroneous precepts of worldly men rather than the spiritual ordinances of Christ. For this reason, the Apostle condemns "philosophy" in general terms, yet recognizes upon a more specific inspection that the love of true wisdom—and therefore the Lover of Wisdom himself—is to be regarded and revered with the highest honor by the wise. Therefore, it is certain that by "philosophy" he means the study of worldly wisdom. For in that passage he confesses Christ to be the true Wisdom, as in whom dwells all the fullness of the Godhead bodily. It follows, then, that he would praise the lover or friend of such Wisdom with the greatest effort, and by consequence, the Philosophy

<column-break/>

which is built upon such a base—upon such a Cornerstone, I say—he would not know how to disapprove. From this it is evident that he intends a twofold Philosophy in that text. The caution he gave to the Colossians regarding the avoidance of "philosophy and vain deceit" referred only to that of the Athenians <note>The Greeks</note>, which is produced from the tradition of men and according to the elements of the world. Truly, he seemed to approve of that which was established upon Christ. Hence the text says, "and not according to Christ," etc. There, he also shows the reason why such Philosophy is to be embraced above all: "Because," he says, "in him dwells all the fullness of the Godhead bodily." Consequently, he says that wisdom descends from the Father of Light, upon whom every creature is founded. It follows, therefore, that he who is a *Theophilos*—that is, a lover of God or a friend of Christ—is a true philosopher, since Christ himself is that true wisdom which is in reality the root and basis of all things.

The sense of this passage from the Apostle is that the word "Philosophy," being a term according to the invention of the Pagans, was to be rejected in respect to its erroneous foundations and rules. This is because it was made and manufactured according to the tradition of unfaithful men, which leads Christians (and even more so the Pagans or Gentiles) into error and away from the true knowledge of God, rather than directing them into the way of truth and the knowledge of divine things. And for this reason, many conditions of various Idolatry have arisen, which act as a cause for the neglect of the true worship of the Creator. Indeed, it leads even to the contempt of His name, so much so that men are incited to the veneration and worship of creatures in place of the Creator, through whom they themselves live and exist. It is for this reason that we are warned to avoid this kind of philosophy with the utmost care. Concerning such philosophers, therefore, who did not place their knowledge upon the Cornerstone, and those Christians who rely on such Pagan fictions:

<margin>Romans 1:18</margin>
The same Apostle says this: "The wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all the ungodliness and injustice of men who suppress the truth of God in unrighteousness. Because what is known of God is manifest to them; for God has revealed it to them. For his invisible attributes are clearly seen from the creation of the world through the things that have been made. Likewise His eternal truth and divinity, so that they are without excuse; because although they knew God, they did not glorify Him as God, nor give Him thanks, but in claiming to be wise they became vain in their imaginations. For they changed the glory of the incorruptible God into an image made like to man, and birds, and four-footed animals, and creeping things," etc. By which things Saint Paul intimates...

<summary>Fludd distinguishes between "True Philosophy," which is founded on Christ as the eternal Cornerstone, and "False Philosophy," which stems from human tradition and leads to idolatry. He uses the writings of St. Paul to argue that worldly wisdom often distracts from the divine truth revealed in creation.</summary>
