# BOOK II of SECTION I

Paul describes how great an iniquity exists among the wise of this world, or the Philosophers, who hide divine truth—or rather, that incorruptible Divinity that dwells within every creature—from worldly men by means of false human inventions. It is as if he had said that the false Philosophers of this world try in every way, using their feigned delusions gathered from the <term>Ethnics</term> <note>The "Ethnics" refers to pagan or non-Christian nations, particularly the Greeks and Romans.</note>, to prevent human darkness from comprehending that essential life or light sent from heaven into all creatures, and especially into man. This light shines in the darkness, even though it is not permitted for those philosophers to discern that divinity within the creatures. Solomon also says of these men:

<margin>Wisdom 13:1</margin>
All men are vain by nature, in whom there is ignorance of God, and who, from those good things which are seen, could not understand Him who is, nor by considering the works did they acknowledge the Craftsman, etc. Moreover, he argues elsewhere that this divine Spirit is in every creature, affirming:

<margin>Wisdom 12:1</margin>
that the incorruptible spirit of God is in all things, etc. This is also confirmed in many other places, as has been said before. Therefore, every Christian has a need to be cautious in reading the philosophy of the Pagans, and to be very certain in his own mind, weighing seriously and repeatedly the opinions of the two aforementioned philosophers <note>Referring to Paul and Solomon</note>. But above all, let him remember the precepts of the former (namely, Saint Paul), who, when he found the worldly Philosophers of Athens worshipping an unknown God, preached to them a new philosophy and wisdom entirely unknown to them: namely, Jesus Christ. This doctrine seemed so foreign to them that they broke out angrily in these words:

<margin>Acts 17:18</margin>
"What does this **babbler** <note>Original: *seminiverbius*, literally a "seed-word sower" or one who picks up scraps of talk.</note> want to say?" Others said, "He seems to be a proclaimer of new demons," because he preached Jesus and the resurrection to them. From this it is clear enough that true wisdom never reached their ears, nor ever took root in their hearts. Indeed, I would wish the reader to consider that the Apostle was thinking of these spurious Philosophers, along with their wisdom or Philosophy, in the place cited before, where he says: *See to it that no one deceives you through Philosophy and empty fallacy*, etc. That is, as it was taught at Athens: namely, with vain fallacies, subtleties, contentious quibbling, and **Protean** <note>Referring to Proteus, the sea-god capable of changing his shape at will; here meaning meanings that shift and change to avoid the truth.</note> distinctions. By such means, such a philosopher, like Proteus, can turn his meaning into any significance, whether true or false. From this, it happens that men are filled with doubts by such doctrine, leaving the plain path of true wisdom to conduct their inquiries through labyrinths and misty, uncertain paths. Are we not taught that the spirit, which is the foundation or the unique and simple subject of true philosophy, must therefore be sought in all simplicity? Is it not said,

<margin>Wisdom 7:22</margin>
that it is modest, sweet, clear, kind, peaceful, and without rivalry? And

<column-break/>

yet we Christians would rather embrace a spirit and a philosophy deformed by quarrels,

<margin>James 3:15</margin>
fallacies, contentious disputes, and ambiguities. True wisdom, therefore, since it is peaceful and relies on no ambiguity, has no need for litigious disputes and quibbles. Nor does it require for its investigation infinite distinctions or vain <term>quiddities</term> <note>A scholastic term for the "whatness" or essence of a thing, often used here to mock overly complex academic definitions.</note> born of human invention, which lead the student into ignorance through their multiplicity rather than introducing him into the light of naked truth. On the other hand, false wisdom so abounds in distinctions, teems with so many subtle evasions, is so subject to sophisticated and contentious disputes, and is composed of such great multiplicity, that in the end it is so difficult and void of good fruit that, in place of the grain of true and essential truth, we find nothing but husks—words, I say, in place of reality. In a word: it appears to be, but is not real. It looks like a body, when in truth it is a mere shadow. This the Apostle also confirms:

<margin>1 Corinthians 2:4; 1 Corinthians 12:12; Galatians 3:5</margin>
*My preaching was not in persuasive words of human wisdom, but in the demonstration of the spirit and of truth.* And elsewhere: *the signs of my apostleship were performed among you in all power, in signs, wonders, and mighty deeds.* And again: *He who gives you the spirit and works powers or miracles in you*, etc. Behold, then, how this wisdom of Christians is accustomed to carry with it power and virtue, which Saint James, in the text cited before, calls "good fruits." In contrast, Saint Paul calls the philosophy of the Pagans "empty fallacy," and consequently bereaved or destitute of good fruits. From this, they seem to conclude that there is no fruitful philosophy, nor any philosopher who has borne good fruit, except that which is occupied in the true and essential wisdom: Jesus Christ. We Christians see that these things are true, and yet in this fleeting age (in which Satan seems to hold dominion), the aforementioned vain and earthly philosophy—which is darkened by deceptive confusion—is held in such high esteem in this world that Christ, who is true wisdom, is continually crucified among His philosophical worshippers because of their ignorance. He is buried in the mists or the dark abyss of that Pagan philosophy, which they seem to worship with such veneration and embrace with such remarkable fervor and devotion, following Aristotle, its inventor, as if he were another Jesus Christ descended from heaven to earth for the salvation of the people and to open the treasure of true science and wisdom to the human race. But observe, I pray, with what characters and colors the Apostle describes such vain philosophers with their contentions and sophistication: *If anyone,* he says, *teaches otherwise and does not acquiesce to the sound words of our Lord Jesus Christ, and to that which is according to godliness...*

...of teaching, he is proud, knowing nothing, but sick with questions and battles of words, from which arise envy, strife, blasphemy, evil suspicions, and the conflicts of men corrupted in mind and deprived of the truth, who think that godliness is a means of gain: From such people, separate yourself, etc. <note>original: "existimantium, quæstum esse pietatem : A talibus separa te"</note> I vehemently desire that any Christian <term>Peripatetic</term> <note>A follower of Aristotle’s philosophy, which dominated medieval and Renaissance universities.</note> who wastes his time according to the laws and customs of Aristotle in vain disputes and quibbling—and who, in his foolishness, hopes to reach the summit of philosophy through such effort—I desire and advise him, I say, to consider these matters patiently (setting aside all bias and envy) and to think seriously within himself. For there is no such custom in the Church of God—that is, the place where true philosophy dwells, in the tabernacles of true <term>Sophia</term> <note>Greek for Wisdom, often personified in this tradition as the divine architect of the world.</note>, or (if you prefer) in the house of sincere philosophy and true wisdom—as the Apostle teaches us. For this wisdom of manifold human invention is so discordant from that true, unique, and simple wisdom of God, that the infinite religious philosophies of this world have sprung up in dissent from that one true wisdom which is from God. Hence it is that there are so many different sects of that philosophy: the Peripatetic, the Stoic, the Epicurean, etc., each of which has attempted to establish and sustain its own sect through infinite disputes and litigious quibbling. This was also the cause of such great errors in the Church of God, among Christians as well as Turks and Jews: for among Christians, it was the origin of many schisms and heresies, all of which nevertheless seem to value the investigation of the one true God (who is eternal unity) and His simple wisdom.

<margin>1 Cor. 11:16</margin>

We conclude, therefore, that there are so many ways of deception in this Christian world by reason of the evasions, distinctions, and Aristotelian sophistries which, like another <term>Proteus</term> <note>A Greek sea-god capable of changing his shape at will; here used to describe how logic-choppers change the meaning of words.</note>, are accustomed to transform the subject of an argument into various and manifold meanings. They frequently strive to hide the truth behind a deceptive veil of falsehood, so that they might turn and change the truth (which is in itself naked and simple) into various appearances, as if shaping a nose out of wax <note>A common Renaissance idiom for distorting a text or truth to fit one's own desires.</note>, according to their own pleasure. Here, then, not only is truth violated, but the simple man of good will is deluded and seduced into evil instead of good. The Apostle depicts this race of enigmatic philosophers or sophists of this age (who, like boastful <term>Thrasos</term> <note>A reference to Thraso, the "Braggart Soldier" character from Roman comedy.</note>, are puffed up in their own imaginations) in these vivid colors: *In the last days,* he says, *perilous times shall*—

<margin>2 Tim. 3:1</margin>

—*approach, etc. Men shall be lovers of themselves, covetous, elated, proud, etc. Always learning and never coming to the knowledge of the Truth; but just as <term>Jannes and Mambres</term> <note>The traditional names for the Egyptian magicians who opposed Moses with their enchantments.</note> resisted Moses, so do these also resist the truth: men corrupted in mind and reprobate concerning the faith; and they shall proceed no further: for their foolishness shall be manifest to all, as theirs also was. But you have followed my doctrine,* etc. Now it is certain that his doctrine was concerned with the true philosophy, the foundation of which was Jesus Christ; the true wisdom, I say, and the Cornerstone, who sustains the entire fabric of the creature and is "all in all," and fills all things with his essential virtue, and finally works all things in all. This doctrine is indeed contrary to the intentions and "rudiments" of the <term>Ethnics</term> <note>Pagan philosophers, specifically the Greeks and Romans.</note>, who establish infinite agents in this world (as has been said), such as Angels, Demons, Stars, Elements, Meteors, Fire, Water, hot and cold, Man, beasts, Plants, minerals, and the rest—all of whom they wish to hold the place of "subordinate acting causes." For they think these things act of themselves and without the assistance of any divinity: when it is nonetheless certain, and decreed by the Sacred Page, that there is no agent besides the one <term>Universal Agent</term> <note>original: "agens Catholicum"; Fludd uses "Catholic" in its original sense of "universal."</note>, indivisible in Essence across the many and almost infinite mansions or organic vehicles of this world, who works all things in all and above all. And this doctrine of theirs has intoxicated the philosophers of the Christian world with such a poison of ignorance and error (those who firmly adhere to that sect), that they say by way of distinction: God is everywhere present *virtually* but not *substantially* or *essentially*. As if, forsooth, the virtue of God could be without His essence, as if it could be separated from His Divinity, which is indivisible! And so they seem to dream that there are "accidents" <note>In Aristotelian logic, an 'accident' is a property that can be changed or removed without changing the essence of the thing. Fludd argues God has no accidents.</note> in God which can be divided from His essence. Or at least they distinguish and say that He works all things *principally* and *mediately*—that is, as the first cause of things—and (they say) there are infinite secondary causes, as we said before, which are accustomed to work of themselves and through themselves. But if this assertion of theirs were true, I wonder how God can be said to fill all things and work all things in all; if He is only the primary or efficient cause of causes, and not the universal cause of all worldly actions, by means of His Word or Spirit, which He sent into the world? But does He not perform His will as much in heaven as on earth? What need is there for more words?

<margin>1 Cor. 8:5-6</margin>
Since the Apostle expressly teaches us: *Though there be those who are called Gods, whether in heaven or on earth (for there are many gods and many lords), yet to us there is but one God the Father, from whom are all things and we in Him, and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and we through Him.* But not in all...

...this science is in those men. This he says: By which speech of the Divine Philosopher <note>original: "Theophilosophi"</note> any wise Christian may be able to discern how opposed he is to that imaginary power and immediate action—whether of Demons and intelligences, or of the stars with their influences, or of the qualities of the elements, or of winds and other meteors, or of other creatures according to the decree of the <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle’s school of thought, who dominated the universities of the time.</note>—since they imply by his word that all acts, whether they be mediated or immediate, are from God the Father through the Son, Jesus Christ. And although creatures of this sort appear in external demonstration to act and operate by themselves and without any more internal and central agent, nevertheless that sacred philosopher of ours teaches us through the Rules of his philosophy (the basis of which is the true wisdom, Jesus Christ) that he can grasp no other truly essential acting cause besides the One from whom all things are, and the Other through whom all things are <note>A reference to the Father and the Son.</note>. He nonetheless acknowledges both of these persons to be but one in essence. For since one agent is nothing but an emanation of the other—and consequently in no way more divided from the essence of the other than a ray of the Sun is from the Sun—it is indeed no wonder if He alone, in a twofold property, operates all things in all without the Essence being changed, 
<margin>Wisdom 12:1</margin>
and this especially because He is in all things essentially (as Solomon holds). This is the firmest and truest assertion of pure philosophy. Therefore, whatever the worldly or Aristotelian philosophers say, and seem to persuade us of by fallacious subtlety, which is opposed to the axioms of true philosophy, we ought in no way to believe them. And to this matter St. Paul seems to agree with a similar thread of speech: *I marvel that you are so soon removed from him who called you into the grace of Christ unto another Gospel. There are some who trouble you, and want to pervert the Gospel 
<margin>Galatians 1:8</margin>
of Christ: but though we, or an Angel from heaven, preach any other gospel to you, let him be accursed,* etc. Therefore, since the doctrine and wisdom of Aristotle is for the most part opposed to the positions and rudiments of true wisdom and pure philosophy, it is not fitting for any pious Christian to give faith to it, insofar as (according to the opinion of St. James) it contradicts the truth and is contrary to the doctrine of the Holy Bible. Therefore, such doctrine or wisdom is said by him to be "spurious, earthly, sensual, and devilish." And hence it is that St. Paul writes these things to his disciple Timothy: *O 
<margin>1 Timothy 6:20</margin>
Timothy, keep that which is committed to thy trust, avoiding profane and vain babblings, and oppositions of science falsely so called: Which some professing have erred concerning the faith.

Grace be with thee.* By which he seems to pre-warn his disciples, so that they might not be captured or deceived by the sophistic allurements of worldly philosophy, which is indeed contradictory to the truth; nor is it peaceful, but full of wordy disturbances and vain disputations. He expressly intimates that such Philosophy must be held as a false science, and not the truth of the matter, no less than other spurious sciences which depend upon it. Furthermore, he also seems to suggest to his disciples that those Christians who profess it with excessive devotion and fervor are introduced—by its cunning and fallacious sweetness—into notable errors regarding the faith, which clings firmly to the anchor of that eternal wisdom. Furthermore, he gives 
<margin>Colossians 2:8</margin>
this same caution to his Colossian disciples in the same sense, which I cited before: *Beware* (he says) *lest any man spoil you through Philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ Jesus,* etc. By which he commands us Christians to leave behind the false Philosophy of Athens, and to embrace that true one which is according to Christ. And for this reason he says, in the same Text: *Walk in Christ, rooted and built up in him,* etc. By which he argues that Christ is the only cornerstone and basis of true Philosophy: Inasmuch as all creatures—indeed, even the whole world—have Him as the foundation for their existence and their essence (which are the subjects of Philosophy). Consequently, it is clear that the foundation of Heathen Philosophy is sandy or mythical <note>original: "fabulosa"</note> and therefore of no value, vigor, or esteem. Hence elsewhere St. Paul says: *Other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ.* But now, to show that this is opposed to the false foundations of the gentiles, the same Apostle proves it thus: *This I say, 
<margin>Ephesians 4:17-18</margin>
that ye walk not as other Gentiles walk, in the vanity of their mind, having the understanding darkened, being alienated from the life of God through the ignorance that is in them, because of the blindness of their heart,* etc. As if he were to say: Do not walk according to the vanity of the philosophy or wisdom of the nations and the Heathens, because they have their understanding obscured by darkness—that is, they are led by a false and imaginary wisdom—and consequently they are alienated from the ways of the true wisdom of Jesus Christ because of their ignorance. 

It remains now, in the next place, for us to proceed to open and unshell the particular errors and false positions of Aristotelian philosophy, so that by this way I may more clearly and brightly expose them to the judicious world by comparing the vanity and falsehood of that system with the goodness and perfection of the other.

# ON MOSAIC PHILOSOPHY. Fol. 15.

# CHAPTER VI.

->*In which the false and erroneous doctrine of the Pagan Philosophers, and especially that of the Peripatetics <note>The school of philosophy following Aristotle, named for his habit of walking while teaching.</note>, is explained; where it is also proven, for certain reasons, that it is built upon the foundations of the wisdom of this world and not upon those of the wisdom descending from God.*<-

---

I hear some of the sharper-witted Aristotelians already now (so it seems to me) replying and saying: How can this wordy man prove that the wisdom which is the foundation of Peripatetic philosophy is not "from above"—that is, from God, who is the Father of Light?

<margin>1 Cor. 1:20. 1 Cor. 3:19.</margin> To discuss this objection, it is necessary that we compare those two wisdoms proposed by the Apostle against each other. First, St. Paul says: *God has made the wisdom of this world foolish.* And elsewhere: *The wisdom of this world is foolishness with God: for God knows the thoughts of the wise, that they are vain.*

<margin>1 Cor. 2:12.</margin> And for this reason, the Apostle says elsewhere: *We have received not the spirit of this world, but the spirit which is of God, and we speak the things that are given to us by God, not in the learned words of human wisdom, but in the doctrine of the spirit, comparing spiritual things with spiritual.* For the natural man <note>original: "Animalis enim homo"; referring to a person guided by their own soul and senses rather than by divine inspiration.</note> does not perceive those things which are of the Spirit of God: for they are foolishness to him, and he cannot understand them, etc.

Having well weighed these words of the Apostle, we must first inquire whether Aristotle was a "natural man" or not. If indeed he is found to be such, what is to be expected from him except worldly wisdom, along with a philosophy such as St. James calls "natural, earthly, and demonic," which in itself is nothing but sheer foolishness?

<margin>Coloss. 2:8, 9.</margin> Since the natural man (to use his words) does not perceive those things which are of the spirit of God—for they are foolishness to him—the Apostle therefore commands us to beware of this kind of philosophy, since it is founded upon the traditions of men and the elements of this world, and not upon Christ. Indeed, he explains Greek wisdom more directly thus, and distinguishes it from that of the Jews and Christians:

<margin>1 Cor. 1:22.</margin> *The Greeks seek wisdom; the Jews seek signs; but we preach Christ crucified,* etc. By these words he argues that the Greeks seek worldly wisdom, which consists chiefly in speculation or contemplation; whereas that of the Jews is occupied in practice—namely, in signs and visual demonstrations—without which they are unwilling to believe. But finally, he names a third Wisdom, namely the true one: Jesus Christ, in whom dwelt the fullness of the Godhead bodily.

<margin>Coloss. 2:9. 1 Cor. 3:11.</margin> And this is that real and sincere wisdom from above, from the Father of Light, which is to be sought with all diligence by Christians; for upon this, every true Philosopher ought to place the foundation of his Philosophy, according to this word of the Apostle: *No one can lay any other foundation*

<column-break/>

*besides that which is laid, which is Christ Jesus.* If, however, the sophists of this age reply that perhaps Aristotle arrived at a knowledge of Christ in some way, or at least looked upon the wisdom of Moses and the Prophets even if from afar, I respond to them: just as the age of Aristotle preceded the incarnation of the Word, so it is also made manifest that he understood little or nothing at all of the Mosaic doctrine—which consists in the creation and ordering of the world through the <term>spagyric</term> <note>An alchemical term referring to the process of separation and recombination; here it describes God "distilling" the world out of chaos.</note> act of the divine word—inasmuch as he taught in his writings that the world had existed from eternity.

I confess that Plato, who was his teacher, was more engaged in the subject of true wisdom, as it is permitted to gather from his writings. But his disciple Aristotle, puffed up with vain glory, through a certain monstrous deviation from the Stoic or Platonic discipline and desiring solely to claim the name of "The Wise One" in the world for himself, named a new wisdom or worldly Philosophy which he afterwards called "Peripatetic" (distinguishing it from others and trumpeting that he was its leader). And so, inflated by a remarkable <term>Philautia</term> <note>Self-love or egoism.</note>, he defiled the truth with infinite fictions and falsehoods produced by his own imagination or concept.

Hence Aristotelian Philosophy arose from both evil and good—or rather, I say, it was forged from false and true, from a little wisdom and a great deal of foolishness. By contrast, pure and simple wisdom is constituted from truth alone, being ordered by the spirit of God alone. Furthermore, if the Peripatetic, Stoic, or Epicurean doctrine had been perfect and according to the institutions of the true wisdom of Jesus Christ, why did those false wise men of Athens <margin>Acts 17.</margin> persecute that true and sacred philosopher, St. Paul, with such hatred when he preached the true wisdom of Jesus Christ to them?

From these things, therefore, it is permitted to gather what kind of wisdom it is upon which Aristotle built his Philosophy: namely, one discovered and handed down from himself, and consequently worldly and human, and not that sincere wisdom which is from God. But to approach the core of the matter more closely: I will compare both wisdoms proposed by the Apostle James with each other, so that you may understand which of them is more worthy and more to be embraced by pious men.

<margin>James 3:15.</margin> James says: *Wisdom that contradicts the truth is not from the Father of Light, nor is it peaceful, nor modest, but is earthly, natural, and demonic.* But Aristotelian wisdom and philosophy is of this sort, for it is litigious and prone to dispute—

He contrasts this with "true wisdom" found in Christ, asserting that Greek philosophy is fundamentally unspiritual and unable to grasp divine truths.</summary>

<header>SECTION I, BOOK II.</header>

of disputes, fallacies, quibbles, and controversies: all of which properties are opposed to the nature and condition of true <margin>2 Timothy 2:23.</margin> wisdom. Hence it was that Timothy was warned by his teacher Paul to separate himself from the company of those who teach a doctrine differing from true wisdom: affirming that those who do so are puffed up with pride and know nothing, but are obsessed with vain questions and wordy contentions, from which arise strife, and so on. But such is the doctrine and philosophy of the **Aristotelian Christians**, as it is their habit and custom to always be occupied with questions, disputes, and quibbles. And this is the reason (as has been said) for such a great "equivocation" <note>The use of ambiguous language to conceal the truth.</note> and a multitude of distinctions, which pave the way for sustaining and defending falsehoods just as much as truths. From this there have arisen among men not only the sects of Philosophers (as we declared above), but even sects of Religions and opinions, from which come disputes and litigious contentions—not only in the schools of the Academies, but even among the different factions of the common people regarding religion. But truly, if their philosophy or wisdom were built upon **Jesus Christ**, the unique **Cornerstone** (who, as he is all in all, is indeed a single and simple essence), then without a doubt both learned scholars and men of humbler or lesser condition would agree in a single unity with Him, who is but one and the same in us all. For in Him and through Him we are made brothers, and even heirs with Him of the eternal kingdom. And again, in Him "we live, move, and have our being" (as St. Paul testifies). We ought <margin>Acts 17.</margin> to know, without any question or dispute, that highest good within ourselves, which the true wise men of every age have sought with such diligence and craved with the "appetite of Tantalus" <note>A mythological reference to Tantalus, who was forever hungry and thirsty but could never reach the food and water just out of reach; used here to describe an intense, unquenchable longing.</note>. Does not Christian philosophy teach us that the kingdom of God <margin>Luke 17:21. 1 Corinthians 6:19.</margin> is within us? And that the worker of all wonders is within us? And that we are the Temple of God and the Holy Spirit? And that we are members of Christ? Since this is so, why should contentions, disputes, and vain quibbles arise among us concerning the ambiguities of many-shaped questions and words? Or why should we corrupt and disturb our more mature senses with dull distinctions? By departing from Unity, we fall away into human inventions and the foolish and **Diabolical wisdom** of this world: for in doing so, do we not plunge ourselves into the abyss of the "multitude," or the pit of ignorance? For the sole and unique effort of truth is to lead us on the right path through the dark clouds of error (in which the foolish wisdom of this world and the philosophy founded upon it miserably involve our intellects) to the fount of unity and harmony, which is eternal wisdom. From this, therefore, we see

<column-break/>

how contrary the wisdom of the Greeks is to that of the Apostles. Thus it is that St. Paul seems to warn his disciple Timothy to avoid profane and vain babblings and the "opposition of sciences falsely so-called": which some, while professing, have erred <margin>1 Timothy 6:20.</margin> concerning the faith. Therefore, all Christians who have their anchor of faith fixed too firmly to Aristotelian philosophy ought to seriously ponder within themselves what their preeminent teacher St. Paul seems to forewarn them with such fervor and zeal: that the over-diligent observation of Ethnic <note>Pagan or non-Christian.</note> philosophy (which consists in strife, questions or doubts, vain wordiness, and the opposition of sciences) is the reason why zealous Christians without understanding are deceived and have erred regarding the faith in true wisdom, as the Apostle testifies.

Furthermore, the Apostle says: *Wisdom <margin>James 3.</margin> contradicting the truth is not from above, but is earthly, sensual, and Diabolical*, etc. <note>original: "animalis & Diabolica"; 'animalis' refers to the 'soulish' or 'natural' man as opposed to the spiritual.</note> Now truly, I am certain that any faithful Christian will strenuously defend and maintain that the Holy Bible is the very fount of truth itself. Since this is so, what will the Aristotelian Christians answer if I plainly and expressly prove that the Aristotelian doctrine is contrary and contradictory to the solid sense and mind of the Sacred Scriptures? It is common among elegant Sophists <note>Here used to mean those who use clever but fallacious arguments.</note> to assert, when some contradiction is found between Greek philosophy and a sacred assertion, that "it is true according to philosophy, but in the Scriptures it is found far otherwise." To them I reply: if any difference is found in the contents of one or the other discipline, there is without doubt a great error to be found in one of them, and consequently one is contradictory to the other. It follows, therefore, that only one of these doctrines must have its origin in earthly and worldly wisdom. Now, I would wish that every pious Christian weigh with diligence whether it is more fitting to adhere to the Word of God, which is the ultimate truth, or to the affirmations and assertions of the Aristotelians, who derived their wisdom from the "father of lies." Others say that men immerse themselves so deeply in the secrets of nature or natural philosophy that they turn from Christians into **Atheists**, as those who (as they say) wish to acknowledge no divinity. We must believe that they understand this of Greek philosophy and not of the philosophy of Jesus Christ; for the latter directs and leads the intellectual spirit of man to the Throne and seat of divine majesty, and constantly persuades him to avoid and leave behind the wretched "multitude" of this world, so that he may be drawn toward that blessed union from which the essence of his spirit was originally extracted. A third kind of men seem to be troubled in mind and take it badly that any philosopher should have a discourse concerning divinity; indeed, they believe it is in...

# SECTION I, BOOK II.

It is a wonder that some of our Academics <note>Scholars or university students.</note>, having been devoted to <term>Peripatetic philosophy</term> <note>The philosophy of Aristotle and his followers, so named because they allegedly taught while walking (peripatētikos).</note> for a space of seven years or more, are so corrupted by its false principles and understand so little of the essential nature of Divinity within creatures, that when they are promoted (after that time has expired) to a higher function or profession—namely, Theology—they are rendered most hostile to those who recognize the mystery of divinity within created things. And although they notice that the Scriptures, in many places, describe the Word of God or the incorruptible Spirit, they nevertheless assert—using Academic distinctions which they receive from plainly pagan philosophers and their agile, obedient commentators—such "clouds of equivocation" around the naked and simple truth, that they drown it in a deeper abyss of doubt and ambiguity than it was in before.

For example: while the entire harmony of the divine Bible is that God is in all and over all, and that the Holy Spirit of discipline is in every thing, some of them immediately respond by making a distinction (as declared above): that He is in all things <term>virtually</term> <note>original: "virtualiter"; meaning by His power or effect, but not by His presence.</note>, but not <term>essentially</term> <note>original: "essentialiter"; meaning by His actual being or substance.</note>. As if, indeed, His power could be distinguished from His essence! Again: where it is said that God works all things in all, they say: "It is true, insofar as He is the principal and primary cause; but," they say, "there are many secondary and subordinate agents which act by themselves and in themselves without the first cause of things—such as Angels, Stars, Elements, Meteors, and composite creatures, etc." 

And so, with Aristotelian sophistications of this kind, they attempt to stain the truth of the matter testified by the Scriptures—which say in simple and plain speech that God works all things in all. For if God, with, in, and through His essential Spirit, fills all things, we must believe that this Spirit works all things in all and in every creature which it immediately fills; and this without any assistance from the creature, since the creature has nothing that it has not received from the Creator. Moreover, what it has received from God cannot be separated from God. For how is it possible that a created "instrument" could, by any act of its own, help its Creator, who fills it and acts and works in it only what and when He wills? 

<margin>Isaiah 44:24.</margin>
The prophet says: *I am the Lord, making all things alone, and none is with me.* Nor does this seem foreign to anyone when the Scriptures themselves testify that He is all in all. And again (as before): *The incorruptible Spirit of God is in every thing.* 
<margin>1 Corinthians 15:25. Wisdom 12:1.</margin>
And the same elsewhere: *In Christ all things are founded through Christ, and in Christ all things are created; all things consist in Him, and He holds the preeminence in all things,* etc. 
<margin>Colossians 1:16.</margin>
He does not mean that this presence of God is <term>by accident</term> <note>A philosophical term meaning a non-essential or temporary quality.</note>, but essentially. Since this is so, it follows that this distinction—along with all others of the same grain—is false when it says God works mediately [through others] but not

<column-break/>

immediately; and consequently, it is false that a creature can act by itself or immediately without the assistance of a divine act. It is as if someone were to say that the divine essence or power could be divisible, or that the divine nature must therefore be partible and separable from the divine root because it is in different "instruments" [organs]. 

I can therefore boldly conclude and make known to all: if Christian scholastics spent those seven years (which they waste in pursuing the discipline of Aristotelian philosophy) in learning the knowledge and doctrine of the true and sacred [philosophy], they would undoubtedly not have wished to err so monstrously in the manner of the pagans. Nor would they, at the end of that time, so monstrously attack the precepts and laws of true wisdom with so many questions, disputes, contradictions, and brawls. Instead, they would be rendered more fit or prepared to proceed in the strict and direct way of seeking and acquiring that **mystic wisdom** which God (according to the Apostle) has revealed and ordained to be revealed in its own time to the elect and those best deserving of God. Thus, at the end of that holy inquiry, following the examples of the Apostles and holy men, they might become as powerful in virtue and power as they currently seem to be influential in this world in their common state—which consists of words alone, without any evident essential effect. 

For they are deprived of that good fruit which usually accompanies true wisdom by the erroneous doctrine of their seductive master [Aristotle]. But lest our Aristotelian Academics believe my words are vain, or publish or reply that this Peripatetic doctrine can bring them greater fruit and utility than any other drawn from the Sacred Text: let me first enumerate in this place those fruits which our **Sacred Philosophy** can confer upon the world. Then, afterwards, let these worldly philosophers see if they are able to extract such real and essential utility from the Aristotelian text. If not, I would have them be silent, and concede the praise and honor to the more worthy wisdom, and relegate the inferior kind to eternal exile from the memory of men. That is to say, let them follow the better Philosophy with the greatest diligence and embrace it with solemn Christian veneration. 

Regarding the fruit, utility, virtue, and power which a wise philosopher can draw from his true philosophy or essential wisdom, we gather these from the sacred context:

# BOOK II OF THE FIRST SECTION

Whether they agree or not. All the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle's philosophy</note> agree on this: namely, that winds, lightning, thunder, comets, clouds, and other meteors of this kind are formed by the attractive power of the sun and other stars; they say that by means of this power, vapors and exhalations are attracted and raised from the Earth and waters into the upper regions of the air. <margin>Velcurio, *Commentary on Physics*, Book 3, Chapter 5.</margin> Hence Velcurio, following the mind and opinion of Aristotle's *Physics* (of which he was a commentator), says: "According as vapors are more or less hot, so they are raised higher or lower by the heat of the sun and other stars, just as we see the sun drinking and attracting water, etc."

But I shall demonstrate that the matter is far otherwise, and I will ensure that anyone endowed with human sense may most easily discern with open eyes that the heat or power of neither the sun, nor the stars, nor fire, nor any living creature has the faculty of attracting anything to itself, but rather of pushing and driving things away from itself. For example: if it were in the power of fire to attract vapors to itself, then it would not permit the smoke of wood and earth-coals to depart so lightly from its embrace. But experience testifies to the contrary: for by it we are taught that the entire office of fire is to rarefy <note>To make less dense</note> the dense subjects of vapors and exhalations, and to render them subtle by penetrating and dividing and expanding their compact parts—not so that it attracts the vapors and smoke thus produced to itself in any way. For we see with our eyes that it drives away those things created by its own action and dissipates them through the expanded spirit of the world.

Also, if we place a linen cloth moistened with water near a fire, we will perceive indeed that the watery substance in it is converted into a smoky vapor by the power of the fire. But truly, that smoke is so far from being attracted by the fire that we observe it being expanded and dissipated everywhere through the cavity of the place without any evident attraction by the fire. It happens in a plainly similar way in the operative nature of the sun: for by its own heat, it thins or rarefies water and moist things and any thick or coarse and combustible substance, and by rarefying them, it expands them. Moreover, that a moist thing reduced to vapor tends upward does not happen from any attractive faculty in the sun and stars, but from 그 natural appetite and inclination by which light things are accustomed to be elevated on high. Therefore it follows that water thinned into vapor, or any solid or oily thing reduced to smoke or exhalation, ascends to the place destined for it by Nature not by any compulsion of an external agent, but spontaneously and by itself; just as, conversely, that which is heavy and weighty makes its motion downward out of its own inclination.

But so that their error may shine forth even more clearly—those who establish the attraction of vapors and exhalations from the earth and sea into the upper regions by solar attraction—I shall refer you to the experience of our experimental instrument, or weather-glass <note>original: *vitri calendari*; an early thermoscope or barometer-like device</note>, by which you will find through ocular intuition that all attraction from the circumference to the center (which is properly called attraction) is produced by cold and not by heat. For we see that by the power of cold, the water enclosed in the glass is elevated upward into the neck of the vessel, and that this happens in the thickening of the air and its reduction into a narrower space of the glass. But on the other hand, we observe that if the sun or fire or a man's hand touches the top of the glass and heats it, then the enclosed air will expand and suddenly fly away from the action of the heat; indeed, it is so far from the air being attracted by heat, that it precipitates and depresses the water (previously attracted by the congealing and thickening faculty of cold) downward by several degrees.

Since this is so, I wish the Christian Peripatetics would consider and diligently notice how poorly they have learned the discipline of their master, which they follow so sacredly and with such affection to this day; let them gather in a few words how immensely and in what a gross manner he erred in the principal argument of his *Meteorology*. What further, then, is to be expected from him, except that his whole fabric should collapse of itself in the eyes of the wise? Briefly I say, that this and many other of his palpable errors are the reason why various disciples of a sounder mind dissent from his spirit and opinion in very many things: namely, in his opinion on the origin of winds, thunder, springs, and other meteors.

For Johannes Fregius, a learned man and very well-versed in the discipline of Aristotle, who gave no small effort to inquiring into the mysteries of nature according to the teaching of the Peripatetics (as appears from the contents of the large volume published by him titled *Physical Questions*), writes these things in that same volume: <margin>Fregius, Book 2, *On the Cause of Winds*.</margin> "Although," he says, "the whole dispute concerning winds, as concerning other meteors, is full of the wonderful works of God, for which no firm and sufficient causes in nature can be brought forward, yet it is profitable to see how far human reason can proceed. The Sacred Scriptures indeed say that God produces the winds from his treasures, whence we hear their blasts, but whence they come or whither they go we know not." Thus he speaks.

<margin>*Margarita Philosophica*, Book 9, Chapter 20.</margin> On the other hand, the *Margarita Philosophica* <note>A famous encyclopedia of the late 15th century</note> (a work indeed of great fame and estimation even among the Peripatetics themselves in respect to that Aristotelian juice which it contains), after a strict inquiry made by it into the nature of lightning and thunder according to the norm of the Peripatetics: and since it was in no way content or satisfied with the reasons brought forward by Aristotle concerning the rise of thunder and lightning, because of their defect and weakness in finding the mystery of such a great miracle in nature; it was compelled to look back to the book of true wisdom to explain this secret, from which indeed Solomon confesses that he [knew] the force of the winds and the change [of seasons...]

It was not for nothing that Aristotle was called *Cacodæmon* <note>original: "Cacodæmon," from the Greek for "evil spirit."</note> by the Greeks, as if he were a malignant and seductive spirit. Indeed, with his subtle inventions and sophistries, he deceived the world, not only in that age but also in the ages that followed, and led it away from the path of truth through the paths of error and ignorance, like a sort of *ignis fatuus* <note>A "will-o'-the-wisp" or deceptive light.</note>. For this sophist, using fallacious reasons disguised with the appearance of probability and truth, imagines those things to be accidents and born of Fortune or Chance, which in reality are from above and, consequently, are essentially and divinely produced by the Holy Spirit. Also, according to his own doctrine, the heaven, the earth, the stars, and the elements were from eternity and not created; and he seems to support this assertion of his with reasons drawn from the quiver of his fictitious philosophy and with inventions prompted by his own brain: saying that "from nothing, nothing is made" <note>original: "ex nihilo nihil fiat," a fundamental principle of ancient Greek philosophy that contradicted the Christian doctrine of creation out of nothing.</note>. Regarding the first matter and the form of natural things, he makes mention of their internal essences entirely according to his own perception; although he is ignorant of the causes of snow, frost, ice, hail, rain, clouds, mists, lightning, etc., he attempts to teach us quite irrationally and by conjecture alone, saying that they are generated in an adventitious manner <note>Coming from outside or by chance rather than from an inherent divine purpose.</note> from vapors and exhalations drawn upward from the earth and water by the heat of the Sun and Stars, attracted into the middle region of the air, condensed by the accidental cold of that place, and reduced into such forms as they have. # SECTION ONE, BOOK III.
# The third book of Mosaic Philosophy, in which the principles of true Philosophy are explained.

### Argument of the book.

In the present book, the author treats generally the true and essential principles of divine philosophy, and expresses in detail how inconstant and differing the Ethnic <note>Heathen or Pagan</note> philosophers were in their opinions regarding the principles of all things. Here he also proves that the most excellent of the Greek Philosophers or Naturalists received the foundations or principles of their philosophy from the true and sacred philosopher Moses in a surreptitious <note>stolen or secretive</note> manner. His philosophy was impressed or outlined by the finger of God, inasmuch as its fiery characters were, as it were, sculpted and depicted in the dark *hyle* <note>original: "hyla"; the primordial matter or "stuff" of the universe</note> through the divine word or eternal wisdom. At the same time, he shows that although these Athenian philosophers usurped these principles of Moses to establish their own philosophy and claimed them almost for themselves—and to cover such a monstrous robbery from the world, imposed new names upon them—nevertheless, because they could neither penetrate nor reach the profound and central understanding of them, nor rightly conceive and apprehend the mystery of the holy wisdom or the Word with mature judgment, they therefore erected nothing but an adulterated structure or philosophy upon those poorly understood foundations. This was surely a vain and fallacious worldly wisdom, which is not hewn from the essential crag or rock of truth and virtue, nor rests upon Christ the only Cornerstone, but proceeds from the tradition of men and is fashioned according to the Elements of this world. It is no different than if we saw a citadel built of straw upon a rock, exposed on all sides to the winds and tossed by every whirlwind and storm. After this, the author explains the true Mosaic principles, which are Darkness, Waters, and Light. Then he teaches that all fullness and emptiness consist in the presence or absence of the lucid and formal Spirit of God. And finally, how two active properties, namely Cold and Heat, arise immediately from the aforesaid principles (namely Darkness and Light), just as on the opposite side two passive natures of the world, namely Moisture and Dryness, seem to claim their origins from the said two actives.

For example, Thales of Miletus, who was held in the number of the seven sages of the Greeks, thought that the waters were the beginning of all things. But Anaximenes with his disciples said that the infinite air was the first cause or source of all. And for this same reason Anaximander thought that this Universal Air was God. And on another side, Zoroaster wishes all things to have their origin from fire and light; as also do the Pythagoreans themselves, who affirm that there is a universal fire in all and above all. And certainly, each of these opinions, if considered rightly and in the proper manner, will be seen to approach the Mosaic truth: For by the power and presence of the Divine fire or light emerging from the depth of the dark abyss, the invisible waters were revealed and manifested, the more subtle portion of which was turned into the vast spirit of the air. ## CHAPTER II.

->*What the Mosaic Principles were—that is, the beginnings of all things: How they were extracted and produced out of nothing. Then, what is understood by this term NOTHING: And finally, the potential Principle, which is the dark abyss or unformed Chaos, is quite effectively described in this place.*<-

---

**T**he <term>Mosaic Principles<note>The fundamental physical and spiritual laws of the universe as derived from the account of creation in the Book of Genesis, traditionally attributed to Moses.</note></term> are plain and evident to those who wisely contemplate the words of the most excellent philosopher, Moses, expressed in the first chapter of Genesis. For before any mention was made of that <term>spagyric<note>A term used in alchemy (often associated with Paracelsus) meaning to separate and then recombine; here it refers to God "filtering" or "separating" the elements of the world out of chaos.</note></term> separation—which was performed by the power of the Word of God or the Spirit of that divine <note>original: "Elohim," a Hebrew name for God.</note> Elohim in the work of the six days of creation—it is said that darkness was over the face of the abyss, and that the earth was without form and void. From these words, it is clear that heaven and earth had not yet been brought into act or essential form, but remained a single unformed thing—that is, a rude, unique, and undigested mass. And thus all things were <note>original: "complicitè," meaning "enfolded" or "folded together."</note> complicitly contained in a single dark abyss, which was indeed as of yet <note>original: "explicitè," meaning "unfolded" or "manifestly."</note> explicitly nothing. 

For example: we see that a great tree, with its root, body, branches, leaves, and fruit, is complicitly contained within a kernel or seed; yet explicitly, we find no such thing there, except in the imagination alone. St. Augustine compares that Mosaic NOTHING (or the "unformed thing") to a "potential speech" which, while it exists only in the mind of the speaker, appears to the listener as nothing—that is, it exists in potentiality alone, but is nothing in act. But when that speech is uttered by a living voice, then that which was previously enfolded in the mind of the speaker is now explicitly apprehended by the listener. Plato compares that state of "Nullity" to a vision in a dream, which, when a man is awakened from sleep, appears as nothing besides the imagination. 

But, because this phrase, *God created all things out of Nothing*, has disturbed the minds of many even most learned men, and has caused them to hesitate quite a bit in understanding its twofold sense, I have proposed to say a few things about "Nothing" itself, and to briefly explain my own opinion on the matter in this place.

The <note>original: "Peripateticorum Princeps," referring to Aristotle.</note> Prince of the Peripatetics says: *From Nothing, nothing is made.* <note>original: "Ex Nihilo nihil fit."</note> This is indeed a learned sentiment and an infallible axiom for a person endowed with such great erudition, provided the meaning of the word "Nothing" is always understood and interpreted in one and the same way. However, I— 

<column-break/>

—resting upon good and secure pillars, assert that if some, led either by presumption or a certain ignorance, fall into the opinion that in these words—*God created all things out of Nothing*—the word NOTHING must be taken for a "negative nothing" or an "absolute nothing" (that which does not fall under the intellect or the capacity of human reason), I now inform them that such a species of "Nothing" was never understood to be the first matter of creation, nor was it at any time accepted by Wisdom. For it is apparent, both by the infallible sense of the Holy Bible and by the sincere light of Nature, that the matter of all things remained as one and the same from eternity in God and with God. And this I shall prove from the divine source as follows:

<margin>Gen. 1.</margin> 
Moses says: *In the Beginning God created the heaven and the earth.* In this sentence, "Beginning" is not to be taken for a negative "Nothing." 

<margin>Rom. 11:36.</margin> 
For the Scriptures teach us in sufficiently clear words that *from him, and through him, and in him are all things.* Therefore, if all things proceed from God the Creator, who is the sum of all Entities, it follows that the matter of heaven and earth—and even the Light that gives form to all things—does not proceed from a "Negative Nothing." 

Again, the Wise Man says: *Almighty Lord, your hand created the orb of the lands* (or as Jerome has it, *the world*) *from unformed matter* 

<margin>Wisdom 11:18.</margin> 
as Tremellius interprets it, or as Jerome explains, *from invisible matter and without form.* Therefore it follows that it was not an absolute "nothing" from which the world was created. 

<margin>Hebr. 11:3.</margin> 
Also the Scriptures say elsewhere: *Through faith we understand that the worlds were framed by the word of God, so that from things invisible* [the visible] *were made,* and consequently not from an absolute "Nothing." Furthermore, if God had not produced and created all things essentially out of himself, but out of a mere and vain negative "nothing," then creation would not belong to God, nor could it be rightly referred to him. That is: if all things had not been essentially in him, and had not received their beginning from him, then it would truly follow that all things were not made by him, but [had] their [own] essence...

# BOOK III OF THE FIRST SECTION.

## CHAPTER III.

### *Concerning the fruit or material principle which, through the presence of the divine spirit, was brought forth from the dark depths of the abyss or the womb of Chaos into the creation of the world; and how the substantial machine of the world was fabricated from it.*

**A**ll things, therefore, in the beginning were contained in an enfolded way <note>Latin: *complicitè*, a philosophical term meaning everything was "folded together" or implicit within God's power</note> within the divine power (as has been demonstrated). In respect to human capacity, this state was formless, empty, and void, insofar as it was contained in one formless and invisible mass of waters. For this reason, it was often called the Mother of Elements and the seed of all things. Just as we see that an entire plant or tree is included within a small, shapeless seed or kernel, and can in no way be grasped by human reason or sense before it explicitly appears from the surface of the earth; so also the primordial water was invisible and without shape or figure, as it was veiled by shapeless darkness. For darkness was upon the face of the abyss, which was called the Prime Matter <note>Latin: *Materia prima*</note>, which possessed no formal act <note>meaning no defined shape or active existence</note> within itself to be considered by human perception; for this reason, it was said to have existed in potential alone. 

Thus, a certain profound philosopher, well-versed in the mystical works of creation, speaks these words: "The Prime Matter, from which the waters went forth, was Nothing, from which the matter of the waters was extracted." But this should not be understood according to human intellect or sense—namely, that God created the waters from a literal void—and yet those words are correctly brought forth from the Scriptures, since in the beginning "Nothing" was visible. But if the wise wish to raise their minds above common understanding to find the origin of the waters through proper contemplation, then they would certainly refuse to deny that before the creation of the waters, there was a certain matter in the supreme mystery—either in the divine power or in the dark and formless abyss—which was the catholic <note>meaning universal</note> or universal treasury-chest of God, from which the waters flowed in creation. And this is confirmed by many passages in the Bibles of the Hebrews. For the 

<margin>Hebrews 11:3</margin>
Apostle Paul, in the place cited before, says: "By faith we understand that the worlds were framed by the word of God, so that from things invisible, things visible were made." From this, it is clear that things which were visible were originally made from things invisible. It is manifest from these points that things which fall under human sense did not appear to the senses primordially, and consequently were estimated in our judgment as if they did not exist. Again, 

<margin>1 Corinthians 1:28</margin>
he says elsewhere: "God chose those things which are not, to destroy those things which are." Hence also that distinguished Kabbalist, Reuchlin, says according to 

<column-break/>

<margin>Reuchlin, *On the Art of the Kabbalah*, Book 1.</margin>
the consensus of others: "It is written," he says, "in the book *Bahir*: 'Nothing is the principle, except wisdom,' and this is the very infinity of the three highest numerations of the Kabbalistic tree, which you have been accustomed to call the three Persons in the divine. This is the most absolute Essence, which, since it is retracted within the abyss of darkness, immanent and at rest, or (as they say) looking toward nothing, is called <term>Ayin</term> <note>original Hebrew: אַיִן</note>, that is, 'Nothing,' or 'Non-Being' and 'No-End' <note>referring to the *Ein Sof*</note>. This is because we, being punished by such a thin poverty of genius toward divine things, judge concerning those things which do not appear just as we judge those things which do not exist. But when that Essence shows itself, so that it is something and truly subsists, then the Dark Aleph <note>the first letter of the Hebrew alphabet, here symbolizing the first movement of creation</note> is converted into the Light Aleph. For it is written: 'As is its darkness, so is its light.'" Thus he speaks.

It is clear, therefore, that although darkness and invisibility appear to our senses to be Nothing in respect to those things which we see by means of light, they are nonetheless all real and Essential before God. Therefore, that NOTHING, or formless vacuum in respect to our weakness and capacity—from which the Waters (which are the material principle of all things) were imaginarily extracted—is seen as a material existence to Him in whose divine power they were reserved. For nothing can be in God which 

<margin>Romans 11:36</margin>
is not an essential reality or something existing, as we are taught by the sacred text: "From Him, through Him, and in Him are all things." Therefore, both the dark matrix of things (the formless womb of the waters) and the watery infant (the moist Nature) which gradually gushed forth from the dark Abyss or formless Chaos by the power of the word or the Spirit of ELOHIM <note>The Hebrew name for God, used here to emphasize the creative power</note>, were really in God before they appeared. That is, they remained in the power of the Almighty and existed in the disposition of His will, no differently than how the number of all things to be built was first in the mind of the Builder. Moreover, that the world was first created from matter of this kind without form is testified by these words of the wise man reported before:

<margin>Wisdom 11:18</margin>
"Almighty, your hand created the world from formless matter" (according to the translation of Tremellius); or (as Jerome interprets it) "from unseen matter." Therefore, it stands clearly enough that the word "Nothing" was taken to mean formless matter, and consequently it was without name and essence, since form is what usually gives a thing its name and being. Or

Now, in truth, the text of my Master Moses seems to clearly confirm that this general matter was the Waters, which the presence of the spirit of Elohim <note>Hebrew: *God*</note> informed in a general way and brought into active being by bestowing the name *Shamaim* <note>Hebrew: *Shamayim*, meaning the Heavens</note> upon them; and that they were the primordial material principle from which the existence of the world was shaped, no differently than a house is fashioned from a rough and formless mass of clay. First, he makes mention of the waters over which the Spirit of the Lord was carried, and this immediately after the naming of the dark abyss and the empty and void Earth; and this especially before any creature was explicitly formed, and before the Spagyric <note>A term from alchemy referring to the divine process of separating, purifying, and recombining elements</note> separation of the first Day had been made. By this, it is clearly argued that the waters were the material Principle of all things, since they were informed or actuated by the Spirit of Elohim: for by the proper name of "Waters" they were infinite before the work of the first Day. Second, it was that same spirit of Elohim which, acting as a kind of midwife, caused that deformed womb to give forth or bring out its offspring, and imparted to it form, action, and life. Again, from the same Chapter of Moses we learn that the waters were the subject of all those separations which were effected in the time of creation by the spagyric or fiery power of that same Spirit or Word of God. Third, that the heavens, which were arranged in the higher region of the world, were composed of the purer, clearer, and more worthy portion of the Waters; while the lower Elemental region was fashioned from their coarser, thicker, darker, and viler substance: and that there was a certain intermediate consistency of theirs marked by the name of Firmament, participating in both extremes, whose office was to divide the subtler or higher portion from the coarser or lower. Then the lowest portion of the Waters

<column-break/>

(which I, not without reason, call the Universal Element <note>Latin: *Elementum Catholicum*</note>) is distinguished into other spheres or orbs, which the learned of the world call by the name of "elements," when in truth they are nothing other than an alteration of the four-fold Universal Element—or the lower waters—made by the various-formed breath of the Divine Spirit, as will be discussed more widely below. We see therefore from the preceding points how the Spirit of Elohim fabricated the entire structure of the world out of that moist nature or Waters. 
<margin>2 Peter 3:5</margin> 
This is also clearly proved from these words of the Apostle: *the heavens*, he says, *existed long ago, and the earth standing out of the water and through the water by the Word of God* etc. But the world is composed solely of heaven and earth; wherefore it follows that the whole world, in respect to its matter, is made of water and through water, but as for its form or essence, it holds this from the Word of God or the Spirit of Elohim, who (as Augustine says) imparted a fiery power or vigor to the waters. Now, since the stars are estimated to be nothing but denser portions of their own orbs, and also since every creature of the Elemental kingdom is composed of elemental matter, it must necessarily follow that both the stars of the firmament and the creatures of the lower world—whether they be meteorological phenomena or of a more perfect mixture, such as Animals, Vegetables, and Minerals—have their existence from the waters. Just as they were brought forth into the light by the mediation of the word of God, so also they consist eternally, and are sustained and preserved in their essence and existence by the eternal word or Spirit of Elohim, just as will be clearly explained to you in the following chapter.

I come now to the description of that Universal principle, whose role is to give life and being not only to every portion of the waters in general, but also to every creature fashioned from them.

We conclude, therefore, that this spirit sent forth from God is the unique essential, primary, and even the final agent in the world: for it is the **Alpha and Omega**, the active principle, the central act of the world-soul <note>original: "anima mundana"; the idea that the world itself is a living being animated by a divine soul</note>, the cornerstone of all creatures, animating, sustaining, and preserving their structures: nor do I know any other essential nature in this my sacred philosophy, besides only that Creator in the creature, or the sacrosanct world-builder in His works, to speak with the Apostle and Solomon: And in this way we have the formal principle of all created things described clearly and graphically enough for the reach of my meager wit, according to worldly reason.

# BOOK III OF THE FIRST SECTION.

# CHAPTER V.

->*On the Full and the Empty: what true Fullness and Emptiness are, and*<-
->*by what reasoning the Heathen Philosophers erred in their*<-
->*inquiry concerning them.*<-

Now that the natures of the two constituent and component principles have been explained—the first being the source of the existence of things, the other the origin of their formal Essence—it is necessary that we understand the properties of the Full and the Empty in the next order, according to true and Christian Philosophy. But before I immerse myself into the heart of this explanation, I must first compare the opinions of the Heathen <note>original: "Ethnicorum"; referring to pre-Christian Greek and Roman philosophers like Aristotle</note> philosophers on this subject with those of the Christian Theo-philosophers. As you have seen from the preceding chapters, there is one principle regarding the material existence of things, which we called the Waters; and another regarding their formal essences. Likewise, we find two opinions concerning the Full and the Empty. The first is that of the Heathens, who believe that all Fullness and Emptiness must be defined in respect to matter or substance which fills the cavity of the world. Therefore, they call that "empty" which is not filled by some material existence. Consequently, where there is nothing of the existence of the waters, they conclude there is a vacuum. Thus, they claim that neither a jar nor a well is truly empty, even if they are not filled with a visible body, insofar as they are filled with air itself, which they recognize as a body. Indeed, they say that air prevents a vacuum in the world and that an eternal fullness fills all things, because its subtle body penetrates everything, and by running everywhere through the world, fills all things with its existence. Therefore, whenever any place is said to be empty, it is nonetheless, in reality, full of air. To these I respond: this dispute concerns things that neither are, nor were, nor ever shall be. For since the waters were that material principle from which all things have their existence—as those things by which, through which, and in which the heaven and earth consist were fashioned, <margin>2 Peter 3.</margin> as the Apostle testifies—it is necessary to believe that the heavens and earth will first fail, and finally the entire mass of created waters (and consequently the material principle of things) will be reduced to nothing, before any such "vacuum" as the Heathens dreamed of will be found in the world. Therefore, I say the question is frivolous when it concerns something that never was and never will be. But on the other hand, the Sacred Scriptures seem to intend another kind of "Fullness" and "Empty," namely those which pertain to the formal or Essential principle. For where the Spirit <margin>Genesis 1.</margin> or *Ruah-Elohim* <note>Hebrew: "Spirit of God"</note> did not appear before the beginning of things, and did not give form to the waters overwhelmed by darkness, there—as has been said—

<column-break/>

was "Nothing," and the earth was "void and empty." Therefore, in that respect, the "Vacuum" was nothing other than the absence of that spirit which animates and quickens all things and gives them form by its presence. Hence it was called the Dark Abyss, a divine potential <note>The author uses "potency" in the Aristotelian sense: something that has the potential to exist but has not yet been "acted upon" to become a real, shaped thing</note> and consequently empty, insofar as it was deprived of all "act" or form. Hence Moses says: *The earth was void and empty.* And John <note>The text cites "Iohannes" but the margin correctly identifies this as Job 26:7</note>: *God stretched out the North over the empty and void space and hung the earth upon <margin>Job 26:7.</margin> nothing*—that is, in the empty and void Abyss, as it was overwhelmed by darkness. God by His wisdom made the heaven and the earth, according to that saying of Moses: *In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth,* where by "the beginning," some of the more learned understand that infinite mystery of the Abyss. Hence also St. John says: *In the beginning was the Word.* <margin>John 1.</margin> For it was from that dark principle (which to human understanding seemed void, empty, and plainly Nothing, though well known to God) that this bright Spirit went forth for the creation of the world, as is evident in many places of the sacred letters. And Hermes Trismegistus says: *There was an <margin>Pimander 3.</margin> infinite shadow in the abyss, and water and an intellectual spirit were within the Chaos by divine power,* etc. It is clear, therefore, that by the appearance of this spirit from the dark Mystery, the darkness was put to flight, the waters were <margin>Job 12:22.</margin> brought into the light, and all things were created by the essential Light emitted by that spirit, according to the words of Job: *He reveals the foundations out of the darkness and brings the shadow of death into the light.* It is as if he had said: from the condition of the void and nothingness He brought back the Waters, which are the material foundations of all things, and converted the nothing and the void into fullness and real existence by the power of the active and bright fullness emitted by the spirit, in which—as the Apostle witnesses—*the whole fullness of the Godhead dwells bodily.* <margin>Colossians 2:9.</margin> Hence the Poet said, and not foolishly: *All things are full of Jove.* <note>The "Poet" is likely Aratus or Virgil; "Jove" or Jupiter is used here as a metaphor for the Divine Spirit</note> And elsewhere: *Jupiter is whatever you see, wherever you move.* Do not the Scriptures also say that God fills all things? And again: *That He is everywhere?* And again: *That He is all in all?* Here, therefore, it is argued that emptiness, inanity, nothingness, and darkness are one and the same thing: namely, the absence of the actual and informing presence of divine power. For all fullness or filling consists in the immediate action and property of the divine power. But God, through His spirit, had not yet shone forth from the darkness for the creation of the world. Therefore it is established that the first and formless matter of the world was, as far as we are concerned, empty and destitute of all actualizing, creating, and informing grace. Whence the void...

...or empty and void, or as it was called, "without form"; as is clear from the previously mentioned words of Moses. "The Earth," he says, "was void and empty," that is, it had not yet tasted of the Spirit of the greatest fullness which gives form to all things. For darkness was upon the face of the abyss: a truly evident proof that this spirit had not yet appeared. But after the appearance of the fullness of the Spirit of God <note>original: "Spiritus Elohim"</note>, the earth was no longer empty and void, but by reason of its participation in the fullness and

divine goodness, the Text says that God saw that the work of that day was good—that is, full of divine goodness. From this, one argues that the earth, which was previously void and empty, was now full by the saving presence of that life and form of the Spirit; that is, overflowing with divine fire and the incorruptible Spirit of God, according to that saying of Solomon: 
<margin>
Wisdom 1.
Wisdom 12:1.
Ephesians 4:10.

"The holy spirit of discipline fills the world." And elsewhere: "The incorruptible spirit of God is in every thing." And the Apostle: "Christ fills all things." By these we can see that all fullness comes from a divine act or the essential presence of the Divine Spirit, whereas, on the other hand, emptiness is said to be present where that formal life granted by the spirit is absent from the waters. This, indeed, cannot happen totally without the absolute destruction of the subject thus deprived of its presence and its reduction into a state of nothingness. Nevertheless, it happens in part, as when this spirit sometimes recedes from a creature—namely, at the moment of death or the corruption of a specific creature. 
<margin>Psalm 104:29-30.</margin>
This is established from the words of the Royal Psalmist: "When God gives to creatures, they receive; when He hides His face, they are troubled; when He takes away their spirit, they expire and return to their dust; when He sends forth His spirit, they are recreated with good," etc. From these things, therefore, it is clear that it is the presence of the Spirit of God which fills man and creatures with the good of Life, and that His absence is the emptiness of life in the human spirit. But this emptiness is properly called "privation," insofar as it follows a preceding positive act. This, then, is the reason why the void and empty are so horrible in the nature of things: namely, because the extreme and absolute absence of the eternal emanation—or the removal of the Spirit from the Waters of the world—can by no means be tolerated. For every thing fashioned from the waters desires to be given form by the greatest appetite of its nature. Wherefore it is an abomination in nature to be deprived of all existence. It follows, therefore, that unless God had filled all things of this world with His spirit of Life, emptiness, void, and deformity would reign everywhere throughout the world, and consequently all things would remain in a state of Nothingness. But because God, by the shining presence of His...

<column-break/>

...emanating spirit, created, sustained, and preserved all things from Nothing; therefore it is evidently clear that there is nothing in this world that is now absolutely empty and void. Even though, before the Beginning of the world, the dark Abyss and the formless matter of heaven and earth were such, as Moses and Job hold. It is manifest, therefore, how vain and impossible "the empty" and "the full" are according to the intentions of the Peripatetic <note>the followers of Aristotle</note> Philosophers, compared to those things understood from the scriptures. For the Empty and the Full are the Mosaic "Potentiality" and "Actuality," whereby, through the reduction of potentiality (as if from Nothing) into Actuality by means of the presence of the Spirit of God <note>Elohim</note>, the void and empty are converted into fullness. Indeed, it is no wonder if Aristotle never even thought about this kind of emptiness or void and fullness, since in one place he says: "From nothing, nothing is made" <note>original: "Ex Nihilo nihil fit"</note>, and in another place he affirms: "Light is a mere accident" <note>a philosophical term for a non-essential property, like the color of an object</note>, and consequently it did not appear to his senses that an accident could take away emptiness or void, or confer it into fullness by reason of its essence. But I now attack the Christian Peripatetics with their own weapons, and with a bolt drawn from their own quiver, I here oppose their assertion. It is a common axiom among them: "The being of an accident is to be *in* something" <note>original: "Accidentis esse sit inesse"; meaning accidents cannot exist on their own</note>. I shall therefore oppose them with a syllogism of this kind: If Light be an accident, then its being is to be *in* or to adhere to a subject. But Light can exist without any adhesion to any subject. Therefore, it is not an accident, but rather the purest and most essential substance of all. The major premise is proved and granted from the words of Aristotle—namely, that the being of an accident is to be *in* something. The minor premise is confirmed by the authority of Moses, inasmuch as he says that Light was produced or created on the first day before every other creature; and consequently, it had no pre-existing matter in which it might adhere. Furthermore, it is beyond
<margin>
James 1.
1 John 1:5.
John 1.
Wisdom 7.
</margin>
human grasp that God would create Accidents in time and order before substances or essential creatures. Moreover, God is called the fountain, origin, and Father of Light, as the scriptures hand down; and His spirit or word is defined as Light, in which there are no darknesses at all. And again, the Spirit of wisdom is said to be the brightness or splendor and power emanating from almighty God. We conclude, therefore, that the true mystery of fullness and emptiness was entirely unknown to the Peripatetics, who were indeed completely ignorant of true wisdom, which (as the Apostle testifies) descends from the Father of Lights. And this appears more manifest in that they falsely taught that the essential light or holy splendor—which is the basis and Cornerstone of the essential structure of every creature—is a mere quality or superficial accident.
