<margin>Job 33:4</margin> inspiration of the Almighty gave me life. From all these things, therefore, it is established that the immediate acting cause in generation and vivification is the Spirit of God in its active or positive property; and consequently its absence or privation is the cause of ruin, death, or corruption: For when the Spirit of the Lord is removed from the corporeal mass or corpse, it leaves it as an unformed and, as it were, shapeless chaos, or an empty and void Earth <note>original: "Terra inanis & vacua"</note> with respect to its preceding species, always decreasing and retreating through the way of Corruption into the point of Nothingness <note>original: "punctum Nihili"</note> from which it proceeded from the beginning; insofar as it is now deprived of its positive and incorruptible spirit: For that spirit either departs entirely, or totally contracts itself to the center, and remains, as far as we are concerned, idle, resting, and doing nothing at the circumference.

Now truly, the difference between the resurrection from the dead—or at least from mortal death into temporal life (for Christ's words concerning the dead Lazarus were that he slept)—and that into eternal life, is this: For as there is nothing that more hinders death than the actual presence of the incorruptible spirit, so also there is nothing that more stands in the way of the perpetuity of living than a corruptible body, or a body subject to death and
<margin>1 Cor. 15:36</margin> corruption: Wherefore it is necessary that that body die, so that by this means it may entirely lay aside impurity and corruption, and put on incorruption, so that by the mediation of the incorruptible Spirit of God it may rise again to eternal life: which purification or cleansing is brought about by the disposition and loosening of the knot or bond of the alterable Element (or according to you, the mutable Elements), and by this way liberating the nobler part of the corporeal mixture from its captivity, so that it becomes pure and clean. Which, when it is done, it follows that through the union of the vivifying spirit it becomes spiritual forever, according to that saying of St. Paul: Someone says, he says: How do the dead rise? With what
<margin>1 Cor. 15:35</margin> kind of body do they come? You fool, that which you sow is not made alive unless it first dies. And what you sow, you do not sow the body that is to be, but a bare grain, as for example of wheat, or of some of the others: but God gives it a body as he wills: Not all flesh is the same flesh, and there are heavenly bodies and earthly bodies: but the glory of the heavenly is one, and that of the earthly is another: so also is the resurrection of the dead; it is sown in corruption, it rises in incorruption: it is sown in ignominy, it rises in glory: it is sown in weakness, it rises in power: It is sown a natural body <note>original: "corpus animale"</note>, it rises a spiritual body, etc. By which he seems to argue that the body must die, so that in that way it may strip off corruption—that is, lay aside the corruptible portion of the impure elements—so that, having been made spiritual in this way, it can be bound into one by the eternal bond of unity, and thus migrate from a weak and corrupted animal condition into a spiritual, virtuous, and incorruptible nature and state. For this reason also he confesses elsewhere that flesh and blood cannot inhabit the kingdom of heaven: Since in their elementary nature they are subjected to corruption and consequently cannot inhabit an incorruptible place: But it is the pure Spirit of both the blood and the flesh which rises, after they have laid aside their gross tabernacles by the incorruptible animal spirit, which makes a tempered life in temporal or momentary creatures—that is, in things compacted from the fourfold alterable Element: But truly to spiritualized and purified bodies he grants eternal life and being, which life is contrary to the natural or animal body: as the Apostle testifies in the same place: For through purification it is changed from an Elementary body into a heavenly or spiritual one. Do we not see, according to that example, that a grain of wheat is so exalted in virtue after it has undergone corruption and is free from the gross bonds <note>original: "ligamentis immune"</note> of the Element, that it is raised high above the surface of the earth toward heaven? Indeed, the spark of incorruptibility <note>original: "scintilla incorruptibilitatis"</note> reigning in it would tend upward toward its homeland if it were not hindered by Elementary matter; and yet, nevertheless, after its corruption, this grain is so exalted that it afterwards abounds with manifold virtue: Just as from the multiplication of its species...

### BOOK IV OF THE FIRST SECTION

We have expressed the series in the creation of the world; the first of which [1. o] signifies the dark Abyss or Divine power, in which state all things were folded together <note>original: "complicita"</note> within God. The second [2. oo] denotes the production of light and waters—namely, the Universal principles, both active and passive. The third [3. ooo] depicts the substance of the ether mixed from light and water—namely, two simple things and the first composite made from them. The fourth [4. oooo] explains the <term>Universal Element: The "Catholic" or universal sublunary element, the basic building block of the physical world below the moon.</term> sublunary Element, or the lower waters, altered in a fourfold way. And these are the simple members of the world, from which all things in the world are afterwards composed. This member shall endure in that state of its existence until the final "Let it perish" <note>Referring to the end of the world.</note>. Here, therefore, we have the bases of all composite creatures; for they are placed upon the foundation [4. oooo] in respect to their substance, while they acquire their form from the Spirit that informs all things and is present everywhere. I shall therefore make my Progression from Generation—starting from the simple Element, altered fourfold through various degrees, to the completion of the "perfectly mixed" substance. For, just as between the starting point and the destination there must be a middle ground which is on the way to perfection but has not yet reached that goal, so that middle ground is not improperly called "imperfectly mixed." Its place is between the simple Element (altered in various forms) or, if you prefer, the 4 Elements, which are simple and absolutely mixed. It is certain, therefore, that on the path of generation between the Elements and the perfectly mixed body, we must encounter a body of a meteorological nature. 

For example: in the Generation of man, his beginning—which is founded upon the aqueous Elemental nature—takes its place in the fifth series of generation: the sperm itself. This is because it is an aqueous or fluid substance, only slightly altered. And just as the entire fabric of the world and the seeds of all things are contained "folded" within the primordial water, yet nothing appears externally except water; so in the sperm, although nothing appears explicitly in the first series except sperm, nevertheless the whole man—namely his bones, flesh, blood, nerves, etc.—are enfolded <note>original: "complicite"</note> within it, and they wish to appear explicitly step-by-step from it, namely in the sixth series. For it will be altered from moisture to solidity with a clear distinction of the three principal members: the Heart, the Brain, and the Liver. In the seventh series, it will remain in the form of an Embryo. And the eighth series will complete the Cube at the second root (2) or of the Square (4) (which in the Universal Element is depicted by the impressions of the four winds) to the completion of the perfectly mixed human creature.

<column-break/>

We see a similar respect in the Great World <note>The Macrocosm or universe.</note>, where the simple Element—namely, the Universal air—appears externally plain and simple in its existence and almost like something invisible; nothing is explicit, yet it contains "folded" within itself clouds, rain, or water, fire or lightning, and heavy stones with Salt, etc. All of these appear explicitly by the power of the four winds, so that vapor holds the first series of generation (the fifth order in the Triangular scale); clouds the sixth; lightning with rain the seventh; and the <term>Thunderstone: Also known as a Ceraunius stone, historically believed to fall from the sky during a lightning strike.</term> eighth, proving the exact rotation of the four forms or windy natures into one mixture. 

But truly, when a man's corpse returns to corruption, then it is necessary that its parts proceed backward in resolution through the same steps by which they proceeded to perfect composition: namely, from the perfect state of 8 to 7, from 7 to 6, and from 6 to 5, until it returns to a slime <note>original: "muccilaginem"</note> not unlike sperm, and is dispersed into the Elemental Nature from which it first arose. There it begins to take on a new form, or to undergo a second generation in another form; for the Spirit of the One who works all things is never idle. Likewise, a stone is resolved into water, water into a vaporous cloud, and a cloud into the air from which it was first derived. This air is that simple Element and consequently requires no further resolution. 

From these things it is clear that the work of Generation proceeds chiefly through degrees of condensation, by means of which the bond of Elemental composition is strengthened. And from this it is also made manifest that the same Universal medicine proceeds by the way of generation from form to form, and from thing to thing; and that the work of corruption happens by the way of Rarefaction <note>The process of becoming less dense; the opposite of condensation.</note>, namely by resolving. This is explained in the manner by which snow, ice, and frost are fashioned by the North winds, and their resolution back into waters and vapors by the contrary blasts. And so you have the material Progression—that is, the alteration of aqueous or aerial matter from state to state or from consistency to consistency.

Now, however, it must be known that the only Craftsman or operator in both of these works is the Spirit of God. For in generation, He emits His rays from the center of the Universal Element or from the interior of the sperm, and moves it toward perfection, and always perseveres in His action until a perfect man is produced. And we have this confirmed by Job: <margin>Job 10:10</margin> *Did you not pour me out like milk, and curdle me like cheese? You clothed me with skin and flesh, and with the kindness of life...*

### BOOK IV OF THE FIRST SECTION

However, the greater part of these philosophers believes that God acts and operates in this world by necessity rather than by any voluntary movement—not only in the generation and preservation of things but also in their corruption and ruin. If this were indeed the case, it would necessarily follow that such an involuntary act in God proceeded from eternity from some other nature more powerful than God, which was either co-eternal with Him or pre-existing Him; or at the very least, that He was forced and driven by some of His own creatures to perform this or that against His own will. 

I shall explain to you in a few words how erroneous this is and how far it wanders from the rules of central truth <note>original: "veritatis centralis" — likely referring to the core principles of Hermetic or mystical philosophy</note>. For in the first place, what (I ask) is more ancient than God Himself or co-eternal with Him? Is it not His nature to have existed before all things? Is there anything in Geometry that is before the point in time or order, or smaller than it in measure? Is any of the numbers in Arithmetic older than unity? From this, it necessarily follows that God is free and voluntary in His actions, since He is and always has been from and in Himself. He held His existence from eternity without respect to any preceding or co-eternal principle, and therefore He was sufficient in and of Himself to work and perfect all things, by Himself, without the help of another from all eternity. 

But the reasons for those opinions of the Heathens <note>original: "Ethnicorum" — referring to non-Christian ancient philosophers like Aristotle</note> are twofold. First, it must be known that God works by His own virtue and essence, and not by some acquired power. Second, because effects in this world appear to be necessary, they conclude from this that they cannot proceed from any cause that happens by chance or from the voluntary will of another. 

Regarding the first point, they argue (as it seems to me) against themselves. For as He acts in His own essence or personally, it is evident that He is moved by Himself, and consequently not by any external compulsion, impulse, or internal necessity. Furthermore, the breadth of unity admits no compulsion or movement against the will, since unity cannot suffer or be acted upon. Moreover, it is not possible for God to be urged to work by means of any external or foreign agent, insofar as He remains fixed, constant, and firm from the beginning. He works in and through Himself alone as the original source of all things, and that by Himself, emitting the formal rays of life according to His pleasure, and drawing them back into Himself again, or withdrawing them, where and when He wills. 

Regarding the second point, I say that necessary effects in no way imply necessity in the first efficient cause. This is because secondary causes, which Plato and others call "Handmaidens" and "servants" <note>original: "Ancillas & servas" — a common metaphor for the laws of nature serving the divine will</note>, attempt to carry out His commands in a necessary order, being driven to that work by Him who is the unity of every multitude, and consequently all in all, so that necessity in 

<column-break/>

<margin>Wisdom 16:22</margin>
created, generated, and corrupted things of this kind depends on the will and free command of Him who created them. We have this confirmed from the fountain of truth <note>the Bible</note> in this way: "Snow and ice endured fire and melted not, that they might know that fire even burned in the midst of water." <note>original: "Ignem mitescit... inter aquas" — a paraphrase of Wisdom of Solomon 16:22, where fire behaves against its nature by God's will.</note> By this it is clear that God does not act upon fire or within it out of forced necessity, but according to His own pleasure. 

Furthermore, when the three servants of God walked untouched and without harm in the fiery furnace despite the violence of the flames, God, out of His free benevolence, operated there against the laws of necessity. Or consider when He made the sun stand still in the heavens in the time of Joshua, or again when it moved backward by fifteen degrees on the dial <note>original: "horologij gradus"</note> during the reign of Hezekiah, contrary to the course of nature and consequently not out of necessity nor by compulsion. 

And that wonderful total eclipse of the sun, which happened at the time of the Savior of the world’s passion, occurred beyond the expectation and capacity of Astrologers and Naturalists. For at that moment, the Moon was found neither in the head nor the tail of the Dragon <note>original: "nec in capite, nec in cauda Draconis" — astronomical terms for the lunar nodes where eclipses normally occur</note>, as that great Astrologer Firmicus <note>Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century writer</note> testifies. Whence it is evident that this was done not by a natural way or by necessity to preserve or sustain the nature of the world. All these effects, I say, could in no way have been produced if God had acted by necessity in the governing of this world. 

From this it is manifest that God operates in this world according to His free will and not by compulsion. But come closer and listen a little (O you vain Philosophers, who believe God, the actor and orderer of all things, to be bound by the laws and chains of necessity): what glory or honor, I ask, can a man attribute to Him for His wisdom, justice, and mercy, if He were forced against His will to provide the things He does? That is, if He were urged by some unknown necessity to create or generate all things, or to form anything according to this or that shape, or even to nourish and preserve Being and finally lead it to the goal of corruption? What thanks, I say, or what worship or adoration would we owe Him, if He does anything in this world by force and impulse? 

And why does Aristotle himself warn us (if this were true according to his intention) that we should offer sacrifices to the roots of nature? Or what benefit would it bring us mortals to pour out our daily prayers and supplications before God for this or that future benefit—a duty which nonetheless Plato, Porphyry, Iamblichus, and Proclus <note>Neoplatonist philosophers who emphasized the importance of prayer and ritual (theurgy)</note> teach to be very necessary—if He cannot be won over and appeased in His anger by prayers, being one who (if it were right to believe them) acts by necessity and against His own will? Or why were Socrates and Pythagoras accustomed—who according to the testimony of the oracle were the most [wise] of their age—

He affirms to his Peripatetic disciples <note>Followers of Aristotle, known as "Peripatetics" because they walked while discussing philosophy</note> that the turbulent and tempestuous wind called *Ecnephia* <note>original: "Ecnephia," a Greek-derived term for a storm-wind that bursts from a cloud</note>, and even the whirlwind itself, are indeed sudden and abrupt winds violently emitted from the clouds. Yet, he is unwilling to admit that hot and dry exhalations can penetrate the middle region of the air because of its coldness. But, to descend deeper into the abyss of his own absurdity: he admits that the cause of "ignited meteors"—such as comets and others of this kind—is a hot and dry exhalation that is earthy, thick, fatty, and oily, and therefore fit to be inflamed and set on fire. Now, he assigns the highest region of the air as the place and seat for the generation of such meteors, namely comets; and yet he seems to deny passage through the middle region of the air to those exhalations that give birth to winds, which are not subject to inflammation and are thin and light in their substance. Can anyone be so lacking in mind and so ignorant of natural effects as not to perceive that coldness would rather resist and hinder a flammable thing of an actual fiery nature (such as the exhalation that produces comets) than a thing or exhalation that is not actually flammable or fiery in itself (namely, that smoke which is said to be the origin of winds)? Again, it appears from the description of comets that their material existence is heavier, more earthy, thick, and compact than that of the winds, and for this reason, it is less suited for ascending and penetrating. Insofar as heavy things, by their own inclination, tend downward more than winds do—for winds are more light and subtle, and consequently suited to tend upward. Therefore, it would be impossible for the thicker smokes that make comets to ascend and penetrate the "diaphragm" of the middle region of air—indeed, to exalt themselves into the third or upper region—as much by reason of their flammable heat as by the thickness and weight of their substance, while on the other hand, thinner and non-flammable vapors would be hindered by the middle region of air in their passage to the heights. Therefore, it is evident how weak, frivolous, and devoid of probability is this assertion of Aristotle in the aforementioned description.

But I come to the examination of the third part of that description. SECTION I. BOOK V.

From what has been said, we can conclude that the definition or description provided by this Peripatetic Philosopher <note>Aristotle, whose followers were called Peripatetics because he famously taught while walking</note>, whom Christians follow with such great veneration, is entirely erroneous and insufficient. This is because winds are creatures more essential and eminent, and more full of divinity, than either Aristotle or any of his followers ever understood. They are not things devoid of internal light and essence, and consequently, they are not merely formed by external, accidental agents through a smoky existence

<column-break/>

springing from the earth. Rather, as Zechariah teaches us, they are created and animated by an Angelic Spirit; they stand before the Lord of the whole earth and are hidden within the power and Treasury of their Lord. From this Treasury, He calls them forth according to His pleasure to fulfill His commands in heaven, on earth, and in the sea—whether for vengeance and punishment, or to offer mercy and kindness to His creatures, as will be discussed more extensively below.

## CHAPTER III.

### *The true definition or description of winds is expressed in this chapter in various forms, according to the sense and intention of Holy Scripture.*

---

Now indeed (as it seems to me), I hear the faction or sect of the Peripatetics murmuring against me and replying in this way: "If," they say, "the stated definition by Aristotle is not good—as you seem to promise by your arguments—assign a better one, if you can. Tell us more essentially what a wind truly is, or how you can correctly describe it according to the doctrine of the Holy Page <note>A traditional term for the Bible</note>." To these men I respond that this can be achieved in many ways, yet always under one and the same essence. In the first place, we can describe it not impertinently in this manner:

->Wind is an aerial Spirit, of a moderate consistency, animated by the inspiration or Spirit of Jehovah, which He brings forth from His Treasuries and sends out to execute His will, whether it be by the way of a curse or vengeance, or of blessing and mercy.<-

<margin>Exodus 15:8. Job.</margin>
Every part of this definition is proven from appropriate passages of Holy Scripture. First, that the external part of the wind is air of a moderate consistency is shown by the fact that the words for air, wind, and spirit are expressed in many places of the sacred letters by a single Hebrew word, <term>Ruach</term> <note>original: "Ruach"; This Hebrew term can mean breath, wind, or spirit depending on the context</note>. Second, that its internal and central soul or action is the divine Spirit, or the inspiration of the Almighty, is very easily indicated from the passages cited before. "By the blast of your nostrils," says Moses, "the waters were gathered together; you blew with your wind and the sea covered them." <note>Exodus 15:8-10</note> And Job: "By the breath of God, the mighty one brings forth ice; by the blowing of God, the frost is thickened," etc. It is as if he had said: God inspired the air with His spirit, so that no discrepancy appears between an Angelic creature and air divinely inspired. For air is called the external and manifest form of an Angel—both good and bad—animated by God to do His pleasure, whether in punishing or in manifesting His kindness and mercy. From this it is clear that its internal essence is the immediate inspiration of God. For this reason (as

to make and refine the waters and reduce the humbler substance of the earth into a vaporous existence; and then we affirm that such substances, having been reduced into the existence of vapors, can climb upward by themselves and without the help of any other force. For, just as heavy things tend downward by an innate appetite, so conversely, that which is light seeks the heights by a natural instinct. Indeed, all of this is clearly demonstrated through the observation of our **Experimental Instrument** <note>This refers to a "weather-glass" or thermoscope, an early device used to show the expansion and contraction of air due to heat, which Fludd famously used to illustrate his cosmic theories.</note>: For, if you place your hand upon its rounded top, the air enclosed in the glass will suddenly expand, and in its expansion it will fly away from the thinning agent; much less will it draw smoky matter toward itself.

From these things it is evident that, although in the eyes of worldly men, vapors or smoke appear to seek the heights—and they therefore conclude that the movement itself away from the earth toward the upper regions must proceed from the attractive power of the sun and stars—nevertheless, this assertion of theirs is proved to be false by ocular experiment. Insofar as we are taught by experience that the nature of light and heat is contrary to attraction, seeing as its sole function is to rarefy <note>To make thinner or less dense.</note>, and by rarefying to dissipate or scatter; whereas, on the contrary, attraction or contraction is nothing other than a certain condensation or gathering together brought about by the property of Cold: as is clearly demonstrated by our glass or Experimental Instrument. But now I shall prove that the foundations of Aristotle—which maintain that clouds are procreated from vapors elevated from the earth to the middle region of the air—are in every way discordant with the truth. It is necessary, therefore, in the first place, to consider that the sense of Sacred Scripture is plainly contrary to this part of the definition: namely, that from which we gather that by faith it is to be <margin>Hebrews 11:2 <note>Typically cited as Hebrews 11:3 in modern Bibles.</note></margin> understood that the worlds were framed by the word of God, so that from invisible things, visible things might be made, etc. Therefore it is certain that neither earth nor water are the visible origins of clouds, but rather the simple substance of the air, or the **Universal Element** <note>original: "Elementi Catholici." In this context, "Catholic" means universal or all-pervading.</note>, condensed into the consistency of a cloud by the opposing blasts of the winds. And this we also have confirmed from various other places in the Sacred Scripture:

> <margin>Job 28:25</margin> For Job says: "God by His wisdom gives weight to the air, and weighs the waters by measure; <margin>Job 26:9</margin> He binds them in thick clouds, He makes laws for the rain and a path for the lightning of the thunders." 

By these words the patient man <note>Job</note> first confirms that God the Father is the radical author of this meteorological work, and that eternal efficient power by which He operates <margin>1 Corinthians 8:6</margin> is the Spirit of His wisdom. This also agrees with that text of the Apostle: "To us there is one God the Father, from whom are all things, and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things." Secondly, it confirms that air is the subject of both fiery

<column-break/>

and watery **meteors** <note>In the 17th century, "meteors" referred to any atmospheric phenomena, including rain, wind, and lightning.</note>: For by the condensation of the air, mist and the consistency of a cloud are made, which then later are converted into rain by an even greater condensation and resolution. But if the air is thinned too much, it is changed into the condition of lightning. I do not say, indeed, that the act of lightning itself is the air; but rather it is an admirable light, which is clothed in air as if in a garment—a wonderful power of the aforementioned wisdom, which manifests itself in many forms within the air, as has been said elsewhere: For where its positive action flourishes more greatly, there the air is rendered more flashing and lightning-like.

Now, truly, that air is the material subject of aquatic meteors is implied by the preceding text in these words: "God by His wisdom gives weight to the air," that is, He condenses it according to His pleasure into mists and clouds. Finally, we draw from the said text that the invisible air is altered in weight and measure into the visible consistency of clouds, which then later melt into rains, and of lightning-bolts, which appear to the eyes through compression. Furthermore, it appears from these things that it is neither Earth nor water, but air alone, from which the substance of the cloud arises.

> <margin>Deuteronomy 28:12</margin> "Jehovah shall open to thee (says Moses) His best treasure, the heavens, by giving rain to thy land in its season." 

From which we observe, first, that by "the heavens" he understands the air: for clouds are procreated in the air, and again: the air is called "heaven" in many places of Scripture, as in "the birds of heaven," etc. From this we conclude that the air itself is the Treasury-chest of God, from which He, according to His pleasure, produces and fashions clouds, as visible things from an invisible thing. Second, we observe that the air is called His "best treasure," and consequently, it is that from which God not only extracts His meteorological creatures, but also that from which some wise men expect their highest good. Moreover, we read elsewhere: <margin>Ecclesiasticus 43:17</margin> "Therefore the treasures were opened, and the clouds and mists flew out like birds." But this is rendered even more evident by this speech: <margin>Job 37:21</margin> "Suddenly the air shall be condensed into clouds, and the wind passing by shall drive them away." By which it is expressly argued that the air is the Treasury-chest of God, from which clouds are drawn out by condensation, and that the heaven is the unique Treasury from which they are extracted: and consequently neither earth nor water, as Aristotle thought. Indeed, if that were true, I would have you notice what an absurd impossibility would follow: For then, since the sun is accustomed to thin the waters in the summer time, it would render the air especially...

<meta>This page continues Robert Fludd’s critique of Aristotelian meteorology. Having previously argued that heat causes expansion rather than attraction, he now challenges the idea that clouds are formed simply by the cold of the "middle region" of the air, proposing instead that clouds are formed by the physical compression of air, often by wind or obstacles.</meta>

### BOOK V OF THE FIRST SECTION.

If the air were thick with a multitude of vapors, a greater irregularity would continually arise to subvert the reasoning of **Aristotle** <note>Aristotle's *Meteorology* was the standard textbook for nearly 2,000 years, but Fludd is part of a 17th-century movement challenging his authority.</note> concerning the generation of clouds. For if his theory were true, we would expect a greater abundance of clouds and rain in the summer time than in the winter, seeing as in that season vapors are more redundant due to the exhalation from ponds, torrents, and rivers caused by the presence of the Sun. But this is proven false by the actual effect. And finally, it is not the heat of the Sun nor of the stars, but the eternal **Spirit of Jehovah**, who has dominion over the **Angelic winds** of the world, in which He moves organically and works all those meteorological alterations in and through the air, as will be declared below. Whence it was said, as above:
> *By wisdom He gave weight to the air, and weighed the clouds by measure, etc.* <note>original: "Sapientiâ fecit pondus aëri, & nubes appendit in mensura" — a reference to Job 28:25.</note>
But I come now to the second doubt.

For the resolution of the second question, I say that there is another mode of condensation of invisible vapor or air into a cloud than the one imagined by **Aristotle**. For where he asserts that this act of thickening occurs because of the contracting cold of the middle region of the air, it is worth wondering why this effect does not also happen at other times—namely, when the winds blow from their own quarters or regions of the earth. For when the Southern winds <note>The "Austri," or south winds, were traditionally associated with rain and humidity.</note> have dominion, we then observe clouds multiplying and rains falling abundantly. I would like to know, I say, from those **Peripatetics** <note>The followers of Aristotle, so named because they walked about while teaching.</note> why vapors should ascend so fluently from the earth and water especially at that time when such winds are accustomed to blow—more so than at another time when they do not have dominion—to procreate such copious clouds in the air. Or why should the coldness of the middle region of the air coagulate or condense vapors ascending in such a way more at that time than at others? Especially since the warm clouds or thick air, mixed with the hot rays of the place, which are driven Northward from the equinox, ought rather to moderate and mitigate the cold of the middle region. I know for certain that they are utterly ignorant of how to respond. Therefore, I will not press them further in this matter. But so that you may better draw out the truth by which air is condensed into clouds, I will explain to you in a few words an experiment I experienced myself, by which I was instructed in the mystery of the generation of mists and clouds.

On my journey from the City of **Venice** toward **Augsburg** <note>Augusta Vindelicorum is the Roman name for the city of Augsburg in Bavaria.</note>, as I made my way among the Alpine mountains and crags one day—with the whole sky of the horizon being quite clear and without a single spot of cloud appearing, and consequently with the Sun shooting its free rays everywhere without any foggy impediment—I noticed a mist gradually grow and increase on the summit of a mountain that was quite tall and steep compared to the others. This happened chiefly on one side of it, against which the rays of the Sun were nonetheless striking strongly, until finally it was reduced into the

<column-break/>

consistency of a dense cloud, which was finally resolved into rain. During this whole time, the air was clear and free of mists and clouds everywhere else, except for that side of the crag, from its peak almost down to its base. At first, I was certainly amazed by the novelty of the thing, and considering the matter seriously with myself, I finally climbed down from the carriage. Grabbing some grass with my fingers, I threw it into the open air so that I might discern the path of the wind. I found that its gusts were directed exactly against that side of the towering mountain. From this I immediately gathered that the stages in the progression from aerial vapor to mist, and from mist to the consistency of a cloud, were caused by the greater or lesser compression of the common and universal air. I realized that the wind, pursuing the fleeing air, had coagulated that portion of the air little by little through pressure and compression, because the height of the resisting crag hindered its flight. In this way, air added to air was altered from an invisible and thin state into a visible and dense form. Whence first a small cloud, and then a cloud according to the shape of the front of the mountain, was generated, which was finally resolved into rain by the heat of the Sun, while all the other air remained clear.

By this, I perceived with open eyes that clouds were not procreated in the manner described by **Aristotle**—namely, from vapor elevated from the earth and water—but by the thickening of thin and invisible air into the consistency of a mist, and from that into a cloud, differing from the small cloud by one degree of density. 
<margin>Job 37:21.</margin> 
Indeed, by this observation, I perceived the assertion of **Job** confirmed, who says: *that suddenly the air will be condensed into clouds, and the passing wind will drive them away.* <note>Fludd provides a Latin paraphrase of Job 37:21 to support his "compression" theory.</note> 

Yet, truly, my spirit still hesitated somewhat in this, considering that mountains and tall crags are not found everywhere to hinder the fleeing air in every place; and yet, on the contrary, we see clouds appear and move even in the middle of deserts and on the open sea, where there are no mountains or crags. Revolving this seriously and often in my mind, I was finally rooted a little deeper in my opinion by another experience. For I thought to myself, not without deliberation, that there is no wind blowing with dominion in the sky that does not have another wind, either opposite or collateral, which meets it in the common or universal element. However, it is not discerned because of the dominion of the more powerful wind, which obscures the actions of the lesser wind no differently than the presence of the Sun is accustomed to obscure the light of a lit candle. Now, indeed, I was instructed by experience that two winds can blow at one and the same time. While being carried many times across the seas, I observed that when the predominant wind decreased a little in its vigor by turns, and pressed the sails of the ship only weakly, the wind opposite to it revealed its own...

## CHAPTER XII.

### How lightning is to be correctly described by the true Philosopher and according to the teachings of Holy Scripture.

Since it is clear from the discussion in the preceding chapter that Aristotle erred greatly and monstrously in his opinion and concepts regarding both the material and formal causes of lightning and thunder, let me here—according to the strength of my meager capacity—be permitted to fish out their true and genuine definition from the deep sea of the Holy Scriptures, so that by this means I may show you their sincere nature and essential origin.

Lightning is a certain fiery air, which is drawn out from the heavenly or aerial Treasury of God <note>The "Treasury" or "Storehouse" (Latin: *thesaurus*) refers to the biblical concept in Job and Psalms where God keeps the wind, hail, and snow.</note> and is animated by His glowing presence, and is sent forth onto the land and sea to execute His will, whether it be for the benefit or the detriment of His creatures.

->Or thus:<-

Lightning is a certain flashing brightness proceeding from the cavity of a cloud, as if from a divine Tabernacle, which is sent from the Throne of Jehovah onto the earth and seas to perform His pleasure.

But if we wish to describe lightning with all its accidents <note>In philosophy, "accidents" are the non-essential qualities of a thing, such as its color or timing.</note> and consequently describe the entire essence of Thunder (which is of a mixed nature), we can perform that according to the Holy Testimony in this manner:

Lightning is a consuming fire, which is kindled by the face or presence of Jehovah, at the sight of whose brightness and touch the clouds pass away, and the Most High thunders or sends forth His voice from heaven, and is accustomed to hurl arrows for the destruction of the impious.

->Or thus:<-

Lightning is a fire flying out from the mouth of Jehovah, sent from His Tent above, in whose sight the waters or clouds (as if fearing and like the disturbed Depths) pass away, and the voice of the Thunder of Jehovah moves in a wheel <note>A reference to Psalm 77:18, where the voice of thunder is "in the whirlwind" or "the wheel."</note>, and fiery coals or His arrows are hurled to execute His will in the heavens and on the earth.

->Or thus:<-

Lightning and also Flashing is a certain pure and bright light made in the upper clouds, which the passing wind has cleansed.

In the first description of lightning, you have it manifested that its **material cause** is the air; the fiery place from which it is brought forth is the Treasury-chest of God, or heaven. The **formal cause** is explained in that it is called a Spirit or fiery air. We make its **efficient cause** the immediate act or divine will. Finally, we detect the **final cause** in it, in that it is sent according to the will of Jehovah, either as a scourge and punishment for mortals, or

<column-break/>

to offer mercy and kindness to them. All of this is brilliantly confirmed from the Holy Testimonies expressed in the preceding chapter.

...produces the works of the wonder-worker: Hence it is said: *From the brightness in his presence the clouds passed, hail and coals of fire; the Lord thundered from heaven, and the Most High gave forth his voice.* <note>The author cites Psalm 17 according to the Vulgate numbering; in most modern English Bibles, this is Psalm 18:12-13.</note> And elsewhere: *The waters saw thee, O God, and they were afraid, and the depths were troubled; a great sound of waters, the clouds gave forth a voice, the voice of thy thunder was in the wheel.* <note>Psalm 77:16-18 in modern numbering.</note> The <term>formal cause</term> <note>The "formal cause" refers to the essential nature or "shape" of a thing—in this case, the crashing sound and flashing light of the storm.</note> is also described therein, because it occurs with a crash and with flashes of lightning. The <term>efficient cause</term> <note>The "efficient cause" is the primary agent that brings something into being.</note> seems to be the lightnings, or rather the fiery gaze of God, animating the lightnings themselves and directing them toward the goal ordained by God. Whence lightnings are like the instruments of God in His wrath, just as a sword is the instrument of a man who strikes, where we say that he has struck with such a blade, and not the blade itself. Therefore, we say that God Himself is the only actor in worldly matters, the very Father of Thunders, who sends out lightnings like His arrows from His Throne. We have placed the purpose <note>The "final cause" or end goal.</note> as the fulfillment of the divine will.

Or finally, in this manner:
Thunder is the voice, or speech, or utterance, or sound proceeding from the mouth of Jehovah, which is directed under the whole heaven, with light, over the ends or borders of the earth. After it, a sound roars, or God thunders with the voice of His excellence, and it cannot be tracked down; after His voice has been heard, He who thunders does wonders with His voice. We have this confirmed thus: *Hear with trembling,* says Job, *the voice or speech or (as another interprets it) the utterance going out from the mouth of Jehovah; He directs it under the whole heaven and His light over the ends or borders of the earth; after it a sound roars, He thunders with the voice of His excellence and it is not tracked down when His voice is heard: God thundering with His voice does wonders.*
<margin>Job 37</margin>

From these things, therefore, it clearly appears—contrary to the insane opinions of the Pagans—that these are not merely "exhalations" nor "vapors" as they claim, nor the sun with the stars, nor earth or water, nor the Elements, nor created nature; but God alone, who is the worker of all wonders, who is the immediate efficient cause of these miracles. This you also have confirmed, as you see, by the sacred scripture, lest you attribute this work (as the Pagans do) either to imaginary "nature," or to the Elements, or to <term>things composed of elements</term>, which must be attributed to the Creator first and before all else. Therefore, conclude that there is the greatest imprudence among philosophers distinguished by the name of Christian; indeed, it is an irrecoverable madness to place such great faith in the vain and lying opinions of the Pagans concerning lightning and thunder. By these opinions, men are easily persuaded that thunders and lightnings are merely incidental things, arising from the natural imbalance of the air or heaven, and not at all sent by divine power. And so, looking only at the effect, they falsely estimate it to be the efficient cause—as if it were just and religious to ascribe the works produced by God the Creator to the creatures themselves. Therefore, I would have you know that I

have written in this place not in a rash manner, but diligently, seriously, and supported by good foundations. For other philosophers, far deeper than I in the abstruse mystery of Jehovah, seem to agree with me: namely, those who, considering the admirable nature of the Lightning-bolt and noticing the hidden reason for the generation of other <term>Meteors</term> <note>In the 17th century, "meteors" referred to any atmospheric phenomena, including rain, wind, and lightning, not just falling stars.</note>, judge them to be not the works of some "secondary nature" (whose reputation the <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy, who sought purely physical explanations for natural events.</note> seem to celebrate with so much praise), but the immediate acts of the most high God, according to the scriptures. We conclude, therefore, that it is evident that the opinion of the Peripatetics, both Christian and Pagan, is wandering and distant from the truth. This opinion says that lightnings are nothing other than hot and dry exhalations, drawn out from the earth and raised into the middle region of the air by the attractive power of the sun and stars, which, being enclosed in a dense cloud, are ignited partly by the collision of clouds and partly by <term>antiperistasis</term> <note>A philosophical term for the intensification of a quality when it is surrounded by its opposite, such as heat growing more intense when compressed by surrounding cold.</note>, which is between the coldness of the place and their own proper heat; from which, afterward, by the eruption of the flame from the cloud, thunders are forced out. I wish that every wise Christian would diligently observe from what has been said before whether the mystery of the Storm, the Whirlwind, and the Thunders depends on a matter of so little weight and value as Aristotle has handed down to us, or rather, on the contrary, whether it does not emerge from the inscrutable abyss of divine depth—since lightnings are handed down by the fountain of truth to be the fiery torches and lights of Jehovah that emanate from His Throne, and since Thunders are called the voices, words, and utterances of the Most High, etc. And for that reason, Jehovah, rebuking the audacity of such worldly philosophers who presume so much to judge His secret actions and to plunge themselves headlong into the depth of the essential causes of Meteorological Mysteries without the assistance and guidance of the divine spirit, and who intend to seduce the world with barely probable arguments, persuading it to believe that such secret Great Works of God proceed from things so foolish and vain, and produced according to the imagination of their own fantasy.

Let me now, in the conclusion of this section (O you Europeans, who so seriously and with such zeal spend your lives in the Christian Religion), turn the sharpness of my pen and the thread of my discourse to you. You, seduced by the false doctrine of Aristotle, think that **Meteors**—and especially lightning and thunder—are things occurring naturally, and consequently, of little or no importance or value, as being produced either by hot or cold imbalance in the air. I earnestly beseech you that you trust in a Christian manner and observe this admonition, which I commend to you as a final farewell to this section. I implore you that you do not reject my aforementioned assertion with either laughter or mockery, nor with contempt, since it has been sufficiently and clearly proved to you that winds, whirlwinds, and storms, and lightning and thunder—indeed, all other Meteors whatsoever—are the immediate works of the hand of God. 

For by this effort of mine, you will not only bring comfort and salvation to yourselves when the terrible crash of clouds (the voice and eloquence of Jehovah) is present with trembling lightning and astounding whirlwinds and storms—by recalling your sins to mind and, moved by penitence, praying to God heartily and humbly that He might not judge these things in His anger and severity—

# ON MOYSES' PHILOSOPHY. Fol. 59.

...understood. Have we not learned from the preceding passages (as witnessed by **David** and the **Book of Kings**) that God, by bowing the heavens, descended and ascended upon the **Cherubim**—that is, an aerial Angel—and by that means, the acting Word of God flew upon the wings of the wind, contracted the clouds, kindled them, and flashed lightning and thundered from heaven? And that He sifted the waters from the clouds and made coals <margin>Psalm 18:9; 2 Samuel 22:8.</margin> fly in the air, and so on? But all of this was unknown to the **Pagan Philosophers**, and for that reason, this discipline of truth is utterly rejected or at least neglected by those Christians who are their disciples. Indeed, the false spirit of **Aristotle** holds dominion in their speech and writings, and seems to claim the primary place in their science. Therefore, although this admonition of mine will perhaps appear vile, vain, ridiculous, and of little or no value to those who firmly and stubbornly adhere to their chimerical imaginations and the subtle teachings of **Aristotle**, yet I would have men of that sort know and understand with a clearer mind that this is a matter of the greatest importance and consequence in the Christian state, as it concerns the honor and Majesty of God. For through this knowledge, true Christians can fundamentally learn the real and essential causes of storms and other wondrous operations of God. They may understand from this that these things do not happen by chance or fortuity, nor by some internal power naturally inherent in them—as the fantastical **Pagans** imagined in their writings—but that they are brought forth from the treasury of Divine Providence and sent down through the action of the Divine Word by means of Angelic ministers. This is done either for the affliction and scourging of the impious, or to remind them of their sins so that, led by fear, they might finally repent. At other times, it is for the benefit of creatures and to provide food for them. Wherefore **Job** says: *If a man considers the expansions of the thick clouds, the crashings in His pavilion; He spreads His light upon it... with these He shall judge the people and give them food.* <margin>Job 36:29-31.</margin> By this he implies that storms occur as much for judging and punishing the people as for giving them nourishment. Therefore, when terrified people hear the voice or speech of the Lord from on high in the thunder, and fearfully behold the flames and flashes of His indignation, or see floods rising beyond reason from excessive rain or snow, or perceive **Comets** <note>In the 17th century, comets and all atmospheric phenomena were classified as "meteors."</note> with corrupted air and are struck with terror, let them be led to repentance. Prostrating themselves humbly before God, let them pour out prayers to the Creator of all things and humbly and penitently implore His help in such great necessity and danger. Let them supplicate Him to mitigate the fury of the storm and, out of His mercy and for the love

<column-break/>

of His Son **Jesus Christ**, turn away its malice from themselves and their families. Let Him suppress the rage of His ministers—the watery, the fiery, and the windy—and finally grant them milder and gentler weather with more fertile rains. May He bless their households, servants, animals, and cattle, along with the fruits of the earth ordained for food, and defend them from the violence of the tempestuous and malevolent Angels who are the instruments of His wrath. On the other hand, whoever neglects this counsel of mine (which is founded upon true wisdom) and chooses to wallow further in his own mud or filth, firmly adhering to the teachings of worldly wisdom (which is foolishness before God), and consequently insists that the great **Meteorological** <term>Meteorology: Here referring to all atmospheric phenomena, including lightning and wind, viewed as divine acts.</term> wonders of God happen in the world contingently and by accident without any internal acting principle—such a person, because he ignores these things as if they were common natural occurrences, will neither fear them (as befits a Christian) nor acknowledge Him who is their immediate author and creator. He is rightly numbered among those whom the Wise Man indicates with this thread of discourse: <margin>Wisdom 13:1.</margin> *Vain,* he says, *are all men in whom there is no knowledge of God, and from the good things that are seen they could not understand Him who is, nor by attending to the works did they acknowledge who was the workman.* And the **Apostle** says of such: *The wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men who suppress the truth of God in unrighteousness...* <margin>Romans 1:18-20.</margin> *for the invisible things of Him from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made, even His eternal power and Godhead; so that they are without excuse,* etc. Let such a man beware, I say, lest God direct His lightnings straight at him, as if from a well-aimed bow. <margin>Wisdom 5:21-22.</margin> For I would have him know that lightnings not only have sense, but are imbued with a certain wonderful and Angelic reason to execute divine commands against the impious and those who despise Divine works. *Do you send the lightnings,* says **Job**, *and they go, and returning say to you: Here we are?* <margin>Job 38:35.</margin> Let that **Irish girl** serve as an example to him, who for her contempt and blasphemy was miserably struck in the very part of her body she chose for her mocking laughter. And that **Peripatetic** <note>A follower of Aristotle's philosophy.</note> of **Shrewsbury**, who out of his derogation of the act of Divine Majesty—so that he might grant fame to the opinion of **Aristotle**—was the only one among many travelers killed on the Shrewsbury plain. Let him look at other examples proving divine power in storms, expressed by me in Section 1, Part 4, Book 4, Chapter 20, and he will see with open eyes that the virtue and power of God reside in the **Meteors**, and that they do not spare those who despise the Divine Name.

# EPILOGUE.

*From these things that have been presented in this first section* (learned Christian reader, endowed with judgment and erudition), *you may be able to discern with open eyes, if I am not mistaken, that immense difference which exists between worldly wisdom (which the* **Apostle** <note>Refers to St. Paul; see 1 Corinthians 3:19.</note> *makes out to be mere foolishness before* **God**) *and that wisdom which descends from heaven from the* **Father of Lights** (which is the essential spirit of wisdom). *And consequently, it may be seen that* **Peripatetic Philosophy** <term>Peripatetic Philosophy: The school of thought based on the teachings of Aristotle. The author argues that because it relies on human reason and physical "elements" rather than divine revelation, it is a "vain deception."</term>, *which is founded upon the wisdom of this world—insofar as it relies on the tradition of men and the Elements of the world, and not on* **Christ** *or the* **True Cornerstone**—*is a vain deception or a deceptive figment. By consequence, that* **Philosophy of the Patriarchs, Prophets, and Apostles**, *which is founded upon* **Christ**, *or the* **Universal Spirit of God** <note>original: "Spiritum Dei Catholicum." The author uses "Catholic" in its literal Greek sense of "universal" or "all-pervading."</note>, *in whom the fullness of the* **Divinity** *dwells bodily, is the only true, real, and essential philosophy which descends directly from* **God**. *Therefore, as a conclusion, let me address you* **Christian Peripatetics** *with these words of* **Moses** *himself (of whose* **Philosophy** *this work of ours is an exact*
<margin>Deuteronomy 30:19.</margin>
*model):* I call heaven and earth to witness against you this day, that I have set before you life and death, good and evil, blessing and cursing: Therefore choose life, so that you and your seed may live and become rich in the knowledge

*A certain Appendix annexed to this first section of Mosaic Philosophy, extracted from a certain German volume printed at Frankfurt not many years ago, the title of which is (A Table of the Revelation of the Divine Majesty comprised in the first chapter of Genesis) which fiercely attacks the doctrine of the Heathens and their Christian disciples.*

## Author’s Preface.

Since it can be hidden from no one endowed with a sound mind how many and almost infinite adversaries of truth are found everywhere in the world (for no enemy is to be found more base or more dangerous than one who is ignorant of true science and wisdom <note>The author is likely referring to "science" in the classical sense of *scientia*, or structured knowledge, rather than modern laboratory science.</note>, a huge multitude of which kind of men is scattered everywhere across the earth), I must believe that in this honest and honorable effort of mine undertaken for the sake of truth, I shall receive nothing as my reward or prize except laughter, cackling, reproaches, curses, satirical attacks, and all types of insults from worldly people—men who are partly blinded by ignorance and partly contaminated at the root by **Peripatetic Philosophy** <term>Peripatetic Philosophy: The school of thought following Aristotle. In this period, many "Mosaic" philosophers viewed Aristotle's reliance on physical causes as a distraction from the direct power of God.</term>. Indeed, I would not know what to do or where to turn, were I not to have Truth herself fighting for me—she who is over all things—or rather, God himself, who overcomes the Devil and his followers. 

But since it is no small comfort to a man surrounded by calamity to have a faithful and **God-taught** <term>God-taught: A translation of the Greek "Theodidaktos," referring to someone whose knowledge comes from divine inspiration rather than human schooling.</term> companion in his difficulties—one who can endure a portion of the arrows drawn from the quiver of spite and malevolence and maliciously shot at him, and who can alleviate his labors and the blows inflicted upon him—therefore, I have chosen one companion in this conflict of mine. I speak of a man quite vigorous in science and a thousand times more deeply immersed than myself in the Mysteries of God and the secret operations of His word. For what I have learned theoretically, by contemplation alone and by diligent reading of the Sacred Scriptures, he has understood not only by speculation and reading, but also by ocular practice and real inspection in the **Table of the Sages** <note>original: "Tabula sophorum." This refers to a mystical or alchemical diagram used to visualize the hidden structures of the universe.</note>, as he himself seems to assert in his aforementioned volume. 

From this source, he has not only clearly and vividly depicted the errors and vanities of the Heathens, but he also fiercely attacks them. For this reason, I have extracted several "members" <note>Here, "members" refers to specific sections or chapters of the work.</note> from the works of that most learned man, which accurately and clearly expose the emptiness of the books of the Heathens, the vanity of their philosophy, and the silliness of their Christian disciples. I have tied these together into a single "bundle," as it were, and made them an appendix to this first section of my *Mosaic Philosophy*. I have done this primarily to indicate to the malevolent people of this age that I was not the first mover or author of such a pious reformation; and secondly, because the master of that volume seems to agree with me in all things and support my opinions exactly. 

For he acknowledges that all things were originally made from water; he confesses that the universe was created by the Word of God and even now, to this very day, is continued, preserved, increased, and multiplied in it. He says that God, without the assistance of creatures, works all things in all things through the Word, and consequently he admits neither any "nature" of the Heathens <note>That is, "Nature" as an independent force acting on its own.</note>, nor their causes, whether secondary or tertiary. He tells us that the air, or the universal heaven, is water (whence I hold it to be the **Universal Element** <note>original: "Elementum Catholicum." In this context, "Catholic" means universal or all-pervading.</note>) and that it is guided by the Word of God through the mediation of Angelic organs. Furthermore, he says that the Angels, as the Word moves them, produce all kinds of meteors and storms in and out of the air, as if from the treasury-chest of God. He concludes that the Word moves the Angels, the Angels move the wind, and the wind moves the air, as is shown in the Appendix...

## The first part of this appendix, extracted from the sixth chapter of the sixth book of the *Table of the Revelation of Divine Majesty*, comprised in the first chapter of Genesis: in which the Author sharply rebukes the doctrine of the Heathens and their Christian disciples.

<margin>Deuteronomy 6</margin>
The writings of the Heathens <note>original: *Ethnicorum*; referring here to the classical Greek and Roman authors</note> have so thoroughly taken the prize in Christian schools that the schoolmasters themselves know or understand little or nothing of the Biblical writings of the Old and New Testaments. This is despite the fact that God, in His first decree—in which He spoke with Moses and the Israelites—commanded that the fear of God be instilled in both the young and the old, and indeed in all the people. They were to call upon Him alone and observe His precepts, ordinances, and decrees. For His servant Moses, by divine command, addressed the entire Israelite people in this way: "These are the precepts, customs, and laws which the Lord your God commanded that I should teach you, and that you should learn and do in the region you are entering to occupy; so that you may fear the Lord your God and observe all His mandates and precepts which I enjoin upon you and your children and grandchildren through all your life, so that you may live long. Hear, O Israel, and observe, so that you may do what God commands you, that it may go well with you and you may be greatly multiplied, just as the God of your fathers spoke to you, in a land flowing with milk and honey. Hear, O Israel: The Lord your God is one. Love the Lord your God with all your heart, and all your soul, and all your strength. And these words which I command you today shall always be kept in your heart; you shall announce them to your children and remember them, and you shall speak of them when you are in your house or walking on the path, when you sit down or rise up. You shall bind them as a sign upon your hand, and they shall be as a memorial before your eyes, and you shall write them upon the posts of your door. You shall fear the Lord your God and serve Him alone. You shall not swear by His name, nor worship the foreign gods of those peoples who surround you. For the Lord your God is a jealous God in your midst, lest the anger of the Lord burn against you and consume you from the face of the earth. You shall not tempt the Lord your God."

<column-break/>

Here you see (my fellow Christians) in what way God opened a school for His children: by ordering, namely, that the fear and precepts of the Lord be presented and instilled in infants right from their cradles. Indeed, they should carry the divine precepts with them in their hearts, remember them, and speak of them, whether they sit at home under their own roofs, or travel abroad through foreign places—whether they are carried, or ride, or sleep, or walk, or rise. Not only must they remember them, but they must also put them into action and arrange their lives according to them with all their strength. And, lest they should ever forget them, but instead always carry them in their present memory, they are commanded to bind the divine precepts as a sign on their hands and to write them for a perpetual memorial on the walls of their houses and the posts of their doors. 

But if they do not obey those divine precepts, but instead go so far as to tempt God—as if the matter were not serious or as if no punishment would be inflicted on transgressors—God threatens them in that case with the most cruel and heavy punishments: that He will wipe them off the face of the earth. Although these things were most rightly ordained by God, you nevertheless allege many empty and futile reasons to the contrary. You claim that the youth can neither perceive nor understand such "difficult matters" regarding God and His divine precepts, and much less can they put them into practice. Therefore, you argue, easier and less difficult things should be presented to them: namely, **Aesop’s Fables**, the **couplets of Cato**, **Virgil’s Bucolics** <note>Pastoral poems by the Roman poet Virgil, often used to teach Latin grammar</note>, and other writings of the Heathens which have been the daily and customary fare in Christian schools until now, on the grounds that they better suit the youth. Furthermore, you say that for the sake of the mind, the comedies of **Terence** and **Plautus** should be read through, and even the books of "Saint" **Aristotle** <note>The author uses "Saint" sarcastically here to mock the high status given to the Greek philosopher Aristotle in Christian education</note> should be handed over—books in which he treats natural and supernatural things and the essence of God, while describing the order of the world and the heavens. From these books, you claim, the youth can draw knowledge of God and His divine creatures...

Afterward, brief interpretations are to be handed to them, so that they may practice them with one another through questions and answers. And although they may not fully understand all these things throughout infancy, they nevertheless perceive this benefit: they can retain them with a firm memory until they grow up, attain mature judgment, and inquire into their true sense and understanding. Furthermore, by this method, they grow accustomed from an early age to speaking of God and hearing others discourse about Him. After these things, higher matters in the **divine law**, the **Prophets**, and the **Psalms** can easily be proposed and drummed into them, and simultaneously the interpretations of the same can be handed down. Thus, through accurate and daily exercise, they may perceive, understand, and retain all those things better and more correctly, since they are distracted and hindered by no **Heathen** follies regarding them. And these things are indeed performed piously: upon such instruction, God bestows the **Holy Spirit** and divine blessing, art, science, and understanding.

But you dismiss all these things and bring forth your **Heathen Doctors**. You must expend much labor and trouble upon them before you can drum that Heathen doctrine into your children and disciples. Simultaneously, your disciples consume a great deal of time—even ten, twenty, and sometimes thirty years—before they drink in and learn those subtle tricks for circumventing others. Yet, when all these things have been so clearly perceived that nothing remains which they have not thoroughly mastered, they are not much more learned than **German Michael** <note>original: *Michael ille germanus*; a personification of the simple, uneducated German commoner</note>, and they know neither God nor His creatures,

### APPENDIX TO THE FIRST SECTION

<margin>Baruch 3</margin>
Oh, you delirious fools! Which of the unclean spirits suggested to you that Philosophy—or, as you call it, "wisdom"—must be sought from the Devil and his sons, the pagan <note>original: *Ethnicorum*; literally "the nations," used here to mean non-Christian, classical Greek and Roman authors</note> deserters of God? This is despite God himself testifying that He alone is the true fountain and source of wisdom. Have you not understood well enough that God has opened only a single school, in which He commanded that He alone be feared, His mandates observed, and He alone be served? How do these things fit together: that you attempt to have a school of sacred literature, and yet simultaneously build a pagan school for the Devil himself? For you cannot serve both God and the Devil. Furthermore, that school of yours, which you call "Theology," does not have a form pleasing to God. For you admit no Teacher into it unless he has first perceived and absorbed the basic elements—or even the total and full foundations—of pagan writers. Indeed, you assert that such a man is finally fit to teach Holy Scripture, so that the Devil sits at the helm <note>original: *ad clavum*; literally "at the tiller" of a ship</note> in both these schools of yours in a horrific way, manifestly and publicly circumventing men and drawing them to himself. Therefore, you yourselves, oh most wretched students, consider these things more deeply at some point; shake off this Diabolical yoke, desert your impious schools, and turn to your God, the most fit schoolmaster <term>ludimoderatorem; a headmaster or teacher of a grammar school</term>, who freely offers and promises you knowledge, arts, and wisdom—nay, even the Holy Spirit and eternal life. For you see that in those pagan schools, the fear of the Lord and Divine precepts and mandates are neither bound to the hand nor inscribed upon walls, posts, or doors—as God otherwise commanded to be done for a perpetual memory of them—and much less does anyone remember them or speak of them at home or in the country, while sleeping, walking, or rising. Instead, the opposite is before your eyes: namely, that all houses, walls, dining rooms, windows, doors, posts, books, cups, plates, small disks, knives, swords, spears, and rings are filled with the maxims and sayings of pagan sages in place of God and the fear of His divine precepts—lest, forsooth, the owners of those things ever forget their Teacher and his doctrine. This is truly to tempt God and one's Lord impudently. For while these men erect pagan schools instead of opening schools to God, and in this way blaspheme God—implying that this business is not a serious matter to Him nor close to His heart—and therefore, because of this transgression of the divine mandate, they need be subject to no punishment at all, they tempt God in this very act: namely, when they invoke Him for the granting

<column-break/>

of the Holy Spirit, yet meanwhile they try out diabolical doctrine. On which account the Lord has sworn that He will destroy those blasphemers and tempters from the face of the earth.

That aforementioned school, which God himself instituted, was meant to be like the Mother and origin of His Israelite Church, from which so many Priests, Levites, Singers, and Deacons came forth. They read, taught, and learned Divine doctrine along with the Prophets and political sanctions in the Church of God—from Moses until the coming of Christ—in such a way that from all these things, by the power of God, they knew all His creatures most fully. They acquired such wisdom for themselves that they certainly foresaw the future: that the Messiah, the true Son of God, would be born of a Virgin in Bethlehem of Judea. And afterward, when Christ was born and went up to the temple in His own time, He found there Teachers and students reading and teaching Moses and the Prophets, without any depravity, corruption, or mixture of pagan doctrine. But because they were unwilling to believe that the true Messiah had already been presented and that the Law and the Prophets had reached their goal and end in the Christ there present, Christ therefore transformed that Jewish Church into the Christian Church, instituted Baptism in place of circumcision, and introduced new schools and Teachers. And they also preached unanimously against the doctrine of the pagans and their idolatry, and referred the people back to Christ alone: namely, that He is the true God with the Father and the Holy Spirit, equal in Majesty, glory, and power. They taught that He assumed true humanity for the sake of our sins, was crucified for our sins, and in this way redeemed us from eternal death; that He rose again on the third day from the dead, ascended into heaven, and sits at the right hand of God, from whence He shall come to judge the living and the dead. This doctrine was in full vigor during the time of the twelve Apostles and for a long time after their departure, with all Pagan Doctrine having been exploded <note>original: *explosa*; a theatrical term meaning hissed off the stage or rejected</note> and many of their books burned—until finally those perverse pagans, who even before the birth of Christ were held in price and authority outside the Church of God, again insinuated themselves among Christians through their books. They mixed themselves in and sowed their poison among them, and by their sophistries turned many Christians away from the Christian faith once it had been recognized and received. Furthermore, they filled all the schools of the Christians with their books, as is observed daily before everyone's eyes in these times of ours. For Satan [did] so much to those pagan Sophists...

Once this is done, the word of God will grow vigorously and remain firm, just as was done in the time of Paul in <margin>Acts 19</margin> Ephesus, where a great many books were burned. Indeed, if anyone wishes to turn away and remove an evil, it is necessary to remove the cause of the evil. If you wish that an infant not be harmed by a knife, the little knife must be taken away and removed from him. Since, therefore, such great damage is brought upon the Christian Church through pagan books, all Princes ought rightfully to apply themselves diligently to this: that at the first opportunity they remove and withdraw the doctrine of the pagans and their books from their schools and burn them with fire. They should also strictly—and under threat of the heaviest punishment—prohibit and forbid the printing <note>original: *impressionem*</note> and distribution of them. Furthermore, they should undertake consultation and deliberation with learned, skilled, and prudent men as to how schools may be established and opened everywhere according to the prescription of the Divine mandate. In these schools, only the fear of God and divine precepts should be taught and read, along with the Prophets, Psalms, Gospels, and the political laws <note>original: *politicis sanctionibus*; refers to the civil and legal codes found in the Pentateuch</note> of Moses. At the same time, it must be observed with the greatest zeal and accurate diligence that this poison and "sophistry" of the pagans does not creep back in secretly or within private walls, thereby overturning the whole business once again. In this way, the devil can be resisted, so that he no longer has the power to stir up such a miserable evil in the Christian Church. For all his works are empty, and he dreams of nothing but the very emptiness by which he leads men away from God. I would wish you, who are students, to be warned of this. Furthermore, it is also a marvel to hear that Jews, Turks, and pagans hate our books so much that they not only do not read them, but they even consider it a crime and a sin if someone should even grasp a single leaf of them with his hand. So greatly, to be sure, do they love and protect their own religion and doctrine,

<column-break/>

lest anything of Christianity be mixed into it. They also rejoice greatly when they hear or see their abominable books held in such high price and honor among us, so much so that they are not only publicly presented in our schools and debated, but even sermons are delivered to the people from the pulpit <note>original: *suggestu*</note> based on them, and their opinions and sayings are cited for the confirmation of our own doctrine and religion. From this, again, a maximum evil emerges: that while we attempt to convert the pagans through our Christian doctrine, we nevertheless meanwhile use the writings of pagans while neglecting the school of God. They conclude that our doctrine is entirely false, and that theirs, by contrast, is true and blameless. Consequently, they prefer to persist in their pagan profession rather than be converted to the true Christian faith—especially since we ourselves, who are Christians, agree with their opinions and thus become "pagan-like." They do not consider that God will not let these "Pagan-Christians" go unpunished. But if anyone wishes to convert the pagans from their idolatry and their false and fictitious doctrine to the true Christian Church, he must proceed by a far different path and method. Indeed, not only must all their books be cast out from the schools and the entire Christian Church and burned, but it will also be necessary to refute, disprove, and break their false dogmas with the solid foundations of Christian truth. On the contrary, one must profess and preach the true doctrine of love and divine precepts, together with the Holy Gospel, with constant and pious zeal. For by this means they will finally learn and understand who God our Creator, Redeemer, Protector, and Savior is, and that their false doctrine and idolatry is entirely displeasing to Him and is condemned. Most of all, they will learn that all those who are not baptized, nor believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God, have no life in themselves but are to be condemned with the Devil. By contrast, those who believe in Christ shall rise again with Him and shall occupy the kingdom of heaven by hereditary right, possessing it for all eternity in the highest joy and gladness before the face of God. Indeed, this is what all Christians most desire: that it might also happen for the pagans, and that they might obtain and possess the kingdom of God together with them, provided they are truly converted to the Christian faith. For the Gospel is lawfully announced even to the pagans, and the gate of heaven is open to all those who turn to Christ and His kingdom and seek it from the heart. From this you now see, you patrons and schoolmasters of "Pagan-Christian" schools, how—
