The type <note>The "type" or "typical world" refers to the physical universe as a reflection of a higher reality.</note> was created above all things in and from one and the same Unity, but in a threefold manner: namely, through the emergence of a single thing like an eternal square from the One (as if from an eternal root), and through the return of that emanation into a Cubic form, for the completion of the *Archetype of all Ideal things*. By this, the three divine properties in a single essence may be easily discerned, as well as the manner in which all things of the *typical* world were folded together and ideally encompassed within that *Archetype* before creation. We conclude, therefore, that according to that ideal image, this *Typical* world was afterwards formed in a triplicity of variety and proportionally adapted, namely, to the pattern of the divine likeness. For, from the unity in its divine and hidden existence—which was originally concealed from us as if in darkness or a potential chaos—there emanated the most brilliant flame of the formal Universal essence; and the spirit of wisdom, proceeding from both, joined that formal emanation with the potential matter of the waters. Thus, by the union of these three—namely, the divine light and the substantial matter of the darkness (that is, the water)—the heavens and the Earth and consequently the whole world existed beforehand, as *St. Peter* <margin>2 Peter 3:10</margin> testifies. But the *Royal Psalmist* <note>Referring to King David, the traditional author of the Psalms.</note> confirms these things best in these few words: *By the Word* (he says) *of the Lord the heavens were made firm, and by the spirit of his mouth all their power.* In this speech he reveals everything: for by the *Lord* he understands the *Father*, from whom are all things; by the *Word*, the *Son*, through whom are all things; and the spirit from the mouth of both as the mediator, by whom all essence and active power in this world is derived.

We can conclude, therefore, that if the unities of the Ideal world are from a single radical unity, extracted like sons from one *Father*, and are included by that same unity (which is infinite in itself), it must necessarily follow that the triple member of this created world must be in and from that unity. This is because the *Typical* world with its members was made in the image and representation of the *Archetype*, which is that eternal monad <note>A "monad" is a technical term for a single, indivisible unit or the Divine One.</note> in which all things exist. Hence it is said, not without justice, by the *Apostle* <note>St. Paul</note> that he is "all in all." <margin>Colossians 3:11; Colossians 1:16; Romans 11:36</margin> And again: "All things are created through him and in him, and he was before all things, and all things consist in him." And elsewhere: "From him, through him, and in him are all things." Whence he is not unjustly called the circumference and the center—the center of all things, whose circumference is nowhere. Hence *Solomon*: "The *Hand of the Almighty* <margin>Wisdom 11:18</margin> made the world out of formless matter." ## CHAPTER III.
*How the lovely and splendid light of Universal and life-giving Love shone forth from the fountain of all goodness, and removed the litigious and hateful darkness from the throne of the obscure Chaos or the deformed Abyss, so that thereafter the most beautiful world might be created out of Nothing by its actual presence and be adorned with its divine beauty.*

It is admirable and beyond human capacity to grasp how from a single Unity in essence, two branches should grow out, differing so much from each other in property and character: namely, darkness, which is the origin of formlessness, error, deformity, contention, privation, and death; and light, which is the vehicle and sole cause of formation, truth, beauty, love, position, and life. It is not for nothing that the Manichaeans <note>A dualistic religious movement founded by the prophet Mani, teaching a struggle between a good spiritual world of light and an evil material world of darkness.</note> held with such confidence that there were two co-eternal principles, one of which they recognized as God, whom they acknowledged as the prince of light and the author of life, sanctity, and all goodness; and they fashioned the other as the devil, whom they repeatedly called the prince of darkness and the origin or beginning of contention, death, sickness, and all evil. And they thought the devil himself was co-eternal with God in his essence, since there can be no goodness which does not have a relation to its contrary, namely malice. By this reasoning (I say) they wish for a God of malice and depravity to be co-eternal in his existence with the God of goodness; by these imaginations of theirs, they not only attempt to exclude the devil from the limbo of creatures, but also to expel unity from the limits of nature and to erect and crown the Dyad or duality (which in the truth of the matter is nothing other than a confusion of unities) in its place. And truly this point or this doubt seemed to be of such difficult discussion and resolution that some of the wiser Poets and Philosophers seemed to have wished to fly somewhat higher in this matter, as if through certain mystical and allegorical expressions of theirs, which they involved in fabulous discourses in an enigmatic manner. Among whom a Poet by the name of Pronapis asserts in his *Protocosmos* <note>The "First World" or "First Order of the Universe."</note> that Demogorgon <note>A deity or being associated with the underworld and the origin of the universe in later classical mythology.</note> (by whom he understands the highest of the Gods) was surrounded on all sides with Eternity and rude Chaos before all things; and he imagines that at a certain time, while Eternity remained in its majesty, he suddenly noticed a great tumult and commotion arising in the bowels of Chaos. Wherefore, so that he might offer help to it in this difficult birth, he stretches out his hand to the one in labor and, by performing the office of a midwife, he caused it suddenly to bring forth a certain monster, deformed and tempestuous, whose name on account of its contentious condition was *Litigium* <note>Strife or Dispute.</note>; which, after it had excited great perturbations and commotions in the air, and attempted with other ambitious things to fly upward and fight against Demogorgon its Creator, was immediately cast down by Demogorgon into the deep abyss. But observing that Chaos had labored again with a new birth, and that in its labors it had sent forth fervent sighs with heavy sweats, he himself did not wish to remove his hand from it until it had brought forth a second birth, in which Pan was born with his three sisters, who were called the *Fates*. When indeed Demogorgon was captured by the remarkable beauty and form of Pan, he made him the presiding officer and governor of all worldly affairs, and commanded his three sisters to obey the mandates of their brother in the manner of handmaidens and ministers. And it followed thereafter that Chaos, now relieved of its burden or that great heap or mass with which it labored, established its Pan (Demogorgon so persuading) upon its Throne. This is that parabolic fable concerning Demogorgon and Chaos commonly recited by the Poets. Their allegory implies that the generation and procreation of all things proceed from the Most High and supreme God the Creator, whom they signify by Demogorgon, to whom Eternity is joined by an indissoluble bond in a single essential society: since he alone is to be called eternal, who is and always was the principle or first cause of all things. And they also imagine that Chaos claims a third place for itself in that eternal society, because it is (according to Ovid's account) that confused and undigested matter or subject from which all things of this world are composed: and for this reason the Ancients handed down that it was co-eternal with God, as being that rude heap from which Demogorgon, the Father of universals, created or formed all things according to his will: and consequently they thought that subject or matter to be the general Mother of all things, from whom and upon whom the Universal Father of all things begat and formed all things: whence...

And yet they seem to agree in this: namely, that God was the primary cause, and they wish for **Chaos** itself to serve in the place of a passive partner to **Demogorgon** <note>A primordial deity in late classical mythology, often associated with the deep or the origin of the gods</note>, so that from her, as if from a universal mother, he might generate all things. Wherefore they conclude that Chaos proceeded from God and is by no means to be divided from him, and also serves him in the place of a female Companion for generation and procreation: not otherwise than **Eve**, extracted from **Adam**, was called a companion and a helpmate to him in the production of the human race. This is the opinion of both the Ethnic <note>Pagan or non-Christian</note> Philosophers and the mystical Cabalists.

But I shall proceed to the explanation of the aforementioned allegory: The **Hand of Demogorgon** signifies divine power; the first-born and deformed Chaos—namely, **Strife** <note>original: "Litigium"</note>—signifies the prince of darkness, who is the Father of opposition and discord. Whence, on account of his ambitious rebellion against the Lord of light and life, he was cast headlong into the whirlpool of the dark **Abyss**. By his second birth, which was **Pan** <note>The god of the wild, here representing the totality of Nature</note>, they indicate the universal nature of the world and the harmonious arrangement of the **Elements**: arguing from this that after that great discord or commotion and through the disturbance which presented itself in the primeval expansion of Chaos, a peaceful concord followed in his second birth, which was as beautiful and acceptable to God in this last birth as the deformed discord was foul, hateful, and ungrateful to him in the first.

By these things, therefore, you may see how all the Elements in the beginning struggled and contended in the belly of confused Chaos. The three **Fates** <note>original: "Parcae"</note> or fatal sisters called **Clotho**, **Lachesis**, and **Atropos**, who were with Pan, denote the three orders of time: namely, the present, the past, and the future. To the care of Clotho the present time is committed, and her office is to spin the thread of life; Lachesis presides over the future time, looking toward that material—whether hempen or linen—which Clotho sets out to spin; and Atropos over the past time, which is irreparable and irrevocable, signifying by the cutting of the thread that the work is finished.

I infer upon this parabolic relation that even if Chaos or the dark Abyss were with God and in God before the creation of the world, nevertheless the infinite and sole eternal unity and radical essence created and produced it out of itself. For He speaks these things in His own person: *I am the Lord, and there shall be no other, forming the light and creating the darkness, making peace and creating evil* <note>Isaiah 45:7</note>. As if he had said: I am the Father of light or of the shining Spirit of wisdom, and I created the Dark Chaos, from which I then introduced into this world both the existence of the world and the harmony of the Elements—that is, strife and peace. So it is evident that there is but one unique eternal unity, which in itself is male and female: and everything that can be imagined, which produced all things from itself and in itself, not otherwise than Adam contained within himself Eve, who was then afterwards the mother of the microcosm. Hence says **Mercurius Trismegistus**: <margin>Divine Pymander</margin> *But Mind, the God, being most full of the fecundity of both sexes, being life and light, brought forth by his word another mind.*

And the scriptures seem to testify to this same thing, saying: *Shall I, who grant generation to others, be sterile?* Wherefore it is manifest that from one and the same radically and eternally existing unity, both the matter and the forms of all things proceed; and that they appear, in respect to their existence and progressions, only "aevial" <note>term: aevial (from 'aevum'), meaning having a beginning but no end, as opposed to 'eternal' which has neither</note>—that is, having beginnings but being without end—even though in their essential root (namely in God, the most hidden unity of unities from which they proceed) they are eternal.

Thus, just as the dark Abyss, or obscure Chaos, and the bright informing Spirit are two opposite principles and contrary to each other in condition and property (for from the dark principle proceed discord, evil, cold, freezing, rest, death, privation, negation, or "un-will"; whereas from the bright region, which is the type of beauty and grace, are derived light, concord, goodness, and will), so also both of these are nothing but general branches rising from one and the same essential unity. Since they cannot exceed the limits of their infinite source, they are in him light and darkness, and consequently differ in no way in their essence from the root from which they spring, which is all in all. Hence the Psalmist says: <margin>Psalm 139</margin> *Darkness is to him* who is only one and the same in himself, from whom, through whom, and in whom are all things. <margin>Romans 11</margin> For his will and his "un-will" are only one in him, who is one simple **Identity**; and that which is his will is both his affirmation and his negation, which are nothing but a unique good in him, who is total goodness. And yet, in respect to the creature, when his negation dominates, he hides the light of his kindly countenance, and the whole is as if darkness, and then he works privatively toward us. For where he hides his face, all things appear deformed, empty, and destitute of essence and goodness. Behold here the negative or privative will, which can rightly be named "un-will" in respect to us, because in his willing in respect to himself, he seems to "un-will" in respect to men, to whom he denies his presence. Behold, here is the effect of negation or "un-will" <note>Latin: *noluntas*, a term coined to describe the opposite of *voluntas* (will), meaning a refusal or turning away.</note> described from this side; for the mental ray does not flow out to the petitioner, but is contracted and reserved within itself. In these two contrary actions, we observe only a single laudable effect in this unity alone: For, although my mind grants through a friendly and merciful emanation of the mental ray, so that it smiles upon the expectation of the petitioner; or if, on the contrary, a certain petition is denied to his great loss or evil, nevertheless, to the mind of both the one refusing and the one willing, both affirmation and negation appear manifest, so that both are to me but one and the same in effect, however much they appear to differ to the petitioner. By the same reasoning, in the eternal and archetypal unity (which is also called the Divine Mind, of which the human intellect or mind is the type and image), the act of both will and un-will is one and the same, and it is nothing but goodness in that which is total and absolute goodness, which admits no contrariety within itself, even though to the creature, who is subject to the effects of both His privative and positive will, the privative or negative action seems evil: just as, on the contrary, His positive or affirmative emanation, being full of kindness and love, is held by the creature as good and consequently received with joy: Are we not taught by holy authority that *good and evil, life and death, poverty and riches are from God?* <note>Sirach 11:14</note> And elsewhere; that, *when God hides His face from the creatures they are troubled, when He takes away their spirit, they expire, and when He sends forth His spirit they are restored by good.* And elsewhere: *Your visitation preserves my spirit.* And again: *Lift up Your face and send light upon us, and it shall cause us to see light and shall make our darkness shining.* And the Prophet:

Again, they call this same unity **Dionysus** during the night, namely in its dark or privative property, asserting that under this title it is accustomed to tear the creature—created or composed during the dominion of Apollo or the daytime—into seven parts: so that they seem to argue that one and the same unity is in essence the author of destruction and corruption as much as of generation and life-giving: Wherefore they assign double names to it, not in respect to its essence, which is unique, but by reason of its properties, namely so that they may distinguish one property of the same essence from another by a variation of the name. Hence it is called by the **Cabalists** <note>Followers of Jewish mysticism</note> in its one property, namely the privative and dark one, **Dark Aleph** <note>original: "Aleph Tenebrosum"</note>, namely, when it contracts its rays into itself or turns its face away from the creature: But in its other property, namely the positive and bright one, they call it **Bright Aleph** <note>original: "Aleph lucidum"</note>; namely when it emits rays of kindness, beauty, and life. From these things, therefore, it appears to Christians that the Heathens or Gentiles, along with the Holy Scriptures, recognized and committed to parabolic writings that it is in the power of one and the same radical unity to save and to destroy, that is, to give life or to take it away, either to will or not to will, and (so to speak) to work all things in all according to its pleasure: And so you have it confirmed that two members of opposite natures gush forth from a single eternal root, and that those members or essential and principal properties act in a contrary manner in the world, and consequently produce effects differing from one another: Whence it is clear that since the waters, from which and through which (as **St. Peter** witnesses) the heavens and the earth formerly came forth from the dark abyss and were as it were the second birth of **Chaos** itself, which the Poets feign to be **Pan** or universal moist nature; it will be very easy for the wise Philosopher to consider that the passive portion of this world inclines toward the property and conditions of darkness by a certain natural instinct, so that if it were not

### CHAPTER IV.

->*In which it is clearly proven, as much by the opinion of the ancients, both Poets and Philosophers, as by the authority of the sacred scriptures and other firm reasons, what the soul of the world is and from what principles it is composed.*<-

At the entrance of this discourse on the Soul of the World, it is my purpose to review the opinions of the ancient Cabalists and mystical Rabbis, as well as the wise Philosophers, concerning this subject—a subject so condemned by certain men unskilled and ignorant of such profound mysteries, yet established and celebrated with such constancy by others who, with the lynx-like eyes of their intellect, have penetrated into the secret bowels of nature and have contemplated its central and eternal essence <note>original: *gentem*, likely a typo for *entem* (being/entity)</note> with due reverence. Then, afterwards, it is my intent to explain that concordance which exists between their opinions and the sense or mind of the sacred scriptures. I begin: it is the opinion of the Cabalists that the great Angel whom they call by the name *Metatron* (which name they interpret as "the Gift of God") is that Universal <note>original: *Catholicus*</note> spirit who universally animates the entire world. Whence <margin>Reuchlin, *On the Art of the Cabala*, Book 3.</margin> Rabbi Moses takes him to be the general "active intellect" from which all particular forms descend. And they maintain that from this universal spirit proceed all virtues—animal and vital as well as natural—which they also call Angels, whose number is infinite in respect to us. Among the Philosophers, Democritus, Orpheus, along with various followers of Pythagoras, did not wander far from these opinions of the Rabbis and Cabalists, differing only in the variety of names; they thought that all things were full of Gods, whom they adored in creatures with various worship and differing ceremonies (by offering sacrifices), yet with such consideration and caution preceding them that they referred all these Gods to the one Jupiter—or rather Jehovah—the eternal unity and Father of all things. Nevertheless, this intention of theirs, being poorly understood by the ignorant, was the chief occasion of Idolatry among the Heathens, inasmuch as under this pretext they venerated the creatures in place of the Creator, or the divinity within the creatures. For this reason Solomon said: *Vain are all men by nature, in whom there is ignorance of God,* <margin>Wisdom 13:1.</margin> *and who from those good things that are seen, could not understand him who is, nor by considering the works did they acknowledge the craftsman, but took the creature for the creator.* By a clearly similar reason, the Platonists called that universal virtue, by whose mediation all things are generated and preserved, the "Soul of the World." The Arabian Astrologers also seem to agree with these intentions, for it is their mind to assign a peculiar soul to every single thing of this world, derived from this general Universal spirit. To this opinion Mercurius Trismegistus, Theophrastus, Avicenna, Algazel, and others—both Stoics and Peripatetics—seem to adhere. Again, Zoroaster and Heraclitus of Ephesus conclude that this world soul is an immense invisible fire, from which and through whose action all things are generated, and by the power of the Spirit "nourishes from within, and Mind, infused through the limbs, moves the whole mass" <note>A famous quote from Virgil's *Aeneid*, Book VI</note> etc.
Marcus Manilius, Boethius, and Augurellus seem to fall into the opinion of Virgil.
Manilius moreover has these words:
*This work, constructed of the body of the immense world,
The Divine force of the soul rules* etc.

*You connect the soul of a triple nature, moving all things,
In the middle.*

From the vitals of the humid nature, a pure and light fire immediately flew forth and sought the heights; the air also, being a light spirit, took its place in the middle region between water and fire; but the earth and water lay so mixed together that the face of the earth, being overwhelmed, appeared nowhere, etc.* By which it is evidently proved that this thin spiritual water or humid nature is no more deprived of a soul than the human spirit is destitute of the vivifying act of life. For, as in the soul of any living creature two things are chiefly required—namely, the agent and the patient—so where one of these is missing, no created soul can exist. Indeed, if the <term>Soul of the World</term> <note>original: *anima mundi*; the spirit that animates the entire universe</note> were the mere inspiration of God without the vehicle of the created humid Spirit (which is the matter of heaven), then that life of the world would be a simple <term>Identity</term> <note>original: *Identitas*; a state of being exactly the same, without variation</note> and of one and the same property; consequently, there would be no variety of action in the world, nor any contradiction or dilation of things in <term>Systole and Diastole</term> <note>The rhythmic contraction and expansion, like a heartbeat</note>, and it would then follow that neither action nor passion would be in the soul. For without a passive nature, an active virtue cannot subsist, just as a passive thing cannot exist without active motion. The Chaos (as has been said) stood in the place of the feminine or passive toward the act of <term>Demogorgon</term> <note>A primordial creator deity or force</note> or God. Likewise, the act or form which proceeds from the emanation or outflow of divine light is the masculine source and spring of action, just as the waters, which are obtained from the belly of Chaos, are the subject of passion. From this, therefore, it is easy to gather first what the Soul of the World is, and consequently of how many and what parts it consists. And again, that it is a creature is declared in this: that it is not Identity, but <term>Alterity</term> <note>original: *alteritas*; "otherness" or diversity, as opposed to the oneness of God</note>, such as is the existence of Angels. Now, that this soul is Alterity, and consequently created, is established insofar as it consists of two things according to the consistency of an Angel; namely, its internal is that light or vivifying flame which proceeds immediately from the bright and splendid emission of the eternal Spirit, while its external is the created <term>aerial spirit</term> <note>original: *Spiritus avialis*; likely a typo for *aerialis*, the subtle vapor of the heavens</note> or the purer and more limpid substance of the upper waters, which is created and animated by the act or virtue of the <term>Divine Spirit</term>. And since the nature of the most essential and never-dying fire of life is said to be everywhere and in every place of the world—for the 
<margin>Colossians 3:11, Ephesians 4, Ecclesiastes 1, Wisdom 12:1, Isaiah 66:1, Wisdom 1</margin> Scriptures say that *Christ fills all things and that he is all in all*; and that the *Spirit of God is in heaven, in hell, in the uttermost parts of the sea, in the night and darkness, etc.*; and that *God poured out his wisdom upon all his works*; and that the *incorruptible Spirit of God is in every thing*; and that *heaven is his throne and the earth his footstool*; and that the *Spirit of wisdom fills the world*—insofar, I say, as He is in every particle of the world and in its universal spirit, so that now, because of His presence, that which was previously vile and deformed is full of dignity. It is certain that it is this alone—the uncreated, eternal, and central Spirit within its external created spirit of the world—which makes the world live. Therefore, this Angelic spirit or this "Alterity" is called the Soul of the World: because it is that universal or general Spirit of the world, animated by the purest and bright Spirit of the upper waters, and animated from the beginning, which gives life to all things. Hence, that question so often agitated among the <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle</note>, and resolved with such poverty of wit, can be fully explained and resolved by this kind of solid speculation: namely, what is the difference between the soul, the divine mind, and the spirit? transgression, because my name is in him, etc.: where by "his name" he understands the Word or the divine Spirit in the external Angelic being, which inspires and animates it, as appears from the preceding passage in Wisdom 10:17. Moreover, that the divine mind, which by its act vivifies the world when taken simply, is an absolute efflux of the mind or eternal unity into the mundane spirit, we gather from this Text: The living word of God divides and discerns the soul <margin>Hebrews 4.</margin> and the spirit: where by "speech" or "word" is understood the mental ray, and by "spirit" is intended the moist and passive nature of the world, which exists by the presence of the word or mental ray; by the removal of which the soul of the creature is annihilated through the disjunction of its parts. Concerning the removal and application of that mental spirit from the soul of the creature, David says this: When God takes back his spirit from the creatures, they expire; when he sends forth his spirit, they are recreated by good, etc. <margin>Psalm 104:29-30.</margin> By which things both the creation of the soul from the union of the mundane spirits with that divine one, as well as the division and separation of the Divine spirit from the mundane spirit, is proved. But now I shall show all this through some definitions of the soul in general by certain Fathers of the Church and Philosophers, both Christian and Gentile, as much in how it relates to a body as how it is considered simply in itself and in its separate condition: Damascenus says: that the soul is a spiritual substance, emanating from divine fountains, simple, indissoluble, immortal, free, incorporeal, and indivisible, lacking quantity, figure, weight, and color. <margin>Damascenus.</margin> To which Saint Bernard also agrees, and Augustine defines it in this manner: It is a divine mind understanding all things, and assimilating itself to all things. <margin>Bernard, Augustine.</margin> And for this very reason some Philosophers maintain that it was formed after the likeness of the spirit of wisdom, which is known to be the image of God: <margin>Wisdom 7.</margin> since it carries with it, and contains in itself, the likeness of every thing: therefore it is defined by them as the likeness of every thing: whence it has the power in itself of comprehending all things. Again, it is assimilated to every thing, insofar as it is one in all. There are also among the Mystic Philosophers those who conclude the nature of the human soul more fully in this definition: The soul is a certain divine light created in the image of the Word, the cause of causes, the first exemplar, a substance of God, and figured by his son, whose character is the eternal word. <margin>Agrippa, Book 3, Chapter 37.</margin> Others define it thus: It is incorporeal, adorned with every beauty, assimilated to the holy Trinity, shadowed by eternal glory; or thus: It is an intellectual spirit always living, always in motion. And according to the duty of its work, it is called by various names: It is called *Life* while it vegetates; *Spirit* while it contemplates; *Sense* while it feels; *Animus* <note>The rational soul</note> while it is wise; *Mind* while it understands; *Reason* while it discerns; *Memory* while it remembers; and when it wills, it is called *Will*.

## OF THE SECOND SECTION, BOOK I.

But all those things are nothing but one essence, though diverse in their properties, etc. Where [one considers] that mind and spirit not according to essence, but in respect to their properties of acting: I, however, have touched upon them as if they were the constituent parts of the soul. I would have you know, moreover, that these later definitions are assigned to it insofar as it converses with the body. Now indeed, if in the proper manner we examine all those descriptions of the essence and properties of the soul, both in its state of liberty <note>The soul's state before or after being in a body.</note> and during the time of its incarceration in the human body, we shall find that they seem in no way to differ from my aforementioned intention.

For first, it is proved that it is the offspring of divinity or of a divine emanation, and then that it has for its external [covering] the most subtle created **spirit of the world** <note>Latin: *spiritum mundi*. A vital, subtle substance believed by alchemists and Neoplatonists to permeate the universe.</note>; which mixture creates that "otherness," or a composition made of two: namely, from the bright emission of the external source and the worldly spirit. Therefore, in the aforementioned definitions, it is called (in respect to its internal part):
*   In the first definition: a **spiritual substance** emanating from the divine source.
*   In the second: a **divine mind**.
*   In the third: an **image or likeness** of divine wisdom.
*   In the fourth: a **divine light** according to the image of the Word and the substance of God, whose Character is the Word.
*   In the fifth: a **likeness of the holy Trinity**, made equal to divine glory.

That this divinity participates with the worldly spirit appears from the sixth and seventh definitions, in which (in respect to its external substance) it is called a **spirit**, which breathes in the body and is the vehicle of the formal act, which is the effect of the power of the divine ray. Therefore, the union of the worldly spirit with the divine mind constitutes the **soul**, so that the soul includes the mind and the spirit—of which the former is uncreated and the latter created—acting as the internal and external of a single "otherness" or Angelic composition.

These things having been considered in the first place, I shall proceed to confirm the aforementioned opinions of the Philosophers and Cabalists by holy testimonies. And first, I shall begin with the great Angel of the Cabalists, **Metatron**, as if a gift of God; whom they say is the Universal <note>Latin: *Catholicum*, meaning universal or all-encompassing in this philosophical context.</note> intellectual agent, from whom all particular forms descend. <margin>1 Timothy 6:13</margin> The Apostle says, *That he himself gives life to all things.* <margin>Proverbs 3</margin> And Solomon: *That the Spirit of Wisdom is the tree of life and the fountain and origin of life.* And if that spirit be the fountain of life, then I would have you look upon these words of the son of <margin>Ecclesiasticus 1:9</margin> Sirach: *God poured out wisdom over all his works and over all flesh according to his gift.* And here was that Universal and Angelic spirit, which God, like a spiritual messenger, sent out from himself in the form of an emanation, to move upon the waters and to inform and enliven them, not only generally in the greater world <note>The Macrocosm/Universe.</note>, but also in every small particle of the same.

And this emanation was in the Word of the Lord, by whom all things were made and quickened, as in whom there was life, <margin>John 1</margin> according to the testimony of St. John. Hence the Apostle says: *Christ fills <margin>Ephesians 4</margin> all things, and is all in all*; and <margin>Colossians 3</margin> in the beginning he made heaven and earth and all things; and those <margin>Hebrews 1</margin> heavens were strengthened by the Word of the Lord, and by the power <margin>Psalm 33</margin> of the spirit proceeding from both, all the virtues of the heavens and consequently of the whole world, and through their mediation the life, act, and preservation of the world arose. <margin>Acts 17</margin> Whence St. Paul concludes, that God, needing nothing, gives life, inspiration, and all things.

And anyone skilled in Philosophy will recognize that the soul is nothing other than that which animates or quickens both the body and the spirit. Why then should we be moved by further doubt, whether the Universal divine spirit, which fills all things and works all in all, be the fountain, origin, and head of life and of the worldly soul, by which it lives, moves, and exists? And consequently, it is the essential life and the central and mental form or **soul of the world** <note>Latin: *anima mundi*.</note>, whose vehicle or clothing is the most thin Universal spirit of the world, which it moves and excites just as the body is moved and driven by the soul itself, or as the spirit of life breathed by God into Adam is moved and driven by the mediation of the subtle airy organ in his body?

<margin>Wisdom 1</margin> What? Does there not exist an eternal and life-giving <margin>Wisdom 12</margin> spirit of wisdom, which is said to fill all things and to be everywhere, and to have in itself the nature of the Universal and first-created Angel? For (according to the Book of Wisdom) *Wisdom was created before all things.* Does it not exist, since it is the Universal soul of the world or the life of all, insofar as it is an emanation of the brightness of the Almighty and the splendor of eternal light, and a spotless mirror <margin>Wisdom 7</margin> of the Majesty of God and the image of his goodness? He who is unique, simple, subtle, remaining in himself and more penetrating and mobile than all things (all of which properties are assigned to the Angel by St. Dionysius and by the Fathers previously cited regarding the soul in its hidden state). Does it not exist, I say, in all things, and will it not fill the celestial spirit of both worlds—namely the greater and the lesser—and will it not produce in them the effects of its quickening and multiplying act? Shall it remain idle and vacant in the creature? Would he send his agile and vivacious spirit into the world only for it to rest and abstain from its active function?

# ON MOSAIC PHILOSOPHY

They hold this to be the Catholic <note>universal</note> intellectual agent, which is nothing other than the universal spirit of wisdom, which God sent forth from His Throne—or, as it is held elsewhere, from His mouth—as the greatest proof and gift of His love and kindness toward both worlds. Indeed, by its presence, the substance of the waters emerges from nothingness, and those waters are led back from deformity and non-existence into action and living beauty. Life and existence are explicitly attributed to those things which were previously implicitly enclosed in the dark shadow of death, as it were. I mean that from the deformed Chaos, or the Dark Abyss, they are brought forth into a pleasant form out of a lethal sleep and a dark rest into living action and motion, and from obscurity into light. And that benefactor to both worlds is deservedly called **Metatron** <note>original: "Mittatron"</note>, or the Catholic Gift of God, inasmuch as by his mediation the universal, deformed "nothing" is rendered into a universal, beautiful "something." But, so that I may better indicate to you the Angelic nature of that supreme intelligence called Metatron—and consequently the Soul of the World—by philosophical demonstration, I would first like you to understand the method by which the ancient philosophers, and especially the Platonists, demonstrate their harmony of the world and its spirit. The **Heptachord** <note>a seven-stringed scale</note> which **Plato** discovered and adapted to prove the Soul of the World consisted of seven strings or properties, partly even and partly odd: namely **1, 2, 3, 4, 8, 9, 27**. Although **Proclus** and **Porphyry** described these proportions in a single line, it nevertheless seems to me that **Adrastus** and **Chalcidius** adapted them more properly to the sides of a Pyramid or Triangle in this manner:

-> **I.** <-
-> **Material proportion in the Dark kingdom.** | **Formal proportion in the lucid kingdom.** <-
-> 1 <-
-> 2 | 3 <-
-> 4 | 9 <-
-> 8 | 27 <-
-> **In creation.** <-

<note>The diagram represents the "Lambda" of Plato's Timaeus, showing the generation of the soul through numerical ratios.</note>

In the cone or summit of this Pyramid, **1** is expressed. Since this unity, insofar as it participates on one side with material existence—namely with 2, 4, and 8—and on the other side has commerce with formal emanation, it is evident that this point or unity (1), from which both different lines proceed, is the source and origin of both matter and form. Whence it is the opinion of both **Synesius** and other Theosophers <note>divine philosophers</note>, departing not at all from the sense of the Scriptures, that God is all that is; for from Him, through Him, and in Him are all things. He is male and female, or (as **Hermes Trismegistus** has it) most fertile in both sexes; He is power and act; He is form and matter. Indeed, he says, there is nothing that He Himself does not exist as. But all of this (as we have said) agrees with the harmony of the Sacred Letters, which acknowledge that God is "all in all and above all," and that "in Him all things consist," and that "from Him, through Him, and in Him are all things." <margin>Romans 11</margin>

The six other corresponding figures look at each other from the material side to the formal side: namely, the even numbers in the material kingdom look upon the odd numbers of the formal kingdom that proportionally suit them. Specifically, **2** looks toward **3**, **4** gazes at **9**, and **8** at **27**. By these correspondences, the species of all creatures with their Harmonies are vividly expressed; and in the first series, it designates in a hieroglyphic-like manner that Harmonic grade of the Soul of the World which was in the beginning and still remains in the same state. For, first, according to the pattern of the Archetype, from the **One (1)** were allotted **Two (2)**, which number is frequently called the "confusion of unities" by the **Pythagoreans**. For this reason, it is the radical and beginning number of imperfection, which, in respect to its confusion and imperfection, stands in the same relation to the unity from which it takes its rise as the lucid eternal unity stands to the dark Abyss or the unformed **Chaos** (which is called by the Poet <note>Ovid</note> a "rough and unordered mass"). It is most rightly called an imperfect number because the efflux of the eternity of light, which is all perfection, had not yet made those potential waters perfect by its presence. And for that reason, the watery matter extracted from Chaos is confused and imperfect in itself, just as the number **two (2)** is judged imperfect in respect to the **three (3)** <note>the Ternary</note>, being nothing but a confusion of unities. This is because all perfection consists of three terms: namely, a beginning, a middle, and an end. Thus, if you choose one unity from the 2 for a beginning and another for a middle, nothing remains for the end, and consequently perfection is lacking. If you place one unity for the beginning and another for the end, then two extremes are present, but the unity for the middle is missing. If you assign one unity for the middle and another for the end, then the beginning will be missing. Therefore, it follows that this number is imperfect, and consequently the waters are imperfect in themselves, as in their constitution the nature of the Dark Abyss (or the mother and the moist nature) is present, but that formal unity is missing, which still contains itself in the cone of the Pyramid or **Isosceles Triangle**. Likewise, if the actual unity...

### SECOND SECTION, BOOK I.

If its own outflow <note>original: *effluxum*</note>, as a beautiful and splendid unity of life, had not been sent forth, the number 2—or the shapeless waters—would have remained in the womb of Chaos in its poured-out, confused, or imperfect state; that is, without the form of any perfect thing. It would be, namely, Nothing, or something existing only in potentiality. Thus the Catholic <note>meaning "universal" or "all-encompassing"</note> matter or water, before it was informed by the luminous unity (which constitutes the third unity), was entirely empty and void. It lacked the presence of the informing Unity, through which it casts off the indisposition of emptiness and vanity and puts on the beauty of fullness. Thus, its emptiness is changed into fullness, its potentiality into act, its darkness into light, and its deformity into a clear, beautiful, and life-giving loveliness; and finally, its imperfection is changed into perfection. And hence it is said that God saw that this creature was good; that is, it was filled with the life-giving essence of divinity, which is absolutely and solely good. By this reasoning, therefore—namely, by the addition of formal unity—the number of confusion and imperfection (which was in the material duality symbolizing Chaos, the mother of matter) is brought forth into the light of the world, and perfection, or the number Three <note>original: *Ternarius*</note>, is produced. For that formal unity, by animating and clothing the upper waters, creates the primary, perfect, and most worthy kind of mixture: by uniting the unity of mental light and the celestial spirit in the Angelic essence, which is then later handed down to animate and inform all worldly things. And this formal union is signified symbolically by 3, or the number Three, which for this reason is called the number of perfection, the number of the soul, or the radical number of form in the course of nature. Hence it is that the Platonists and Pythagoreans express matter, which is imperfect in itself, by even or imperfect numbers. Just as in the Archetypal world <note>the world of divine ideas</note> designated by 1, 2, and 3 in the form of the Holy Trinity, there appear only three Ideal dimensions in a single divine or eternal nature and essence. In the manner of their progression, these designate in the Algebraic art <note>original: *arte Cossica*, referring to early algebra</note> the root, the square, and the Cube, which signify the supreme soul, the spirit, and the body of the world as depicted ideally in the Archetype. And it is clear that these three seem to arise from a single 1 or unity: For by multiplying 1 by 1, 1 is produced, and itself, which are two, like a simple ideal square; and again by multiplying that square unity by itself, there arise 2 and one, which make 3, or the cube of simple unities, which proves the perfection of the Ideal world that is in God. So, if we take the radical and simple number of two unities for the root, we produce—according to the aforementioned Archetypal pattern—the created Typical world. That is, let us seek the three dimensions of matter—namely, Length, breadth, and depth—through the progression from the root to the square, and from the square to the Cube of matter. The root of matter, therefore, was 2: For although the supreme unity multiplies and expands itself into 2, thereby proving its first-born; nevertheless, because the Holy Spirit of illumination was not yet emanating, all things were dark as far as we are concerned. Therefore, we must imagine that the multiplication of matter in this world is nothing other than the multitude of formal light in the abyss of water; for the more matter exists, the closer it approaches its root 2, or dark Chaos. Conversely, as it is made thinner through the wealth and abundant presence of the luminous formal emanation, the closer it approaches the root of formal unity. This Mystery being rightly understood, I say, all science—even in the most abstruse Philosophy—can be most easily discerned. The root of matter, therefore, which is 2, signifies dark Chaos; but the root of form, which is 3, seems to prove that the root 2 (which designates the dark waters) is animated through the formal and splendid emanation or extension of unity or 1. And so the first (1) or the binary number was completed and the soul of the world was created or revealed—namely, through the Angelic emission or outflow. In this way, the *Metatron* <margin>Ecclesiasticus 1</margin> of the Cabalists, or the Gift of God, or the soul of the world, was first produced, which according to their traditions is called the first creature or the first of all things created. This indeed agrees perfectly with the Syriac: "Wisdom," it says, "was created before all things: God created her in the Holy Spirit." And in and through that Angelic creation, all other Angels were also made. Whence it is said: "Christ is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature, in whom all things were brought forth in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, <margin>Colossians 1</margin> whether they be Thrones, or Dominions, or Powers; all things are through him and in him, and he is before all things, and in him all things consist," etc. Behold, here you have described the true Catholic Spirit, which not only made all things but is all things, inasmuch as he gives them life, since all things are in him; but he also does the will of the Father in every creature he has formed. Hence he is called by the Rabbis *Metatron* or the Gift of God, <margin>Mag. I.</margin> and his name shall be called (says the Prophet) the Angel of Great Counsel. <margin>Mag. II.</margin> Therefore, by multiplying 3 in him, we shall have the created formal square, <margin>Mag. III.</margin> which signifies the 9 orders of Angels, who are said to be varied in property <margin>Mag. IIII.</margin> according to the disposition and property of that holy outflow, <margin>Mag. V.</margin> which is sent forth from the infinite source of light to operate in manifold ways in this world. <margin>Mag. You see now, how far and by what proportions, both spiritual and material, the Platonic **harmony of the world** extends itself; and also from these things you may observe, that where that Harmonic proportion is not present between matter and form, it is necessary that there be both a bodily and spiritual dissonance or discord, and consequently **Antipathy**.

We see, moreover, that the **root of life** is fixed in the Angelic composition or "alterity" <note>original: *alteritate*—the state of being 'other' or the first step away from divine unity</note>: namely, in the mixture of simple, eternal, and uncreated light and pure spiritual matter: so that **eternal wisdom** is the first act and essential soul of the Angels, and the eternal or Angelic Spirit is the act and essential life of the Starry celestial heavens and their influences, and the Stellar influence is the life and soul of the winds or Elements (for the force of life is rained down by the **Olympic Intelligences** into those elementary ones) or the presiding spirits of the winds; and the spiritual emanations or outflows from the four winds inform the **Universal Sublunary Element** or the lower waters in a fourfold way. And then afterwards the Element, according to the property which the predominant wind assigns, informs in many ways the **meteors** or Meteorological impressions, from which then afterwards the composed Elemental things are made. By this reasoning, they draw their whole essence and way of living in many forms from the divine source, and that by reason of the difference of the organs through which and in which He acts indifferently in this world.

From which it appears, that God in the beginning first animated the higher heaven or **Empyrean** and the intellectual spirit—which heaven is the seat of the Angels—which we compare to the **root**, where 2 is animated by 3 through the addition of 1 (or formal light) to matter 2. And the Empyrean heaven (I mean the Angelic Spirit) animates the stars and the ethereal region, pouring its influences into the Olympic intelligences, which we refer to as the **square**: and the starry heaven is as it were the male and multiplier in the Elemental heaven and its creatures, which we compare to the **Cube**.

Truly, not only the abstruse **Cabalists**, but also the deepest of the Philosophers have left an everlasting memory of that most perfect and most formed root, or the **ternary number** <note>The number three</note> with its three dimensions; not that of the merchant or the one commonly known in Arithmetic, but that of a purely spiritual and essential Character in formal numeration, which proceeds from a certain circular revolution and square and cubic multiplication. And for this cause, those most skilled in the secrets of nature have founded their formal and **Mystic Arithmetic** and Geometry upon that subject, which are not occupied with common or vulgar subjects, but totally in the deep meditations of true **Cabala**, **natural Magic**, and **essential Alchemy**. These sciences—which the ignorant common people rashly and without legitimate cause condemn under those titles—are called by the more secret craftsmen **Elemental, Celestial, and Super-mundane science**: both because they treat of the natures of "separated" (as they say) intelligences and substances, and because they are the most worthy of all, insofar as they are occupied with the knowledge of the Creator.

For the greatest perfection, in which a man can most glory, is that he attains to a certain knowledge of God: Whence the Prophets say: *Let not the wise man glory in <margin>in Jeremiah ch. 9 <note>The text says p. 23, likely a volume reference, but the quote is Jeremiah 9:23-24</note></margin> his Wisdom, and let not the strong man glory in his strength, nor let the rich man glory in his riches; but let him who glories glory in this, that he understands and knows God.* And certainly these are those three mystic sciences, which are appropriated to the knowledge of the **three worlds** (I mean the Intellectual, Celestial, and Elemental): which worlds, according to the sayings of the Cabalists, are represented by these three letters of the name **אדם Adam**. They also relate to the three parts of man or the **Microcosm**, namely the intellect, the soul, and the body, which is subject to alteration and corruption.

**Rabbi Zour** <note>Likely a reference to the Zohar</note>, founded upon these bases, says that there are three things which correspond to each other in that ternary dimension, which are formed after the example of the **Archetype** or radical Idea: namely, the **Tabernacle of God** which Moses erected, the **Temple of Solomon**, and the **human body**: and that according to the type of those numbers which are applied to them, namely the **vocal** or operative, which is the extract of the measure for the formal Elemental world; the **formal**, which is the extract from the vocal for the celestial; and the **rational** or divine, which is the extract from the formal for the intellectual: all of which is made apparent through the description of the Tabernacle. exposed to meteorological disturbances, and was subject to almost perpetual alterations of the air. And to this part of the Tabernacle, the common race of men and even beasts frequented in a constant vicissitude of life and death, by reason of the continuous sacrifices and burnt offerings <note>original: *holocaustorum*</note> which were offered in that place. And therefore, that region, signifying the material cube, most rightly refers to the **Elemental world**, which is composed of matter or thicker water, like a fluid and inconstant substance: and for this reason, it is properly called the world of darkness. Hence, therefore, Apollos calls the Devil the Prince of Darkness, and elsewhere calls him the prince of this world. This region also refers to the human body.

The second portion of the Tabernacle, which was gilded on all sides and adorned and illuminated by the candelabra of seven lights, is the **Symbol of the starry heaven** with those seven distinguished lights themselves, namely the planets. And this heaven, as it is between two extremes—namely the Empyrean <note>The highest, fiery heaven</note> and the Elemental middle—so indeed it participates in both extremes, namely in water and in fire: and hence it is that the heaven is called by the Hebrews **שמים** *Schamaym* <note>Heaven</note>, as if from **אש** *Esch*, fire, and **מים** *Maym*, Water; and by the Greeks *Ether*, as if fiery air. But the existence of its water is therefore incorruptible: because its appetite is so intoxicated by the formal nectar sent down from above, that it is forgetful of all alteration: moreover, it receives its motion or activity from that same eternal efflux, which according to the saying of Solomon is more mobile than any moving thing. 

<margin>Wisdom of Solomon 7.</margin> 

And in truth, it is the first Universal <note>original: *Catholicus*</note> mover, who is said to preside over the *primum mobile* <note>the "first moved" sphere in Ptolemaic astronomy</note>, by whose act all the inferior Intelligences are moved, and they carry their glowing fires with them in a circuit: not otherwise than we see that all outer wheels, being as it were dead by themselves, are observed to be moved by the motion of one central wheel, inasmuch as that wheel is their life. From these things, therefore, we can gather why that region of the world is called Heaven, and the Sphere of Equality, namely by reason of its mixture from an equal portion of form and matter: Also, why it is called the **Sphere of the Soul**, namely, because it is composed of the pure and incorruptible spirit of the waters, which is feminine and passive, and of the bright fire or eternal act. For the Divine Mind acts by means of such a moist nature, which is its Vehicle or organ, and expresses and exercises its vivifying property in this world. Hence, therefore, even the Heathens recognize that all life consists of innate heat and radical moisture, of which the former is active and from God; the latter is passive and from the prior spirit of the waters, which some call the *quintessence*. This region, therefore, refers to human life or the soul, and has a close relation to the square, both formal and material, which is something intermediate between the root and the cube.

The third portion of the Tabernacle is the *Holy of Holies* <note>original: *Sanctum Sanctorum*</note> or signifies the super-celestial or intellectual or Empyrean spirit, which is almost nothing else than pure and sincere fire, and is handed down by the Fathers of Theology to be the seat of the Angels and of souls, who are the immediate ministers of their great Lord and Prince of Light. And this is witnessed by the presence of the two Cherubim, who cover the mercy seat with their wings. This heaven refers to the human intellect, which is called by the Hebrews *Neshamah*, by the Greeks *Nous*, and by the Latins *Mens* <note>Mind</note>, which has dominion over the human soul. Thus, as it may be seen, that in the Great World <note>the Macrocosm</note> the Angelic Heaven, which is most formal, fiery, and full of divine light, is like the soul of the ethereal heaven. For through it and from it that region receives its life, motion, and existence, and by a similar proportion the ethereal or celestial heaven is the life or soul and agent in the Elements of the heaven itself. For by the mediation of the Sun, Moon, and other Stars, which rain down their influences and roots upon the earth, the earth and water and all creatures in them act, live, generate, and multiply: so that the heaven is estimated by all Philosophers to be the male, and the sublunary Element the female, whose matrix is the earth and water. For the earth and water receive influences like the seeds of the male, and thus all generations in the earth and water are made. For the earthly body cannot work without the aerial impression or contact: indeed, man himself requires (as the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle</note> maintain) celestial assistance for his generation: Whence Aristotle says: *The Sun and man generate man.* Furthermore, all Philosophers also seem to agree in this, namely, that the higher things act upon the lower like a male upon a female. And it is common among the more skilled Cabalists through the Axiom 

<margin>Reuchlin, book on the Art of the Cabala.</margin> 

of the representation of higher things. And certainly a very learned man, well-versed in such abstruse science, affirms that the age-enduring or Angelic heaven was created according to the pattern of that eternal or Ideal one: and the images of it have their Ideal likenesses in and from the brighter celestial heaven: and the images and actions of the Stellar world were first depicted or outlined in the intellectual and Angelic heaven: and the icons of its rainbow obtained their origin from the radical exemplar, or principle existing in the Archetype. I conclude, therefore, that both Theologians and mystic Philosophers agree in this, namely...

<header>ON MOSAIC PHILOSOPHY. Fol. 78.</header>

# ON MOSAIC PHILOSOPHY.

It is evident that God delights in the number three <note>original: "numero ternario"</note>, which is the first odd number in arithmetic progression. For we Christians worship a Trinity of persons in unity. And Aristotle says that by a certain natural instinct, we are instructed to revere God himself according to the number three. Nor is this said without consideration, since in the Ideal world there were three properties extracted from unity (as we proved above), according to whose exemplar the real world was afterwards fabricated, so that the Trinity in the Divinity was the root of the entire formal position of the world. For by the root 3, the intellectual and Angelic world was designated; by the square 9, the celestial world; and by the Cube 27, the Elementary world, just as we can elicit from the aforementioned doctrine of Plato. 

But as far as the opinions of the Rabbis and Cabalists <note>Practitioners of Jewish mysticism (Kabbalah)</note> are concerned, they considered the quantitative proportions of that same triad differently. For the Cube of the root 3 consists of three 9s, or nine-fold numbers: indeed, they take those three 9s and join them in arithmetic order thus: 9. 9. 9. which constitute (999) nine hundred ninety-nine; so that, according to the arithmetic rule, the first nine toward the right is a simple digit or digital number, which by reason of its simplicity, formality, and essentiality, is attributed to the nine orders of Angels. The nine (9) standing in the middle seems on one side to participate more in form or simplicity, and on the other in matter; and for that reason, they attribute it to the nine orbits or spheres of the starry heaven. The third (9) nine-fold number, which is placed in the hundreds position, signifies a deeper and more material composition, which belongs to the Elementary world: all of which numbers and even the regions of the world finally terminate in man, who is like a passage <note>original: "meatus"</note> according to the image of unity from the elementary things themselves to celestial things, and from those to intellectual things. 

Finally, if unity—in which the philosopher Leucippus placed the highest good—be added to the aforementioned three nines, it constitutes the complete number of a thousand, which is the cube of 10, and the end of all numbers according to the calculation of the Hebrews. Also Aleph, which is 1, produces the denary number <note>the number ten</note>, beyond which (as Aristotle says) no one has ever found a number. Therefore, according to the pattern of the aforementioned type, the ancient or Mosaic light made a partition of fruits and goods arising from the earth to be divided into three parts: of which it assigned the hundredth part as material and coarse power to the Laity and the profane; the tenths to the Church and the Priests; and finally unity, or the tenth part <note>The "tithe of the tithe"</note>, for God, who as he is all things, so indeed he is nothing but one. 

But to the purpose: the Cabalists have adopted the name of their Angel (whom they, along with the Platonists, refer to the soul of the world) to this triple triad or formal proportion; namely 999. From this they argue for the radical, square, and cubic extension, or the emanation of the divine form into the depth of matter: and consequently, it is demonstrated that he is the Alpha and Omega, the life-giver of all, who is present to all and penetrates through all. For the letters or elements of the word *Mitattron Sarphanim* <note>Metatron Sar ha-Panim, the "Prince of the Countenance" in Jewish mysticism</note>, which signifies the prince of faces (who is taken for the soul of the world), according to the calculation of the Hebrews, ascend to 999. And therefore this name with its letters imports this number, but nevertheless with this consideration: that the etymology of the word through interpretation signifies **THE GIFT OF GOD**. For what [greater gift] could God give to his potential creatures and generally to the entire world, than the eternal spirit of his wisdom, or his first-born? So that by means of his essential presence, something might be made as if out of nothing; and that by putting away the deformity and emptiness of the waters and reducing their potential into act, and dividing them into heaven and existence, they might be preserved by essence and vital faculty. 

This was therefore the true and Universal <note>original: "Catholicum"</note> Gift of God, whose incorruptible nature is in every thing, to preserve it; <margin>Wisdom 12:1</margin> and it fills all things, so that it is never lacking to creatures: <margin>Wisdom 1:7</margin> and, just as this spirit is more mobile than any thing, <margin>Wisdom 7:24</margin> so it works all things in all, according to the will of that unity which sent it forth. For this reason, and in respect of his office and insofar as he was a sent spirit, not undeservedly and not without good consideration was this name of the Universal Angel imposed upon him, as Scripture witnesses. We can also demonstrate in another way that the world itself and its soul were created according to the image of the Archetype in this manner:

->God.......1 Light.<-
->Heaven.......3 Sphere of equality.<-
->Earth.......2 Darkness.<-

In which demonstration one may contemplate how from 1, which was light, in which there are no shadows, there would arise 2, which existed before the appearance of light, as far as we are concerned...
<column-break/>
...darkness.

## OF THE SECOND SECTION, BOOK I.

Between these two extremes is placed a third <note>The number 3 is used here to denote the Trinity or the third mediating principle</note>, like a peaceful and charity-filled unity, which is the lovely medium for joining the two extremes—namely light and darkness—into a perpetual friendship. This is the divine spirit of love and concord which, residing in the middle between those two principles (both in position and in condition), unites and joins the divine formal fire with the moist material nature or spirit of darkness. Thus, those two natures, once opposed, remain in one sympathetic accordance; and for this reason, that formal trinity <note>original: "ternarius"</note> is called the bond of the Elements, connecting strife and friendship with the chains of concord.

This excellent harmony of the world-soul <note>original: "anima mundana"</note> has been explained by me elsewhere most aptly by means of two Pyramidal figures, one of which is formal and the other material. The base of the formal Pyramid is contiguous with the fountain of divine light, and that Pyramid denotes the lucid emanation of the spirit that informs and enlivens all things, from the lucid source into the existence or unformed matter of the world; so that its cone penetrates even to the center of the dark earth or abyss. From the region of the base of the material Pyramid (or in the place of the water) is the diameter of the earth, which passes from east to west through the center of the earth as if in a place most opposite and remote from the formal base: its cone, however, ascends even to the center of the base of the formal Pyramid, as you have it depicted here.

Now indeed, where the intersection is made in the middle between both Pyramids, I have drawn the arc of a circle: since the portions of both the formal and material Pyramids are equal at the point of intersection. I therefore, according to the opinion of the Platonists, call the Sphere or orb passing through that intersection the **Sphere of Equality**, and in another respect the **Sphere of the Soul**, which has its position directly in the middle of the stellar heaven. For this reason, it is called the ether or fiery air <note>original: "æther seu igneus aër"</note>; as if one were to say, an equal portion of the spirit of the waters and the formal fire descending from God the Father of Light, as was said. And therefore, as I placed it in the preceding demonstration (3), in the center or middle of the line—namely between the unity of divine light (1) and the dark Chaos or the unformed and confused duality (2)—so in the world was placed the spiritual body of the visible Sun of this typical world. In this Sun, the invisible and uncreated Sun of the Archetypal world placed His Tabernacle, and for that reason, it is rightly called the **Sphere of the Soul** by the Platonists. And certainly, it gives forth powerfully by effect from the Solar influence. Furthermore, in respect to its eminent beauty, it is clearly established that it abounds with the blessed sparks of divine light. Again, daily experience teaches even the rustic and the farmer that it is a most bright organ, through which and from which He who enlivens all things pours out and distills the effects of His kindness, or the divine nectar of life, into the lower regions daily. 

Now truly, that most perfect and excellent concordance of life remains and has its seat in the middle of the line, like a string <note>original: "Chorda"</note> extended from the unity (the center of the formal base) to the duality (the center of the material base): as if it were the string of the **Symphonic World-Monochord** <term>Monochord: a single-stringed instrument used by ancient theorists to demonstrate the mathematical ratios of musical intervals</term>. I prove and demonstrate this through musical consonances in this way: The most perfect consonance in Music is the **Octave** <note>original: "Diapason"</note>, since it approaches more closely than all others to the nature of sacred unity. For it is the half-part of the unison, and consequently is most aptly compared to the emanation of the most holy life which arises from unity. Therefore, it is not wrongly called the Idea or image of unity; and as unity, though it be but a single essence in the divinity, comprises three persons representing the three consonances of Archetypal Harmony, so also the Octave comprises under itself (or in its dimension) two other musical concordances, namely the **Fifth** <note>original: "diapente"</note> and the **Fourth** <note>original: "diatessaron"</note>. Now, that this most perfect consonance consists and is placed in the middle of the unison, and produces its two concordances in the unison by its central position, we prove in this manner. Let a **Lute** <note>original: "Barbiton," a stringed instrument similar to a lyre or lute</note> or some other musical instrument consisting of strings be taken, and let a string be struck...

...any string of it openly and will give the voice of a Catholic or universal unison. For, as the string is one, so the sound will be absolutely unique in itself and will behave as the Father of harmonies, of which the firstborn and most orderly will be the Octave <note>original: "Diapason"</note>, which is procreated from the belly or center of the Unison in this way: Press the string constituting the Unison exactly in the middle, and then both half-portions of the string will relate to each other in a double proportion, namely as 2 to 1. And thus the Octave, being the most perfect harmony, serves to demonstrate that the perfection of the Octave resides in the Solar seat; and consequently, that the formal and living concord of the whole world—as if of a monochord <note>a single-stringed instrument used to demonstrate mathematical proportions of sound</note> (whose spirit I relate to the string of the monochord) extended from the seat of God even unto the earth—exists in that middle and central place no differently than the heart, which is the seat of human life. And yet, through the rays of the Sun, this life or soul of the world is made Catholic <note>meaning "universal" in the Greek sense</note> and fills all things: not otherwise than the vital blood expands universally through the fabric of the microcosm <note>the human body as a reflection of the universe</note> by means of the veins and arteries. But now, I fear lest I have pursued this point—namely, proving the soul of the world—too far; therefore I leave it, so that I may approach more closely to the subject at hand, and all the more because in the fourth book of the first section, where I maintained that translation of St. Jerome to be true, namely: GOD PLACED HIS TABERNACLE IN THE SUN, I treated the Solar mystery more fully; now indeed I shall proceed to the second opinion of the Philosophers.

The ancient Philosophers, Democritus, Orpheus, along with the Pythagoreans, asserted that all things are full of Gods: yet they refer all these Gods to a single supreme Jove <note>Jupiter/God</note>: where by "Gods," they intend the divine virtues infused into all things, which Zoroaster called divine Allurements <note>original: "Illices"</note>, and Bishop Synesius called symbolic attractions; others call them souls, others "powers" <note>original: "fortes"</note>, upon which the virtues of things depend. In this they seem not to err much, except that they distinguish the divine essence into the divinities of Gods: yet they appear to excuse themselves and purge themselves of this error in that they refer all those Gods to the one Jove: by which relation they seem to acknowledge the continuity and indivisibility of the soul with the divinity. Therefore the Platonists and all those Philosophers who share their opinion agree with the scriptures in that they confess the divine essence to be in every thing; they agree with Orpheus and Democritus in every thing, except in this: that the former said the spirit was Jove, and that these latter repeatedly call the virtues possessing the creatures "Gods"; the former name them "particular souls," which by relation have a continuity with the soul of the world: Not otherwise and in the same sense the scriptures say, that the incorruptible Spirit of God is in every thing. <margin>Wisdom 12:1</margin>

I conclude therefore, that since the soul of the world has for its internal part a splendid emanation of eternal unity, and for its external part a subtle Catholic spirit of the waters or a moist nature—which serves it in place of a moist vehicle or material organ, in which and through which it operates spiritually everywhere and in every thing—we ought to recognize that there is a certain species of contrariety even in the Catholic soul of the world itself, without which there would be no action or passion in the created soul. But insofar as it is created from the luminous soul or uncreated active nature, it tends toward the Deification and exaltation of the created Spirit, if it adheres to it: and from the created passive spirit, which is the offspring of the obscure and dark abyss or Chaos, and therefore is easily inclined toward moving the nature of darkness. It is no wonder if, by reason of the various conditions of that spirit, there are present to it sometimes good passions and sometimes evil passions, which operate in an opposite or contrary manner not only in the heavens and the earth of the macrocosm <note>the great world/universe</note> and its creatures (whether celestial or Elemental, whether animals, vegetables, or minerals), but also in the lesser world, which is man: As will be declared in the first chapter of the following section of this book. But first I deem it worth the effort to untie and shell out <note>to explain clearly</note> the true mystery of the particular soul of the microcosm: and then afterwards to show how all other souls of creatures—animal, vegetable, and mineral—proceed and are derived from that Catholic soul of the greater world, and are preserved and multiplied in their state of life by it. Since this doubt has not yet been fully and clearly discussed by the more excellent Philosophers until this day: and consequently this discourse of mine ought not to be belittled even by the most learned of this age, or inspected lightly and negligently.

Nor was it sufficient that Adam should put on a microcosmic body, namely a mass of clay or earth for his material or elemental portion, unless that divine Spirit sent from God into the world had breathed a portion of its divinity—namely, the breath of life—into it, by which mediation he moved, lived, and existed in the human state.
